name: Dani Ortega
bio: Dani Ortega has been banned from Starlight Mall four times and has come back five. She skates the drained fountain in the dead wing, knows every service corridor and loose ceiling tile, and can rebuild a cracked deck with nothing but duct tape and spite. She is loud, fearless and very funny, especially when she is scared, which she will never admit. She has a hopeless crush on the girl who works the Corn Dog Castle counter and has been 'about to talk to her' since August. Her flaw is that she would rather eat concrete than ask for help, and she picks fights with things twice her size because somebody has to.

perk.name: Fountain Diver
perk.text: Dani skates the dead wing's dry fountain every morning and pockets whatever the mall rats dropped: +1 quarter each dawn.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 16-year-old Chicana girl with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver hoop through one eyebrow, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee, cuffed black jeans, checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, a battered skateboard with hot pink griptape, caught mid-ollie over the railing of a drained mall fountain at night, flannel flying, a roll of silver duct tape raised in one fist like a weapon, dead neon store signs glowing behind her

neutral.line: Mall cop's on break in six minutes. That's our window.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Chicana girl with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver hoop through one eyebrow, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee, cuffed black jeans, checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, a battered skateboard with hot pink griptape, board tucked under one arm, chewing gum, one eyebrow cocked, an empty mall corridor behind her

happy.line: Did you SEE that? Tell me you saw that. Nobody ever sees that.
happy.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Chicana girl with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver hoop through one eyebrow, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee, cuffed black jeans, checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, a battered skateboard with hot pink griptape, laughing with her head thrown back and both fists up, pink tips of her hair flying

scared.line: Okay. Not scared. Just skating backwards really, really fast.
scared.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Chicana girl with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver hoop through one eyebrow, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee, cuffed black jeans, checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, a battered skateboard with hot pink griptape, eyes wide, gripping her skateboard in front of her like a shield, lit by a flickering fluorescent tube

angry.line: You touch my friends again and I'm taping you to the ceiling.
angry.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Chicana girl with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver hoop through one eyebrow, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee, cuffed black jeans, checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, a battered skateboard with hot pink griptape, teeth bared, ripping a strip of duct tape off the roll with a snap, jaw set

sad.line: Everybody says I'm too much. Then they bail. Whatever. It's fine.
sad.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Chicana girl with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver hoop through one eyebrow, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee, cuffed black jeans, checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, a battered skateboard with hot pink griptape, sitting on the rim of the dry fountain, board across her knees, staring at the scuffed tape on her shoes

determined.line: Board's taped, laces are tight. Let's go break something that deserves it.
determined.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Chicana girl with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver hoop through one eyebrow, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee, cuffed black jeans, checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, a battered skateboard with hot pink griptape, one foot on her skateboard, pulling a pink bandana up over her nose, eyes narrowed

meet.title: The Dead Wing Ramp
meet.place: The dead wing, Starlight Mall
meet.text: Behind the arcade, past a sawhorse that says CLOSED FOR RENOVATION since 1984, a girl with a hot-pink undercut is carving the drained fountain while a security guard named Gus wheezes after her. She shoots past you, flips you a roll of duct tape and hisses, "Hold this. You never saw me." Then she vanishes up a pillar. Gus is coming around the corner, and her board is still spinning in the fountain.
meet.art: A 16-year-old Chicana skater with warm brown skin and a crooked grin, a shaved undercut with a long black flop of hair dyed hot pink at the tips, a silver eyebrow hoop, an oversized black-and-pink flannel over a ripped black tee and checkerboard skate shoes wrapped in silver duct tape, clinging to a pillar above a drained mall fountain in a dusty half-lit dead wing, tossing a roll of duct tape down to a teenager, her skateboard spinning upside down in the empty basin, a heavyset security guard rounding the corner, dusty skylight beams, medium wide shot

choices.label: Send Gus running with a fake lost-kid emergency

success.text: "My little brother's in the food court and he's eating a whole Orange Swirl cup with a FORK!" Gus lumbers off at full speed. Dani drops from the pillar and stares at you. "You lie like a professional. Okay. You're in."
success.art: A pink-haired skater dropping down from a mall pillar, laughing and pointing at a teenager, a security guard running away in the distance

failure.text: Gus squints at you, then at the spinning skateboard, then at the duct tape in your hand. You're both marched out the side door. In the parking lot Dani is cackling. "Loading dock's unlocked tomorrow. Same time."
failure.art: Two teenagers sitting on a curb in an empty mall parking lot, one holding a skateboard and laughing, a mall security door slammed behind them

choices.label: Grab her board and drop into the fountain

success.text: You drop in, wobble, nearly die, and somehow carve all the way around the fountain and out the other side. Dani whoops so loud a pigeon falls off a light fixture. "That was the ugliest thing I've ever seen. Do it again. You're with me now."
success.art: A teenager wobbling through a drained mall fountain on a pink skateboard, a pink-haired skater whooping on the rim, a startled pigeon mid-flight

failure.text: You eat it hard. Dani slides down, peels a strip of duct tape and slaps it over the rip in your sleeve like a field medic. "Rule one, learn to fall. Come back tomorrow, I'll teach you." Gus's flashlight finds you both.
failure.art: A pink-haired skater kneeling to duct-tape a fallen teenager's torn sleeve inside a dry fountain, a security flashlight beam sweeping toward them

choices.label: Help her fix the cracked deck before Gus finds it

success.text: You show her how to lay the tape crosswise so the crack can't spread. She tests it with one stomp and grins. "Okay, genius. Anybody who can fix a board can come with me." She splits the change she found in the fountain with you.
success.art: Two teenagers crouched behind a planter, crisscrossing silver duct tape over a cracked skateboard, coins scattered on the tile

failure.text: The tape sticks to everything: the board, your hair, Dani's flannel, a passing pigeon. Gus finds you both in one glittering silver knot. Dani is laughing too hard to run. "Tomorrow," she wheezes. "Bring scissors."
failure.art: Two teenagers hopelessly tangled together in silver duct tape beside a cracked skateboard, a security guard standing over them with his hands on his hips

arc.title: Rehearsal
arc.place: The dry fountain in the dead wing, Starlight Mall, noon
arc.text: Dani is skating slow circles in the drained fountain, talking to a cardboard corn-dog mascot she rescued from a dumpster. "Hi. Hey. Hi. I'm Dani, I skate, you fry things, we should..." She sees you and nearly eats concrete. "You heard none of that." The food-court costume contest is Friday, and she has been about to ask Marisol from the Corn Dog Castle to go with her since August.
arc.art: A teenage skate punk girl with a hot-pink undercut and a duct-taped board, skating circles in a dry mall fountain while rehearsing a speech to a battered cardboard corn-dog mascot propped on the fountain lip

choices.label: Put on a paper hat and play Marisol so she can practice

success.text: "Welcome to Corn Dog Castle, can I take your order?" Dani gets through the whole invitation without falling off the fountain once. She punches the air. "I can talk to a corn dog. That's PROGRESS."
success.art: A teenager in a folded paper food-counter hat playing the cashier while a skate punk girl delivers a nervous speech, both standing in a dry mall fountain, the girl punching the air

failure.text: You play Marisol a little too well. You hand Dani an imaginary corn dog with such sincerity that she panics and orders forty of them. She lies flat on her back in the fountain. "I'm gonna be single forever. Tomorrow we go again."
failure.art: A skate punk girl lying flat on her back in a dry mall fountain with her arms flung out in despair, a teenager in a paper hat holding out an imaginary snack

choices.label: Buy a lemonade and scout what Marisol is into

success.text: Tucked behind Marisol's name tag is a stub from the Glitter Box midnight movie, and she is doodling a skateboard on the order pad between customers. Dani grabs your arm hard enough to bruise. "She draws BOARDS?"
success.art: A teenager at a neon corn-dog stand counter sipping lemonade, glancing at a smiling teen cashier doodling a skateboard on an order pad, a movie ticket stub tucked behind her name tag

failure.text: Marisol catches you staring. "Are you Dani's friend? The one who keeps walking past forty times a day?" You flee with your lemonade, mortified. Then it hits you: Marisol has been counting.
failure.art: A teenager hurrying away from a neon corn-dog stand clutching a lemonade cup, face red, while a teen cashier in a paper hat watches them go with a curious little smile

choices.label: Tell her to skip the practice and walk over right now

success.text: Dani gets as far as the napkin dispenser, says "Cool hat," and skates away at top speed. But Marisol calls "Thanks!" after her, and Dani glows like a jukebox for the rest of the afternoon.
success.art: A skate punk girl rocketing away from a food-court counter on her board with a huge stunned grin, a teen cashier in a paper hat waving after her

failure.text: Dani marches straight over, and Gus the security guard spots her halfway there. You both bolt through a service door. In the cinderblock corridor she laughs it off a little too hard. "See? Too much. This is why."
failure.art: A skate punk girl and a teenager catching their breath in a gray cinderblock mall service corridor, a security guard's flashlight beam sweeping past the door window

arc.title: Snapped
arc.place: The loading dock behind Starlight Mall, 5 p.m.
arc.text: Dani's board lies on the loading dock in two clean halves. She tried the twelve-stair set nobody has ever landed, so she would have something to show Marisol on Friday. Her elbow is scraped raw and her eyes are red, and she says she is fine three times before you even ask. "Forget Friday. Everybody says I'm too much, then they bail. Why would she be any different?" She would rather eat the asphalt than ask anybody for help, and you can see it costing her.
arc.art: A skate punk girl sitting on the edge of a concrete loading dock at sunset with a scraped elbow, a snapped skateboard in two halves beside her, a teenager sitting down next to her

choices.label: Splint the broken deck together with glue, a shelf board and her tape

success.text: Wood glue, a splint cut from a busted display shelf, and about a mile of duct tape. The board is hideous and it rides. Dani does one long carve across the lot and comes back quiet. "You didn't ask if I was okay. You just stayed. Thanks."
success.art: A skate punk girl carving across an empty mall parking lot at sunset on a hideous patched skateboard splinted with wood and silver tape, a teenager cheering from the loading dock

failure.text: The patch holds for exactly one push before the board folds like a lawn chair. Dani laughs for the first time all day. "It's so ugly. It's perfect. It's dead." Then, quietly, she admits she was scared of Friday before she ever hit the stairs.
failure.art: A patched skateboard folding in half under a skate punk girl's sneaker in a parking lot, the girl laughing with her hands over her face, a teenager laughing beside her

choices.label: Offer to chip in for a new deck as a loan

success.text: She refuses three times. You offer it as a loan, interest payable in one skating lesson. Dani glares at the sky, then sticks out her hand. "Asking for help is the worst feeling in the world. Fine. Once."
success.art: A skate punk girl and a teenager shaking hands on a concrete loading dock at sunset, the girl scowling at the sky with a smile tugging at her mouth, coins and a crumpled bill between them

failure.text: "I don't need charity," she snaps, and pushes off on half a board. Ten minutes later she rolls back, sits down beside you without a word, and stays until the parking-lot lights buzz on.
failure.art: A skate punk girl and a teenager sitting side by side in silence on a loading dock as parking-lot lights flicker on at dusk, half a skateboard resting across her knees

choices.label: Tell her what you see: she isn't too much, she's exactly enough

success.text: Dani stares hard at the asphalt. "Say that again, but slower." You do. She laughs, wet and loud, wipes her face on her flannel and asks if you will come Friday as backup. "Not to talk. Just to stand there."
success.art: A skate punk girl wiping her eyes on her flannel sleeve and laughing on a sunset loading dock, a teenager beside her with a steady hand on her shoulder

failure.text: It comes out as "You're a LOT, but in a good way." Dani snorts. "Wow. Put that on a greeting card." But on her way out she picks up both broken halves of the board and carries them home instead of throwing them away.
failure.art: A skate punk girl walking away across a dusky mall parking lot carrying the two halves of a snapped skateboard under her arm, glancing back with a reluctant grin

arc.title: The Ask
arc.place: The Corn Dog Castle, Starlight Mall food court, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Dani is in her best flannel, her undercut freshly buzzed, the patched board under her arm. Marisol is wiping down the counter beneath a giant fiberglass corn dog in a cowboy hat. Dani looks at you, deadly serious. "If I bail, you push me. If I eat it, you tape me back together. Deal?" Then she takes a breath and rolls forward.
arc.art: A skate punk girl in her best flannel holding a patched skateboard at the edge of a neon mall food court, a fiberglass corn dog in a cowboy hat above a counter where a teen cashier is wiping up

choices.label: Skate the food-court slalom beside her for courage

success.text: You carve through the tables side by side, and Dani kicks her board up into her hand right at the counter. Marisol applauds with a mustard bottle. Dani asks. Marisol says yes, and adds, "I've been waiting since August. I thought you hated corn dogs." On the way out, Dani shows you how to fall without getting hurt, and you finally get it.
success.art: Two teens skating a slalom between food-court tables, a skate punk girl kicking her board up into her hand at a neon counter where a delighted cashier claps with a mustard bottle

failure.text: You wipe out into a tray of nachos. Dani wheels back to help you, and Marisol vaults the counter with a fistful of napkins. Kneeling in the cheese, Dani asks. Marisol is working Friday night, but she grins. "Saturday, though? The rink?" It isn't the plan. It's better.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled in spilled nachos on a food-court floor, a skate punk girl and a cashier in a paper hat kneeling on either side with napkins, the two girls grinning at each other

choices.label: Hang back by the arcade and let her do it alone

success.text: She walks over. Not skates: walks. She talks, Marisol laughs, and then Marisol writes her phone number on a paper corn-dog boat. Dani crosses the food court back to you in what feels like slow motion, then screams directly into your shoulder.
success.art: A skate punk girl screaming happily into a teenager's shoulder by a glowing arcade entrance, clutching a paper food boat with a phone number on it

failure.text: Dani freezes halfway and comes back. "I can't." You remind her who she is, and she goes again, and gets out one "Hi" before Marisol's manager calls her into the back. But Marisol slips her a napkin on the way: TOMORROW? RINK, 7. Dani holds it like a holy relic.
failure.art: A skate punk girl holding up a napkin with both hands like a treasure at a food-court counter while a teen cashier is waved into the kitchen by a manager, glancing back over her shoulder

choices.label: Help her unfurl a giant duct-tape heart from the balcony

success.text: A six-foot silver duct-tape heart unrolls from the second-floor railing. The whole food court whoops. Marisol covers her face, laughing, and nods yes before Dani even gets the words out. Gus the guard decides he needs to check something very far away.
success.art: A huge silver duct-tape heart unrolling from a mall's second-floor balcony railing over a neon food court, a skate punk girl and a teenager leaning over the rail, a cashier below covering her laughing face

failure.text: The heart peels loose and flutters down directly onto Gus. You are both escorted out: Dani's fifth ban. But in the parking lot, Marisol comes running after you in her paper hat. "Was that for ME? Yes. Obviously yes."
failure.art: A teen cashier in a paper hat running across a mall parking lot toward a skate punk girl and a teenager, a crumpled silver tape heart draped over a grumbling security guard by the doors

reactions.slasher: Big guy with a knife? Cool. I've got a skateboard and zero sense of self-preservation.
reactions.paranormal: Ghosts can't catch me. They float. I roll.
reactions.creature: Everything's got a soft spot. Even that. Probably. Somebody find it before I do.
reactions.tech: Can I hit it with my board? No? Then what good is it?

name: Marcus "Mix" Bell
bio: Marcus Bell got the midnight-to-six shift at KGLM because the last overnight DJ quit after something breathed on the call-in line, and Mix has never been happier. He runs the board, does his calculus between songs, and talks to the whole sleeping valley in a voice like warm velvet. He can name the label, year and B-side of almost any record ever pressed, and he notices instantly when a song plays wrong. On air he is smooth and fearless; in person he is shyer than he lets on, a little vain about his record collection, and secretly afraid nobody is really listening. He wants to program a station in Oakland someday and play everything.

perk.name: Dawn Dedication
perk.text: Every sunrise, Mix plays a song for you on the air, by name, no matter what happened in the night: +1 nerve each dawn.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 17-year-old Black young man with deep brown skin and an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck, a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, pleated black slacks, polished loafers, a stack of vinyl records under one arm, leaning into a hanging studio microphone with one hand on the headphones, records fanned out behind him like a purple and gold halo, a radio tower blinking red against a midnight sky

neutral.line: You're listening to KGLM 103.3, and I'm listening right back.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old Black young man with deep brown skin and an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck, a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, pleated black slacks, polished loafers, a stack of vinyl records under one arm, relaxed in a radio booth, one hand resting on a mixing board, red ON AIR light glowing behind him

happy.line: Oh, that's the good stuff. That's a B-side, baby.
happy.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old Black young man with deep brown skin and an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck, a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, pleated black slacks, polished loafers, a stack of vinyl records under one arm, grinning wide and holding a vinyl record up to the light like treasure

scared.line: That's not static. Static doesn't breathe.
scared.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old Black young man with deep brown skin and an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck, a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, pleated black slacks, polished loafers, a stack of vinyl records under one arm, pressing the headphones tight to his ears, eyes wide, lit green by the glow of the board meters

angry.line: Nobody cuts into my signal. Nobody.
angry.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old Black young man with deep brown skin and an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck, a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, pleated black slacks, polished loafers, a stack of vinyl records under one arm, jaw tight, finger jammed on a glowing red switch, a crackling speaker in the background

sad.line: Four in the morning, a thousand people listening, and nobody calls.
sad.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old Black young man with deep brown skin and an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck, a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, pleated black slacks, polished loafers, a stack of vinyl records under one arm, alone in a dark booth, chin on his folded arms beside a silent telephone with unlit buttons

determined.line: Cue it up. We're going live, and we are going loud.
determined.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old Black young man with deep brown skin and an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck, a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, pleated black slacks, polished loafers, a stack of vinyl records under one arm, sliding a fader up with one finger, headphones on, staring straight ahead

meet.title: Dead Air
meet.place: The KGLM 103.3 booth at the base of the water tower
meet.text: The KGLM booth is a cinderblock box under the water tower, papered with album covers. Mix Bell is supposed to be asleep before his overnight shift, but he is hunched over the request line, receiver to his ear. "Every afternoon at three," he whispers, "somebody calls and hums a song. Same song. I know every record in this building and I don't know this one." He holds out the receiver. A girl is humming a slow dance, very sweetly, from very far away.
meet.art: A 17-year-old Black DJ with deep brown skin, an easy smile, a crisp high-top fade, a thin gold chain, big padded headphones around his neck and a purple satin station jacket with a gold lightning-bolt patch over a white tee, holding out a telephone receiver to a teenager in a cramped cinderblock radio booth papered with album covers, afternoon sun slanting through a small window with a water tower outside, warm medium shot

choices.label: Listen hard and name the song she is humming

success.text: "'Hold Me Till the Morning,'" you say. "The slow dance from the old prom records." Mix stares, then dives into the archive and comes up with a dusty 1966 single. "Nobody knows that record. NOBODY." He presses a mixtape into your hands. "You're on my crew now."
success.art: A teenage DJ holding up a dusty vintage 45 record in triumph inside a radio archive, a teenager beside him holding a cassette mixtape

failure.text: You guess a song from a cereal commercial. The humming stops. The caller laughs softly and hangs up, and the turntable behind you starts spinning on its own, empty. Mix lifts the needle with a shaking hand. "Come back tomorrow. I'm finding this record if it kills me."
failure.art: An empty turntable spinning by itself in a radio booth, a teenage DJ reaching for the tone arm, a telephone receiver dangling off its hook

choices.label: Grab the mic and fill the dead air with a fake weather report

success.text: "Tonight in Glimmer Falls, clear skies, light fog, and a ninety percent chance of something in your closet." Mix laughs so hard he has to mute the board. "Okay, you've got a radio voice. You're coming on my show. And my crew. Mostly my crew."
success.art: A teenager speaking dramatically into a studio microphone while a teenage DJ doubles over laughing at the mixing board, an ON AIR sign glowing

failure.text: You open your mouth and nothing comes out. The microphone squeals with feedback that sounds almost like a scream, and the station manager bangs on the glass. Mix mouths "tomorrow" and gives you a thumbs-up you don't deserve.
failure.art: A frozen teenager in front of a squealing microphone, a red-faced station manager pounding on the booth window, a DJ giving a sympathetic thumbs-up

choices.label: Trace the call on the old station switchboard

success.text: You follow the lit line through a nest of cables to a number Mix looks up in the phone book. It belongs to a pay phone in the old Glimmer Falls High gym, disconnected in 1966. Mix whistles low. "Okay. You and me are figuring this out together."
success.art: Two teenagers bent over an old switchboard with tangled cables, a phone book open between them, one finger on a listing for a gymnasium pay phone

failure.text: You pull the wrong cable. Every line on the board lights up at once, and from every receiver comes the same slow breathing. Mix yanks the power cord. In the silence he says, very calmly, "New rule. Come back tomorrow, when it is more daylight."
failure.art: A radio switchboard with every button lit up red, a dozen phone receivers off their hooks, a DJ yanking a power cord from the wall

arc.title: Take Twelve
arc.place: The KGLM booth under the water tower, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Mix is splicing a demo tape for KBRV, a new all-music station in Oakland looking for an overnight host. It has to be postmarked by Friday. He has recorded his intro eleven times and hates every take. "Every one of them sounds like me pretending to be me," he says, and drops his headphones on the board. The reel-to-reel hisses, waiting for take twelve.
arc.art: A teenage DJ in a cinderblock radio booth papered with record sleeves, slumped over a mixing board beside a spinning reel-to-reel tape machine, headphones tossed down, a crumpled script on the desk

choices.label: Sit in the guest chair and be the one person he's talking to

success.text: He stops talking to the microphone and starts talking to you. Take twelve is warm and easy and a little funny, and halfway through he catches himself grinning. "Oh. That's what I sound like when I mean it."
success.art: A teenage DJ leaning into a microphone and grinning across a radio booth at a teenager in a worn guest chair, the reel-to-reel spinning, warm lamplight on the record sleeves

failure.text: You sneeze in the middle of the perfect take. Mix laughs so hard he has to put his head on the board, and for a minute the nerves are gone. Then he rewinds, and you watch them come right back.
failure.art: A teenage DJ with his forehead resting on a mixing board, laughing helplessly, while a teenager in the guest chair covers their nose, the tape reel rewinding

choices.label: Dig through the station archive for the perfect opening record

success.text: In a box marked LOCAL you find a 1959 doo-wop single by a Glimmer Falls group that recorded in this very booth. Mix holds it up to the light like a diamond. "Opening with the station's own history? That's not a demo. That's programming."
success.art: A teenager kneeling among dusty cardboard record boxes in a radio station storeroom, holding up a vintage seven-inch single while a teenage DJ gasps with delight

failure.text: The box marked LOCAL turns out to be the station manager's polka collection, forty records deep. Mix plays one out of pure despair and you both lose an hour to the accordion. The demo is still not done.
failure.art: A teenage DJ and a teenager sitting on the radio booth floor surrounded by stacks of polka records, a turntable spinning, both looking dazed

choices.label: Rip up his script and tell him to just talk

success.text: You tear the script in half before he can stop you. Mix stares at the pieces, then at the red ON AIR light, then leans in and talks about the valley at four in the morning: the truckers, the night nurses, the kids who can't sleep. It's the best minute of tape he's ever made.
success.art: A teenage DJ speaking into a microphone with his eyes closed under a glowing red on-air bulb, torn halves of a script fluttering to the floor beside a teenager

failure.text: With no script, Mix freezes for nine full seconds of dead air, then says, "Uh. Hi. Radio." He puts his face in his hands. Later, though, he tapes the torn halves of the script to the wall above the board, and he doesn't take them down.
failure.art: A teenage DJ with his face in his hands at a silent mixing board, a teenager wincing beside him, torn script halves on the desk under a glowing red light

arc.title: Automation
arc.place: The KGLM parking lot under the water tower, 5 p.m.
arc.text: Mix is sitting on the bumper of his secondhand hatchback with a memo crumpled in his fist. Starting in November, KGLM's overnight shift goes to a satellite feed called Hit-O-Matic: no host, no requests, no B-sides. "Doesn't matter," he says, too lightly. "Nobody's listening at four in the morning anyway." And there's a second thing he finally admits: he hasn't told his mom he applied to Oakland at all.
arc.art: A teenage DJ sitting on the bumper of an old hatchback under a looming water tower at dusk, a crumpled memo in his fist, a teenager standing beside him with hands in pockets

choices.label: Dig out the call logs and prove the overnight listeners are real

success.text: You count every logged call since September: three hundred and twelve. Truckers on Route 49, night-shift nurses, a baker who starts at three. The station manager grumbles and grants one month's reprieve if the call-in special goes big. Mix reads the number over and over.
success.art: A teenager running a finger down columns of a handwritten call log on a cluttered desk, a teenage DJ reading over their shoulder in astonishment, a grumpy station manager in the doorway

failure.text: Half the logbook is pages Mix filled in during the breathing calls, every line in shaky capitals. The station manager goes pale and shoos you both out. Mix laughs, a little hollow. "Great. My biggest fan is a ghost."
failure.art: A station manager recoiling from an open logbook full of shaky handwriting, a teenage DJ and a teenager being waved out of a cramped radio office

choices.label: Talk him into sending the B-side demo, not the safe one

success.text: He has two tapes: one plays the countdown hits, the other plays everything he loves. You make him listen to both in the car. When the B-side tape ends, he ejects it and writes OAKLAND on the label in marker. "If they don't want this one, they don't want me."
success.art: A teenage DJ writing on a cassette label in the front seat of a hatchback, a teenager in the passenger seat, a second cassette tossed onto the dashboard

failure.text: He listens to your pitch, nods, and slips the safe tape into the envelope anyway. "Safe gets jobs." But he doesn't seal it. The flap stays open on the dashboard all the way home.
failure.art: An unsealed manila envelope with a cassette inside resting on the dashboard of an old hatchback at dusk, a teenage DJ staring at it with both hands on the wheel

choices.label: Sit with him on the tower's bottom platform and just listen

success.text: Up on the first platform, with the whole valley turning gold, he says it: he's afraid nobody has ever really been listening. You tell him about the night you couldn't sleep and his voice was the only thing on. He goes quiet. "You never called." "I was listening."
success.art: A teenage DJ and a teenager sitting on the low platform of a water tower above a suburban valley at golden hour, legs dangling through the railing, talking quietly

failure.text: The wind picks up and the platform hums under you, and neither of you can find the right words. You sit there anyway until the streetlights come on below. When you climb down, he says, "Thanks for not leaving."
failure.art: Two teens sitting in silence on a water tower platform as dusk falls and streetlights blink on in the suburb below, the wind tugging their jackets

arc.title: Request Line
arc.place: The KGLM booth, the live afternoon special, 4 p.m.
arc.text: The station manager gave Mix two live hours this afternoon: a call-in special, recorded straight onto the Oakland demo. If the phones stay dark, the tape is dead air and the overnight show goes to the satellite. Mix straightens his collar for a room with no camera. "If nobody calls, I'm reading the phone book on air until somebody does." The ON AIR light flicks red.
arc.art: A teenage DJ in a pressed collar at a radio mixing board, a bank of unlit telephone request lines on the wall beside him, the red on-air bulb just switching on

choices.label: Run to the pay phone and rally the whole crew to call in

success.text: The lines light up: Glory requests a torch song, Bea wants to know if dinosaurs had radio, and then a stranger calls, a trucker who says Mix got him home through the fog last winter. Mix's voice cracks on air and he lets it. It's the best tape he will ever make, and by the end you know how to talk to a room you can't see.
success.art: A radio booth's whole wall of telephone request lines blazing with light, a teenage DJ laughing into the microphone with tears in his eyes, a teenager holding up a scrawled list of callers

failure.text: The crew all calls at the exact same second and jams the switchboard. For one awful minute there is nothing. Then a single line clears: a night nurse who listens every shift, calling on her break. Mix sends the tape with one call on it. It's the right one.
failure.art: A tangled radio switchboard with every line flashing at once except one steady light, a teenage DJ leaning toward it with a hand pressed over his heart

choices.label: Pull up a second mic and co-host the special with him

success.text: You do a ridiculous weather report, he does a smooth comeback, and by the second song you are bickering like a morning-zoo team. The phones start ringing just to join the bit. Mix mouths over the board: "We're GOOD at this."
success.art: A teenage DJ and a teenager sharing two microphones in a radio booth, both mid-laugh, phone lines lighting up one by one behind them

failure.text: You talk over his best line, he talks over your punchline, and the first caller asks if the station is "okay." Mix waves you off the mic and finishes alone, warm and steady. Afterward he admits that watching you flail made him braver.
failure.art: A teenager pulling back from a microphone with a wince while a teenage DJ smoothly takes over the broadcast, one phone line glowing on the wall

choices.label: Leave the phones alone and let the valley answer on its own

success.text: Nothing for one long song. Then a single line lights. Then three. Then all of them: strangers, every one, asking for B-sides by name. Mix stops cueing records and just reads requests for twenty minutes straight, grinning like the sun came up early.
success.art: A teenage DJ standing up at his mixing board in amazement as an entire wall of telephone lines blinks on one after another, a teenager beaming in the doorway

failure.text: Two calls in two hours, both wrong numbers. Mix talks anyway, to the dark, to whoever is out there, and somewhere in the second hour he stops sounding scared. He mails the tape at five. "Even if it's just you," he says, "that's an audience."
failure.art: A teenage DJ talking softly into a microphone in a dim booth as late light fades, a single unlit phone on the wall, a teenager listening from the guest chair

reactions.tech: Static that talks back is still static. I can mix it out.
reactions.paranormal: I always said dead air wasn't dead. Nobody believed me.
reactions.dream: Can't sleep? Tune in. Can sleep? Maybe tune in anyway. Just this week.
reactions.cult: Everybody chanting the same thing? Worst playlist I ever heard.

name: Delphine Hart
role: Head librarian and keeper of the town record
bio: Delphine Hart rides a cherry-red 1971 motorcycle to work, wears cardigans like armor, and knows exactly where every lie in Glimmer Falls is filed. She kept the occult stacks open when the library board wanted them locked, and she shushes people with a look that could stop a werewolf. In 1966 she was eighteen and in love with Roz Vance, the prom queen, and on prom night Roz was taken from her by a cruel prank the town decided to forget. Delphine still wears the ring they bought each other at the county fair. She is dry, deadpan, guarded and quietly furious, and twenty years of grief have taught her to answer every question but the ones about herself.

perk.name: Card Catalog Mind
perk.text: Delphine knows where every story in this town is shelved: the case board shows your odds of finding each clue.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a freckled 38-year-old Irish American woman with a sharp jaw and steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck, dark jeans, worn leather motorcycle boots, a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her left hand, standing beside a cherry-red motorcycle on the library steps at dusk, a stack of old yearbooks under one arm and a motorcycle helmet in the other hand, a faded prom banner rippling in the wind behind her

neutral.line: Shh. Not because of the rules. Because something in the stacks is listening.
neutral.art: Portrait of a freckled 38-year-old Irish American woman with a sharp jaw and steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck, dark jeans, worn leather motorcycle boots, a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her left hand, one finger raised to her lips, tall shelves of old books fading into shadow behind her

happy.line: Oh, now that is a first edition. Don't breathe on it.
happy.art: Portrait of a freckled 38-year-old Irish American woman with a sharp jaw and steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck, dark jeans, worn leather motorcycle boots, a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her left hand, a rare small smile, holding a battered antique book open with gentle hands, warm lamp light

scared.line: I've heard that song before. In 1966. I hoped I never would again.
scared.art: Portrait of a freckled 38-year-old Irish American woman with a sharp jaw and steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck, dark jeans, worn leather motorcycle boots, a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her left hand, face gone pale, gripping the edge of a reading table, a slow dance playing from somewhere unseen

angry.line: The board can ban the book. They cannot ban what happened.
angry.art: Portrait of a freckled 38-year-old Irish American woman with a sharp jaw and steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck, dark jeans, worn leather motorcycle boots, a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her left hand, slamming a heavy ledger shut, glasses swinging on their chain, eyes blazing

sad.line: She was going to wear blue. I still have the corsage, you know.
sad.art: Portrait of a freckled 38-year-old Irish American woman with a sharp jaw and steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck, dark jeans, worn leather motorcycle boots, a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her left hand, turning the silver ring on her finger, a pressed blue corsage in a glass case beside her

determined.line: Get your jacket. The library is closing early, and we're going riding.
determined.art: Portrait of a freckled 38-year-old Irish American woman with a sharp jaw and steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck, dark jeans, worn leather motorcycle boots, a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her left hand, pulling on a motorcycle helmet, keys in hand, jaw set

meet.title: Boxing Up the Occult
meet.place: The occult stacks, Glimmer Falls Public Library
meet.text: A memo from the library board is taped to the end of the occult stacks: REMOVE ALL MATERIALS BEFORE HALLOWEEN. Ms. Hart is packing them into banker's boxes as slowly as a person can pack anything. She does not look up. "If you're here for the Stephen Kingsley, it's checked out until 1990," she says. On the cart beside her is a 1966 yearbook, and her thumb keeps turning a silver ring around and around.
meet.art: A freckled 38-year-old Irish American librarian with a sharp jaw, steady gray eyes, gray-streaked chestnut hair in a short practical shag, tortoiseshell reading glasses on a beaded chain, an oxblood cardigan over a black turtleneck and worn motorcycle boots, slowly packing occult books into cardboard boxes between tall shelves, turning a thin silver ring with a small purple stone on her finger, a typed memo taped to the shelf end and a 1966 school annual on a book cart, a teenager at the end of the aisle, warm lamp light, medium shot

choices.label: Help her 'lose' the most important books before the board comes back

success.text: You slide the best grimoires behind the encyclopedias in the children's section, spine-in. Ms. Hart watches you work, and for the first time something like a smile crosses her face. "The board never goes into the picture-book room. You have instincts. Come by after closing."
success.art: A teenager sliding old leather books behind a row of children's encyclopedias in a colorful kids' section, a librarian watching with a faint smile

failure.text: A board member in a pastel suit catches you with three grimoires under your shirt. Ms. Hart takes the blame instantly and coldly. Later, on your way out, she murmurs without looking at you, "Come back tomorrow. Bring a bigger backpack."
failure.art: A stern woman in a pastel suit pointing at a teenager holding stacks of old books, a librarian stepping between them

choices.label: Ask, gently, about the ring she keeps turning

success.text: She is quiet a long time. Then she opens the yearbook to a girl with a cloud of dark hair and a laugh you can see from twenty years away. "Rosalind Vance. Roz. She could dance like gravity was optional." She closes the book softly. "I've never said her name out loud in this building. Thank you."
success.art: A librarian showing a teenager a black-and-white 1966 yearbook photo of a laughing girl, a silver ring catching the lamp light

failure.text: Her face closes like a book. "That's private." The lights in the aisle flicker, and from somewhere deep in the stacks comes the scratch of a needle on an old record. She goes white and turns away. "Maybe tomorrow, kid."
failure.art: A librarian turning her back in a dim library aisle as the overhead lights flicker, a teenager standing alone among the shelves

choices.label: Find the book she has been hunting for in the uncatalogued shelves

success.text: Misshelved under DEMONOLOGY you find the 1966 Glimmer Falls High prom program, a dried blue petal pressed inside. Ms. Hart takes it with both hands. "I've been looking for this for twenty years." She clears her throat. "You're useful. That's the highest compliment I give."
success.art: A teenager holding out a faded prom program with a pressed blue petal to a librarian between dusty shelves

failure.text: The uncatalogued shelves lean in like they are reading over your shoulder. A book leaps off the top shelf and lands open at your feet on a page of nothing but the word STAY. Ms. Hart shelves it with a snap. "That one bites. Come back tomorrow."
failure.art: A heavy book lying open on a library floor with a single repeated word filling its pages, shelves leaning ominously over a startled teenager

arc.title: The Corsage
arc.place: Ms. Hart's office behind the circulation desk, closing time
arc.text: Delphine unlocks the bottom drawer of her desk and lifts out a florist's box. Inside, wrapped in tissue from 1966, is a corsage of blue cornflowers gone brown at the edges. "She was going to wear blue," she says. "I was going to wear my brother's suit. One slow song, in front of everyone." She sets the box between you like evidence. "It's falling apart. I don't know whether to keep it or let it go."
arc.art: A librarian in a cardigan with a silver ring on her hand, opening an old florist's box on a lamp-lit office desk to reveal a faded blue cornflower corsage in yellowed tissue, a teenager seated across from her

choices.label: Help her press the petals so they last

success.text: You lay each petal between blotter sheets and weigh them down with the unabridged dictionary. Delphine watches every move. "Twenty years that dictionary has done nothing but hold a door open," she says. "Finally, it's useful."
success.art: Blue flower petals laid carefully between sheets of blotting paper under a huge open dictionary on a library desk, a librarian and a teenager leaning over it by lamplight

failure.text: A petal crumbles to blue dust between your fingers, and you start to apologize. Delphine just gathers the dust into an envelope and writes ROZ, 1966 on it in her tidy script. "She would have laughed at both of us."
failure.art: A librarian's hands sliding a small envelope of blue flower dust into a desk drawer, a teenager watching apologetically, an old florist's box open between them

choices.label: Ask which song they were going to dance to

success.text: "'Hold Me Till the Morning.'" She hums two bars before she catches herself, cheeks pink. She has never been able to listen to it since. You mention that a DJ at KGLM found the 1966 single, and she goes very still. "Does he," she says. "Does he really."
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan humming with her eyes closed behind a lamp-lit desk, one hand over the silver ring, a teenager smiling across from her

failure.text: She says the title, and then she can't say anything else. You sit together in the lamplight while the wall clock ticks. When the closing bell rings, she squeezes your hand once. "Tomorrow. I'll tell you tomorrow."
failure.art: A librarian and a teenager sitting in silence in a dim office after hours, a wall clock above them, her hand resting briefly on theirs

choices.label: Suggest she wear the corsage at the front desk, tonight

success.text: She pins the brittle corsage to her cardigan and works the desk until close. Three patrons compliment it. To the last one, a teenage girl with a stack of poetry, she says simply, "It was a gift," and doesn't look away.
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan with a faded blue corsage pinned to it stamping books at a library circulation desk, a teenage girl with a stack of poetry admiring the flowers

failure.text: Her hands shake too much to work the pin. She sets the corsage back in its tissue and closes the lid gently. "Not yet. But soon." She looks at you over her glasses. "Thank you for thinking I could."
failure.art: A librarian closing the lid of an old florist's box with gentle shaking hands, a straight pin left on the desk, a teenager beside her

arc.title: The Missing Page
arc.place: The locked local-history room, Glimmer Falls Public Library, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Delphine opens the 1966 yearbook to the spring dance page. One photo is gone, sliced out with a razor so neatly you could miss it. "The board took it the week after," she says. "It was Roz and me at the county fair, the day we bought the rings." In the back of the room is a cabinet the library board sealed in 1966, and in twenty years she has never been allowed to open it. Today she is wearing the pressed cornflowers in a locket.
arc.art: A librarian in a cardigan and a teenager in a cramped local-history archive room, an old yearbook open to a page with one photo neatly cut out, a sealed wooden cabinet in the background

choices.label: Find the key the board hid

success.text: The key is taped under the seat of the board chair's own reserved armchair. Inside the cabinet: the missing photo, and a 1966 petition with forty-one student signatures asking for a dance in Roz's name. The board buried it. Delphine reads every name. "Ten of them still live in this town. I check out their books."
success.art: A librarian reading a yellowed handwritten petition beside an open wooden cabinet, an old photograph of two smiling girls at a county fair in her other hand, a teenager holding up a small brass key

failure.text: You find the key, but the cabinet holds only the board's minutes: NO MEMORIAL. MATTER CLOSED. Delphine's jaw sets. "Closed. Like a book nobody's allowed to read." She photocopies the page and files it under Injustice, Local.
failure.art: A librarian holding a single typed page of old meeting minutes beside a nearly empty cabinet, jaw set, a teenager beside her holding a brass key

choices.label: Help her put Roz's photo in the front display case

success.text: The fair photo goes into the Local History case by the front doors, with a card: ROSALIND VANCE AND DELPHINE HART, 1966. Delphine's hands are perfectly steady. Within the hour, a teenage girl stops in front of it and stands there a very long time.
success.art: An old photograph of two girls laughing at a county fair inside a glass library display case by the front doors, a librarian and a teenager stepping back to look, a teenage girl pausing to stare

failure.text: The case lock jams, and a board member in a pastel suit comes clicking down the hall. Delphine slips the photo into her cardigan pocket, over her heart. "Not like this," she murmurs. "When we do it, we do it on our terms."
failure.art: A librarian tucking an old photograph into her cardigan pocket beside a jammed display case, a woman in a pastel suit approaching down a library hallway

choices.label: Ask what she never got to say to Roz

success.text: "That I'd have danced with her in front of God and the whole PTA." Then she laughs, actually laughs, loud enough to break her own rule about voices in the library. "Twenty years and I've never said that out loud either."
success.art: A librarian laughing with her head tipped back among archive shelves, holding a locket on a chain, a teenager grinning beside her

failure.text: She answers by reciting the overdue-fine schedule, in full. You let her. When she runs out of fines, she stands quiet in the dust a long while and says one word: "Everything."
failure.art: A librarian standing very still among dusty archive shelves with her hand over a locket, a teenager waiting patiently beside her in the dim light

arc.title: The Last Dance
arc.place: The library reading room after closing, lamps low
arc.text: The long oak tables are pushed against the stacks. Mix has brought a turntable and the 1966 single, Glory is at the door handing out paper programs, and a dozen neighbors stand awkwardly between the card catalogs, three of them gray-haired names from the petition. Delphine wears her ring and the locket of pressed cornflowers. "I don't know how to start," she says. "I was supposed to have someone to start with."
arc.art: A library reading room after hours with oak tables pushed against the shelves, lamps glowing low, a turntable on the circulation desk, neighbors of all ages gathered, a librarian with a locket standing in the cleared center

choices.label: Offer your hand for the first verse

success.text: You dance the first verse, badly, and pass her to Glory, then to the old petition signers, then to Bea standing on her shoes. By the last chorus the whole room is turning around her, and Delphine is in the middle with her eyes closed, smiling, as a warm draft smelling of gardenias moves through the stacks. Afterward she teaches you how to find what a town tried to forget.
success.art: A librarian dancing with her eyes closed and smiling at the center of a circle of neighbors in a lamp-lit library reading room, a faint warm glow drifting between the bookshelves

failure.text: You step on her foot on the very first beat. She laughs out loud, in the library, and Glory cuts in, and then the whole room follows. You watch from the edge as Delphine dances for Roz with the living town. It doesn't matter who started it. It started.
failure.art: A teenager watching from the edge of a lamp-lit library reading room as a towering drag queen twirls a laughing librarian, neighbors joining the dance behind them

choices.label: Read the 1966 petition aloud before the needle drops

success.text: You read all forty-one names. When you finish, one of the gray-haired signers says, "We should have done this then." Delphine answers, "We're doing it now," and nods to Mix. The needle drops, and she asks the signer to dance.
success.art: A teenager reading aloud from a yellowed petition in a lamp-lit library, a gray-haired neighbor wiping his eyes, a librarian offering him her hand as a DJ lowers a turntable needle

failure.text: Your voice cracks halfway down the list. Delphine takes the paper from you and finishes it herself, steady as a stone, every name. Then she folds it into her pocket and nods to Mix. "That one was mine to read anyway."
failure.art: A librarian reading from a yellowed petition in a steady stance in a hushed library reading room, a teenager beside her, neighbors listening in lamplight

choices.label: Cue the record yourself and let her choose how it begins

success.text: You drop the needle in the right groove. For the first bars, Delphine dances alone in the center, with the empty air, the way she planned to in 1966, and nobody in the room laughs. Then she holds out her hand to all of them.
success.art: A librarian dancing alone with her arms around empty air in the center of a hushed library reading room, neighbors watching tenderly, a teenager at the turntable

failure.text: The needle skates to the end of the record with a terrible scratch. Silence. Then Delphine says, "Again. We have waited twenty years. We can wait for a needle." The second time it lands, and the room exhales and starts to dance.
failure.art: A teenager wincing over a turntable in a lamp-lit library while a librarian raises one patient hand, neighbors waiting in a loose circle around her

reactions.paranormal: The dead aren't monsters. They're overdue. Let's find out what they want returned.
reactions.cult: Every cult I've ever read about started the same way: somebody banned a book.
reactions.cosmic: Shelve it under Unknowable. Right next to the library board's budget.

name: Toby Nakamura
bio: Toby Nakamura is shooting his masterpiece, Attack of the Cul-de-Sac, on a shoulder camcorder he borrowed from the AV club in September and has not returned. He works weekends at Rewind Video rewinding returns for store credit, knows four recipes for fake blood, and can tell you how every effect in every monster movie was done. His grandmother tells him ghost stories from Hiroshima prefecture over tea; his father thinks horror movies are a waste of a good mind. Toby's flaw is that he would rather film the monster than run from it, and he directs his friends like they are his cast. He is sweet, intense, a little bossy, and braver behind a lens than anywhere else.

perk.name: Take Two
perk.text: Toby yells "cut!" and everybody resets: reroll one failed daytime roll each day.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round, earnest face, a messy black bowl cut falling into big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo, khaki cargo shorts with every pocket stuffed with tapes and batteries, white tube socks pulled to the knee, a bulky shoulder-mounted camcorder with a red recording light, kneeling low in the middle of a foggy suburban street at night with the camcorder on his shoulder, its red light glowing, a giant shadow looming in his viewfinder and reflected in his glasses

neutral.line: Okay, hit your mark. No, the other mark. The tape mark.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round, earnest face, a messy black bowl cut falling into big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo, khaki cargo shorts with every pocket stuffed with tapes and batteries, white tube socks pulled to the knee, a bulky shoulder-mounted camcorder with a red recording light, squinting through the camcorder viewfinder, one hand directing, a video store horror aisle behind him

happy.line: That was the best practical effect I have ever seen and it was REAL.
happy.art: Portrait of a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round, earnest face, a messy black bowl cut falling into big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo, khaki cargo shorts with every pocket stuffed with tapes and batteries, white tube socks pulled to the knee, a bulky shoulder-mounted camcorder with a red recording light, bouncing on his toes, camcorder raised overhead in triumph, glasses askew

scared.line: The light's red. It's recording. I'm not stopping. I'm not stopping.
scared.art: Portrait of a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round, earnest face, a messy black bowl cut falling into big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo, khaki cargo shorts with every pocket stuffed with tapes and batteries, white tube socks pulled to the knee, a bulky shoulder-mounted camcorder with a red recording light, pale and sweating, camcorder still steady on his shoulder, red record light reflected in his wide eyes

angry.line: You don't get to be in my movie. You get cut.
angry.art: Portrait of a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round, earnest face, a messy black bowl cut falling into big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo, khaki cargo shorts with every pocket stuffed with tapes and batteries, white tube socks pulled to the knee, a bulky shoulder-mounted camcorder with a red recording light, lowering the camcorder slowly, glaring over the top of his glasses

sad.line: My dad says horror movies are a waste. He's never watched one with me.
sad.art: Portrait of a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round, earnest face, a messy black bowl cut falling into big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo, khaki cargo shorts with every pocket stuffed with tapes and batteries, white tube socks pulled to the knee, a bulky shoulder-mounted camcorder with a red recording light, sitting on a video store step-stool, camcorder in his lap, staring at a blank TV screen

determined.line: Fresh tape, full battery. Roll camera.
determined.art: Portrait of a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round, earnest face, a messy black bowl cut falling into big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo, khaki cargo shorts with every pocket stuffed with tapes and batteries, white tube socks pulled to the knee, a bulky shoulder-mounted camcorder with a red recording light, snapping a new tape into the camcorder, jaw set, record light blinking on

meet.title: Extra Wanted
meet.place: The horror aisle, Rewind Video
meet.text: In the horror aisle of Rewind Video, a kid in a yellow windbreaker has taped an X to the carpet and is lying on his back, filming up at the shelf of slasher tapes. "I need a scream," he announces to nobody. "A real one. Mine sounds like a teakettle." He spots you. "You. You have a screaming face. Also, my tape from last night came out weird and I think I filmed something I didn't film."
meet.art: A 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a round earnest face, a messy black bowl cut and big wire-rimmed glasses, a yellow windbreaker over a teal-and-white striped polo and khaki cargo shorts stuffed with tapes and batteries, lying on his back on the carpet of a video store horror aisle with a bulky shoulder camcorder aimed up at shelves of lurid horror tapes, a tape X marked on the floor beside him, a teenager standing over him, purple aisle light, medium shot from above

choices.label: Hit the mark and give him a classic scream-queen scream

success.text: You throw your hands to your face and let rip. The whole store goes silent. From the counter, the old clerk applauds slowly. Toby lowers the camera, awed. "That's a take. That's a PRINT. You're in my movie. You're in my crew."
success.art: A teenager screaming dramatically on a tape mark in a video store aisle, a boy filming with a camcorder, an elderly clerk applauding from the counter

failure.text: Your scream cracks into a squeak halfway through. Two kids in the comedy aisle laugh. Toby pats your shoulder with total sincerity. "No, that was honest. Honest is good. We'll reshoot tomorrow."
failure.art: A blushing teenager in a video store aisle, two kids snickering behind a shelf, a boy with a camcorder giving an earnest thumbs-up

choices.label: Help him rescue the tape the store VCR ate

success.text: You wind the crinkled tape back with a pencil and play it in the back room. There is Crystal Street at 3 a.m., and in the corner of the frame a tall shape in curlers, walking through a front door without opening it. Toby whispers, "We're going to need a bigger crew. You're it."
success.art: Two teenagers in a cluttered video store back room staring at a small TV showing grainy night footage of a suburban street and a shadowy tall figure

failure.text: The VCR eats your sleeve too. When you finally pull free, the screen shows one frame of you, asleep in a pink salon chair you have never sat in. Toby ejects the tape very carefully. "Okay. Tomorrow. We look at this tomorrow."
failure.art: A small TV in a dark back room frozen on a grainy still of a teenager asleep in a pink salon chair, a jammed VCR chewing a sleeve

choices.label: Distract the manager so Toby can film in the stockroom

success.text: You ask the manager to explain the difference between Beta and VHS, and he gives you twenty uninterrupted minutes. Toby emerges from the stockroom glowing, with a cardboard cutout of a swamp monster under his arm. "You're a natural producer. Welcome aboard."
success.art: A video store manager lecturing a teenager while gesturing at two tape formats, a boy sneaking out of a stockroom behind them with a cardboard monster cutout

failure.text: The manager sees straight through you and catches Toby elbow-deep in the stockroom. You're both sent out to the curb. Toby, unbothered, films the sunset. "Rejection builds character. Come back tomorrow. I'll storyboard it."
failure.art: Two teenagers sitting on a curb outside a neon video store at sunset, one filming the sky with a camcorder

arc.title: No Ending
arc.place: The back room of Rewind Video, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Toby has two VCRs wired together on a card table, cutting Attack of the Cul-de-Sac tape to tape. Everything is done except the ending. The monster is a garbage bag, a mop head and two ping-pong-ball eyes, and he cannot figure out what it wants. "Every great monster has a reason," he says, rubbing his eyes. "Mine has a mop."
arc.art: A teenage boy in a yellow windbreaker hunched over two wired-together VCRs on a card table in a cluttered video-store back room, a homemade garbage-bag monster with a mop-head wig slumped on a chair beside him

choices.label: Pitch him an ending

success.text: "What if it just wants to be invited to the block party?" Toby goes completely silent. Then he starts scribbling. "It's lonely. It's a lonely mop. That's devastating. That's CINEMA."
success.art: A teenage boy scribbling furiously in a notebook in a video-store back room, a teenager beside him gesturing at a homemade mop-headed monster costume

failure.text: "And then it was all a dream?" Toby gasps like you insulted his whole family. But the horror on his face is useful: by the time he stops sputtering, he knows exactly what his ending is NOT.
failure.art: A teenage boy clutching his chest in theatrical horror in a cluttered back room, a teenager shrugging beside a garbage-bag monster costume

choices.label: Ask what his grandmother says about monsters

success.text: "Baachan says most ghosts in her stories are just people nobody said goodbye to." He stops. Looks at the mop. Looks at you. "I'm filming her telling one. As the prologue. She's going to love being in a movie."
success.art: A teenage boy holding a shoulder camcorder and staring at a homemade monster costume in sudden inspiration, a teenager smiling beside him in a video-store back room

failure.text: He opens his mouth and realizes he doesn't know. He has heard all her stories, but he has never asked her what she thinks they mean. He writes ASK BAACHAN on his hand in marker, a little ashamed.
failure.art: A teenage boy writing a note on the back of his hand in marker at a cluttered card table, a camcorder beside him, looking thoughtful

choices.label: Put on the garbage-bag suit and be the monster for a reshoot

success.text: You lumber down the horror aisle in the garbage-bag suit, knock over a cardboard cutout, and make a real customer shriek. Toby is crouched behind the camera, glowing. "That's the shot. You're a natural mop."
success.art: A teenager in a homemade garbage-bag monster suit with a mop-head wig lumbering down a video-store horror aisle, a customer shrieking, a boy filming on a shoulder camcorder

failure.text: You trip over your own garbage-bag feet and take out an entire display of aerobics tapes. The manager comes running. Toby, still rolling, whispers, "Keep going, this is gold," and you are both sent outside to think about it.
failure.art: A teenager in a garbage-bag monster suit tangled in a toppled display of exercise videotapes, a boy still filming with a camcorder, a manager rushing in

arc.title: The Camcorder
arc.place: The Rewind Video counter, 5 p.m.
arc.text: Toby is rewinding returns with way too much force. His dad came in at lunch, saw the AV-club camcorder, and said it goes back to school on Monday, and that the movie is over until after the PSAT. "He said it's a waste of a good mind," Toby says. "He's never even watched one with me." His grandmother is sitting in the folding chair by the door, waiting to walk him home, pretending not to listen.
arc.art: A teenage boy furiously rewinding videotapes behind a video-store counter, a shoulder camcorder in its bag beside him, an elderly Japanese American woman in a cardigan sitting patiently by the door

choices.label: Help him shoot the last shot today, before the camera goes back

success.text: You sprint to Crystal Street with the monster suit and the camera and get the final shot at golden hour: the lonely mop at the edge of the block party, someone finally holding out a paper plate. The light is perfect. Toby lowers the camera. "Okay. Now I'm done. Now he can have it."
success.art: A homemade mop-headed monster standing at the edge of a suburban cul-de-sac at golden hour while someone offers it a paper plate, a boy filming from the curb with a camcorder

failure.text: The battery dies halfway through the take. You both sit on the curb in the monster's shadow. "Maybe he's right," Toby says. Then a kid from down the street wanders over and asks if you're making a real movie, and Toby sits up straight. "Yes. Yes, we are."
failure.art: A teenage boy and a teenager sitting on a suburban curb at sunset beside a dead camcorder and a slumped monster costume, a curious younger kid approaching

choices.label: Help him write down what he'd say to his dad if he weren't scared

success.text: It takes six drafts. The last one is three lines long: "I'm premiering my movie Thursday at seven. Please come. Then you can decide." Toby folds it carefully and puts it in his dad's lunch thermos bag. His hands are shaking. He's smiling anyway.
success.art: A teenage boy folding a short handwritten note at a video-store counter, crumpled earlier drafts around him, a teenager beside him giving a thumbs-up

failure.text: Every draft turns into a screenplay where his dad is the villain. By the fifth he crumples it and sighs. "He's not a villain. He's just tired, and scared I'll be poor." It isn't a letter, but it's the truest thing he's said all week.
failure.art: A teenage boy surrounded by crumpled notebook pages at a video-store counter, resting his chin in his hands, a teenager sitting beside him

choices.label: Suggest he show his grandmother the footage first

success.text: His grandmother watches on the store TV, laughs out loud at the mop monster, and says something in Japanese. Toby goes very still and translates: "Your father drew monsters too, when he was your age. He kept them in a shoebox." Toby has never heard this in his life.
success.art: An elderly Japanese American woman laughing in front of a small store television showing a homemade monster movie, a stunned teenage boy beside her, a teenager watching them both

failure.text: She falls asleep in the first five minutes. Toby laughs so hard he has to sit on the floor. When she wakes up at the end, she pats his hand. "The mop was very sad. Good." It's a review, and he takes it.
failure.art: An elderly woman dozing in a folding chair in front of a video-store television, a teenage boy laughing on the floor beside her, a teenager grinning

arc.title: Premiere
arc.place: The Rewind Video TV wall, after closing
arc.text: The store's wall of twelve display TVs is cued to the same tape. Folding chairs fill the new-release aisle, the crew is passing popcorn, and Toby is pacing in a borrowed blazer two sizes too big. In the front row he saved two seats: one for Baachan, who is already there with a thermos of tea, and one for his father, which is empty. "We start at seven," he says. "No matter what." It's 7:02.
arc.art: A video store after hours with a wall of twelve glowing television sets, rows of folding chairs filled with friends holding popcorn, a teenage boy in an oversized blazer pacing beside one conspicuously empty front-row seat

choices.label: Stall the crowd with a live pre-show introduction

success.text: You give the most dramatic introduction in Rewind Video history, and right at the big finish the bell over the door jingles. Mr. Nakamura, still in his work clothes, takes the empty seat. During the mop's last scene he laughs out loud, and afterward he asks Toby how he did the slime. On the way out, Toby teaches you how to make a movie with nothing but nerve and borrowed gear.
success.art: A tired man in work clothes laughing in a front-row folding chair before a glowing wall of televisions, a teenage boy in an oversized blazer turning to stare at him in disbelief

failure.text: Your pre-show runs long and the crowd gets restless, so Toby rolls without him. Halfway through, the bell jingles. His dad stands in the back by the new releases for the second half. At the end he says, "Run it again. From the start. I missed the start."
failure.art: A man in work clothes standing at the back of a dark video store by the new-release shelves, lit by a wall of televisions, a teenage boy looking back at him from the front row

choices.label: Run to the Nakamura house and bring his dad yourself

success.text: You find Mr. Nakamura on his porch, holding Toby's three-line note, not sure he's really wanted. You tell him he is. He grabs his coat. You slip in together just as the title card hits the screen, and Toby, who sees, forgets his next line completely.
success.art: A teenager and a man in work clothes slipping into a darkened video store together as a wall of televisions lights up, a teenage boy at the front turning around open-mouthed

failure.text: The house is dark; he's working late. You sprint back to find the credits rolling and Toby filming the audience's applause. The next morning, though, Toby calls you at seven a.m.: his dad borrowed the tape before work. "He watched it twice. He wants to see the shoebox monsters too."
failure.art: A teenage boy filming a cheering audience with a camcorder in a video store as end credits glow on a wall of televisions, a breathless teenager arriving at the door

choices.label: Tell Toby to start without waiting

success.text: Toby looks at the full room and realizes the movie belongs to the people already here. He dims the lights. The crew screams at all the right parts. Mid-credits, the bell jingles, and his dad stands in the doorway, late but there, asking if there's a second showing.
success.art: A video store wall of televisions showing end credits while a cheering crowd applauds, a man in work clothes standing in the doorway, a teenage boy in an oversized blazer turning toward him

failure.text: Toby starts, but he keeps glancing at the door and misses his own cue to dim the lights. Baachan reaches over and holds his hand. At the end, the empty chair has a bag of rice crackers on it, with a note in his father's handwriting: WORKING LATE. SAVE ME A COPY.
failure.art: An empty front-row folding chair holding a bag of rice crackers and a folded note in a dim video store, a teenage boy and his grandmother holding hands beside it

reactions.creature: Is that a practical effect? Please tell me that's a practical effect.
reactions.slasher: Okay, rule one: never split up. Rule two: I'm filming all of it.
reactions.tech: Ghosts in the videotape? I KNEW my tracking was fine.

name: Glory Hallelujah
pronouns: she/her in drag, he/him out of it (Gordon)
role: Drag queen and revue mother of the Glitter Box
bio: Out of drag he is Gordon Pike, who keeps the Glitter Box's books, teaches Tuesday tap, and fixes the boiler with a wrench and a prayer. In drag she is Glory Hallelujah, six-foot-four in heels, sequins and steel, mother of the Saturday revue and of every stray kid who wanders in looking for somewhere to be themselves. In 1961, nineteen-year-old Gordon sat in Frieda Krueger's salon chair and got his first real haircut, and Frieda told him to be bold. Glory has been bold ever since. She is devastatingly funny, generous to a fault, and keeps a grudge like a scrapbook. Her flaw is that she will turn any hurt into a punchline before she lets anyone see it land.

perk.name: Mother's Morning Read
perk.text: Glory calls at dawn to tell you exactly how fabulous you were last night: +1 nerve each dawn.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old white drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, dramatic magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes, a floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe at the shoulders, elbow-length gold satin gloves, rhinestone chandelier earrings, holding a rhinestone microphone, striking a triumphant pose center stage under a single spotlight, one gloved arm flung up to the rafters, sequins blazing, a red velvet curtain parting behind her and fog rolling at her feet

neutral.line: Darling, the show starts at eleven, and so does the haunting.
neutral.art: Portrait of a tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old white drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, dramatic magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes, a floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe at the shoulders, elbow-length gold satin gloves, rhinestone chandelier earrings, holding a rhinestone microphone, seated at a lighted dressing-room mirror, one gloved hand adjusting an earring

happy.line: Now THAT is what Mother calls a performance!
happy.art: Portrait of a tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old white drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, dramatic magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes, a floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe at the shoulders, elbow-length gold satin gloves, rhinestone chandelier earrings, holding a rhinestone microphone, laughing with her head thrown back, gloved hands clasped at her chest, confetti in the air

scared.line: I have played to drunk Shriners and a fire marshal. I can survive this. Probably.
scared.art: Portrait of a tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old white drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, dramatic magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes, a floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe at the shoulders, elbow-length gold satin gloves, rhinestone chandelier earrings, holding a rhinestone microphone, clutching the rhinestone microphone to her chest, glitter lashes wide, a shadow falling across the stage

angry.line: Honey, I will take off these earrings, and you do not want that.
angry.art: Portrait of a tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old white drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, dramatic magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes, a floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe at the shoulders, elbow-length gold satin gloves, rhinestone chandelier earrings, holding a rhinestone microphone, unclipping one chandelier earring with a deadly calm stare, jaw set

sad.line: Frieda told me to be bold. I never got to tell her I listened.
sad.art: Portrait of a tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old white drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, dramatic magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes, a floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe at the shoulders, elbow-length gold satin gloves, rhinestone chandelier earrings, holding a rhinestone microphone, sitting on the edge of the stage in her gown, wig slightly askew, holding a faded salon appointment card

determined.line: Wigs on, hearts out. We open in five.
