determined.art: Portrait of a tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old white drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, dramatic magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes, a floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe at the shoulders, elbow-length gold satin gloves, rhinestone chandelier earrings, holding a rhinestone microphone, pulling on a gold glove finger by finger, chin high, spotlight rising behind her

meet.title: The Closing Number
meet.place: Backstage, the Glitter Box Playhouse
meet.text: Backstage at the Glitter Box smells of hairspray, mothballs and fresh coffee. A towering queen in a half-zipped magenta gown is pacing between racks of costumes. "Trixie dropped out. Nightmares, she says, every night, somebody trying to cut her hair." She whirls on you, takes you in from shoes to scalp, and her eyes stop on a single gray streak in your hair you didn't have last week. Her face changes. "Well," Glory says softly. "Sit down, sugar."
meet.art: A tall, broad-shouldered 44-year-old drag queen with a strong square jaw, a towering platinum-blonde bouffant wig, magenta eyeshadow and gold glitter lashes in a half-zipped floor-length magenta sequin gown with gold fringe, pacing backstage between racks of costumes and bulb-ringed mirrors and stopping to study a teenager by the stage door who has a single new gray streak in their hair, warm bulb light, medium shot

choices.label: Learn Trixie's closing number in one afternoon

success.text: Kick, turn, fan, dip, and you hit the final pose exactly on the cymbal. The chorus erupts. Glory dabs her eyes with a glove. "Mother is weeping. Somebody put this child on the bill, and somebody get this child on my crew."
success.art: A teenager striking a dramatic final pose on a small stage while a chorus of drag performers cheers, a tall queen dabbing her eyes with a gold glove

failure.text: You turn left on the kick and land in the orchestra pit, which is one upright piano. Glory hauls you out by the collar. "Tomorrow, same time. Bring sneakers, not ambition." She is laughing, which helps.
failure.art: A teenager tangled on top of an upright piano below a small stage, a drag queen in sequins leaning down laughing with an outstretched hand

choices.label: Tell her about the salon chair in your dreams

success.text: When you mention the shears, Glory sits down hard on a costume trunk. "Frieda Krueger cut my hair in 1961. Told me to be bold." She takes your hand. "Whatever's wearing her face now, she was kind to me once. We are going to figure this out together, you and Mother."
success.art: A drag queen sitting on a costume trunk holding a teenager's hand, an old salon appointment card on her knee, dressing-room bulbs glowing

failure.text: Glory laughs too loudly and too long and changes the subject to wigs. She sends you off with a hug that is a little too tight. On the bus home you find a long silver hair on your sleeve that isn't yours. Come back tomorrow; she'll be ready.
failure.art: A teenager on a city bus at dusk picking a single long silver hair off their sleeve, the glowing marquee of a small theatre receding through the window

choices.label: Help the costume crew mend a torn gown before curtain

success.text: You hold the seam while the crew stitches, and you find the loose sequins nobody else could. Glory zips into the gown, twirls, and points at you with a gloved finger. "This one stays. Anybody who saves a gown is family."
success.art: A drag queen twirling in a repaired sequin gown backstage, a teenager holding a spool of thread and grinning, sequins glittering in the air

failure.text: You sew the gown to your own jeans. Twice. Glitter gets in places glitter should not be. Glory snips you free with great dignity. "Darling, come back tomorrow, and come back without a needle."
failure.art: A teenager accidentally stitched to a magenta sequin gown, a drag queen snipping the thread with tiny gold scissors, glitter everywhere

arc.title: Big Hallelujah
arc.place: Glory's dressing room, the Glitter Box Playhouse, 3 p.m.
arc.text: Glory's signature wig, a towering auburn creation she calls Big Hallelujah, sits on its foam head, and since Saturday it has been going gray, one strand at a time. She will not look at it in the dressing-room mirror; she checks it in a hand compact, turned away. "It's the humidity," she says, which it is not. "Mother is not superstitious. Mother is simply... reorganizing."
arc.art: A towering drag queen in a satin robe in a cluttered dressing room, peering into a small hand compact with her back to a bulb-lit mirror, a huge auburn wig on a foam head streaked with strands of gray

choices.label: Restyle Big Hallelujah with her, curl by curl

success.text: You hand her pins while she teases and rolls. Instead of hiding the gray, she weaves it in, and by six o'clock Big Hallelujah is a shimmering silver crown. Glory turns it on the foam head, slowly. "Bold," she says. "That's what Frieda would have said."
success.art: A drag queen and a teenager restyling a towering wig on a foam head into a shimmering silver crown, bobby pins and rollers scattered across a vanity

failure.text: The curling iron sizzles a whole hank of fake hair into a puff of smoke. Glory waves it away. "That is the most dramatic thing to happen to that wig since 1979." She laughs. Her hands, though, are trembling.
failure.art: A small puff of smoke rising from a towering wig on a foam head, a drag queen in a satin robe waving it away with a fan and laughing, a teenager holding a curling iron sheepishly

choices.label: Strut the gray wig down the hallway like a runway, then ask what's really wrong

success.text: You sashay the gray wig down the backstage hallway and Glory shrieks with laughter. Then, quietly, with the door shut, she tells you: when she looks in the mirror this week, she doesn't see Glory. She sees a frightened teenager in a pink salon chair in 1961.
success.art: A teenager strutting down a narrow backstage hallway wearing an enormous gray-streaked wig, a drag queen in a satin robe doubled over laughing in a dressing-room doorway

failure.text: She out-jokes you three punchlines deep, then four, and every time you get close to the real thing she tosses another one. Finally she pats your cheek. "Nice try, sugar." But she keeps the wig on its stand facing you, not the mirror.
failure.art: A drag queen in a satin robe patting a teenager's cheek affectionately in a bulb-lit dressing room, a gray-streaked wig on a stand between them

choices.label: Gently turn her chair so she faces the mirror

success.text: She looks. For one second, in the glass, there's a teenager with a brand-new bold haircut grinning back at her from 1961. Glory breathes out, long and slow. "Oh," she says to the reflection. "There you are."
success.art: A drag queen in a satin robe gazing into a bulb-lit mirror, her reflection briefly replaced by a grinning teenager with a bold 1961 haircut, a teenager standing behind her chair

failure.text: She flinches and throws a feather boa over the mirror before you can blink. "Not today, darling." There's a long silence. Then she pulls up a second stool and pats it, which means you're allowed to stay.
failure.art: A pink feather boa flung over a bulb-lit dressing-room mirror, a drag queen turning away from it, a teenager hesitating beside an empty stool

arc.title: The Covered Mirror
arc.place: The Glitter Box office, out of drag, 5 p.m.
arc.text: Out of drag, Gordon Pike sits at the office desk in reading glasses and a cardigan, doing the books in pencil. The mirror on the office wall is covered with a bedsheet. He opens a scrapbook to a 1961 Gazette clipping about the Shear Delight dye scare. "I was nineteen," he says. "When the PTA came for her, I sat in the back of the hearing and said nothing. I was afraid if I stood up for her, they'd ask why." He has never forgiven himself.
arc.art: A tall middle-aged man in reading glasses and a cardigan at a cluttered theater office desk with an open scrapbook of old newspaper clippings, a bedsheet draped over a wall mirror behind him, a teenager seated nearby

choices.label: Tell him that nineteen-year-old Gordon was scared, not wrong

success.text: He's quiet for a long time. Then he takes off his glasses and rubs his eyes. "Glory would have said that," he says. "I keep forgetting she's me. She's been telling me that for twenty-five years."
success.art: A middle-aged man in a cardigan holding his reading glasses in one hand and smiling sadly at a teenager across a theater office desk, an open scrapbook between them

failure.text: He deflects with a long story about the boiler, and you let him tell it all the way through. When it's over, he closes the scrapbook. "Thank you for not laughing," he says, and means it.
failure.art: A middle-aged man in a cardigan gesturing with a wrench while telling a story in a cramped theater office, a teenager listening patiently, a closed scrapbook on the desk

choices.label: Pull the sheet off the mirror together

success.text: The sheet slides to the floor. In the mirror is Gordon at forty-four, in a cardigan, a little gray at the temples. He looks for a long time. Then he says, "Hello, you old queen," and laughs so hard he has to sit down.
success.art: A middle-aged man in a cardigan laughing at his own reflection in a newly uncovered wall mirror, a bedsheet pooled on the floor, a teenager grinning beside him

failure.text: The sheet snags, and for half a second his reflection moves a beat behind him, gray all over. He yanks the sheet back up. "Not yet," he says. But he leaves one corner of the glass uncovered, and he doesn't fix it.
failure.art: A wall mirror half uncovered by a snagged bedsheet in a theater office, a faint gray reflection lagging behind a middle-aged man in a cardigan as he pulls the sheet back

choices.label: Search the clippings for what Frieda actually said

success.text: Under three layers of yellowed tape you find it: one line the Gazette quoted from Frieda before the eviction. "Every face in this town deserves to be seen." Gordon reads it four times and copies it onto an index card for his vanity.
success.art: A teenager peeling back yellowed tape on an old scrapbook clipping, a middle-aged man in reading glasses leaning in close, copying something onto an index card

failure.text: The clipping crumbles at the fold, right where the quote should be. Gordon smooths the pieces flat with one finger. "Well. I suppose I'll have to remember it myself," he says, and slowly, he does.
failure.art: Crumbled pieces of a yellowed newspaper clipping on a desk, a middle-aged man in a cardigan smoothing them flat with one finger, a teenager watching quietly

arc.title: The Song
arc.place: The Glitter Box stage, dress rehearsal, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Glory is in full drag for the first time all week, Big Hallelujah restyled in silver, sequins blazing under the work lights. Frankie has rolled the big gold-framed mirror from the lobby to center stage. Glory has added a number to the revue, "I Am What I Am," and she means to sing it not to the house but to her own reflection. "If I'm going to look at her," she says, "I'm doing it with a key change."
arc.art: A towering drag queen in a blazing sequined gown and a silver bouffant wig standing center stage in an empty theater, facing a huge gold-framed mirror under bare work lights

choices.label: Stand beside the mirror and hold her gaze through the first verse

success.text: She sings to the mirror. Her reflection is Glory, then Gordon, then a teenager with a bold new haircut, all three singing along. At the key change she laughs mid-note, and the mirror is just a mirror again, and it is hers. Afterward she shows you how to meet your own eyes without flinching.
success.art: A drag queen singing to a gold-framed mirror on an empty stage, her reflection layered with a man in a cardigan and a teenager with a bold haircut all singing together, a teenager standing beside the frame

failure.text: Your knees knock and you look away at the key change. Glory doesn't. She finishes alone, eyes locked on her own eyes, steady to the last note. Then she turns to you, breathless. "Mother had it from here, sugar. But thank you for standing up there."
failure.art: A drag queen holding the final note with her eyes locked on her own reflection in a gold-framed mirror, a teenager beside the frame looking down at the stage floor

choices.label: Run the follow spot from the booth with Frankie

success.text: You hit every cue. On the key change the light hits the mirror and throws Glory's reflection twenty feet tall across the back wall of the theater, sequins and all. Over the headset Frankie whispers, "Oh, that's gorgeous. Keep it there."
success.art: A follow spotlight striking a gold-framed mirror on stage and throwing a giant sparkling reflection of a singing drag queen across the theater's back wall, a teenager at the spotlight in the booth

failure.text: You swing the spot too fast and hit Glory square in the eyes. She closes them and sings the rest by feel, chin up, and somehow that's the moment: she isn't singing to the mirror anymore. She's singing to herself.
failure.art: A drag queen singing with her eyes closed and her chin raised in a too-bright spotlight on an empty stage, a gold-framed mirror beside her, a teenager wincing in the booth

choices.label: Throw on a backup-singer wig and join her for the chorus

success.text: You slide in beside her in a borrowed beehive and hit the oohs right on time. Glory catches your eye in the mirror and winks, and for the whole chorus there are two people up there who are not afraid of their reflections.
success.art: A teenager in a borrowed beehive wig singing backup beside a sequined drag queen in front of a gold-framed mirror, both reflected side by side, mid-wink

failure.text: The beehive slides over your eyes and you walk straight into the mirror. It doesn't break. Glory catches you by the collar, laughing so hard she misses a line, and you both end up laughing in the glass together.
failure.art: A teenager with a beehive wig slipped over their eyes bumping into a gold-framed mirror on stage, a drag queen catching them by the collar and laughing, both reflected in the glass

reactions.camp: Oh, honey. You brought camp to a drag queen? Pull up a chair, I'll show you how it's done.
reactions.slasher: A man with a blade and a grudge? Darling, I have survived the Shriners and two fire marshals.
reactions.dream: I have been dreading my dreams since 1961. Wake Mother when it's fabulous.
reactions.cult: Matching outfits, chanting, one leader? Sweetie, that's just a bad chorus line.

name: Frankie Fontaine
bio: Frankie Fontaine came up from Fresno at nineteen with a suitcase, a toolbox and a new name she had picked out at fourteen, and Glory Hallelujah handed her a headset the same night. Five years later she runs the Glitter Box: the fly system, the projector, the fog machine, the fuse box that should have been condemned in 1974. On Saturdays she hosts the midnight double feature as Frankie Fright, in a lab coat and a beehive, heckling the screen. She can rig anything from a pulley and gaffer tape. She is sarcastic, organized to the minute, and terrible at resting; her flaw is that she carries everyone's problems and forgets to set them down, and she would rather rewire a building than say she is tired.

perk.name: Safety Line
perk.text: Frankie rigs a harness for everything: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp, freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil stuck through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top, black work pants with a tool belt of gaffer tape, pliers and a flashlight, scuffed combat boots, perched on a catwalk high above a theatre stage, one hand gripping a rope line and the other holding up a glowing flashlight, the headset mic at her lips, a projector beam cutting through fog below her

neutral.line: Places in five. And somebody find me the fog juice.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp, freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil stuck through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top, black work pants with a tool belt of gaffer tape, pliers and a flashlight, scuffed combat boots, clipboard in hand, headset on, glancing up at the theatre rigging

happy.line: Cue's clean, lights are hot, nobody's on fire. Perfect night.
happy.art: Portrait of a 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp, freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil stuck through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top, black work pants with a tool belt of gaffer tape, pliers and a flashlight, scuffed combat boots, grinning and leaning back against a lighting board covered in glowing sliders

scared.line: That's not one of my cues. I didn't rig that.
scared.art: Portrait of a 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp, freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil stuck through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top, black work pants with a tool belt of gaffer tape, pliers and a flashlight, scuffed combat boots, frozen with the flashlight raised, its beam shaking, pressing her headset to one ear

angry.line: Get off my stage. Get OFF my stage.
angry.art: Portrait of a 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp, freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil stuck through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top, black work pants with a tool belt of gaffer tape, pliers and a flashlight, scuffed combat boots, pointing a wrench like a sword, headset mic bent toward her mouth

sad.line: I built this whole place into a home. Sometimes I forget to live in it.
sad.art: Portrait of a 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp, freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil stuck through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top, black work pants with a tool belt of gaffer tape, pliers and a flashlight, scuffed combat boots, sitting alone in an empty theatre seat with her headset around her neck, a single ghost light on stage

determined.line: Standby lights. Standby sound. Standby kicking its butt. Go.
determined.art: Portrait of a 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp, freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil stuck through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top, black work pants with a tool belt of gaffer tape, pliers and a flashlight, scuffed combat boots, hand poised over a big switch on the lighting board, eyes narrowed, mic at her lips

meet.title: The Extra Frame
meet.place: The projection booth, the Glitter Box Playhouse
meet.text: The projection booth is a hot little box full of film cans and fuses. A woman in a headset is halfway up a ladder rewiring the projector lamp, a pencil in her teeth. "Don't touch anything," Frankie Fontaine says around it. "Last Saturday, in the middle of the second feature, somebody spliced a frame into my reel. One frame. Everybody in the house screamed and nobody could say why." She points with her pliers at a reel on the rewind bench.
meet.art: A 24-year-old Portuguese American trans woman with light olive skin and a sharp freckled nose, long dark curls in a high side ponytail with a pencil through it, a black headset with a boom mic, a cropped black stage-crew jacket over a cyan tank top and a tool belt of gaffer tape and pliers, halfway up a ladder rewiring the lamp of a big film projector in a hot cramped booth full of film cans, a reel resting on a rewind bench in a pool of lamp light below, a teenager holding the ladder, medium shot

choices.label: Hold the ladder and pass her the right tools

success.text: Wire strippers, needle-nose, the blue tape, not the black. You're one step ahead every time. Frankie climbs down and looks at you like you're a new piece of equipment she didn't know she needed. "Okay. You can be on my crew. You're the only person who's ever handed me the right pliers."
success.art: A woman in a stage headset climbing down a ladder and taking a pair of pliers from a teenager in a cluttered projection booth

failure.text: You hand her the wrong wire. There is a pop, a shower of sparks, and every light in the Glitter Box goes out. In the dark, Frankie sighs. "Tomorrow I'm teaching you color codes. Bring a notebook."
failure.art: A dark projection booth lit only by a falling shower of sparks, a woman on a ladder silhouetted against the flash

choices.label: Search the reel for the spliced-in frame

success.text: You find it under the loupe: a single hand-painted frame of the Heartstone, glowing, with a crowd of tiny people around it all looking up. Frankie leans in close. "That's the roundabout on Crystal Street. Somebody wants us to see that." She hands you a spare headset. "Welcome to the crew."
success.art: A teenager peering through a magnifying loupe at a strip of film held up to a lamp, one tiny picture glowing purple with a tiny painted geode

failure.text: You hold the frame up to the lamp and it starts to bubble and burn, the way film does when a projector jams. For one second, in the browning celluloid, you see your own face. Frankie pulls it away. "Okay, enough for today. Tomorrow."
failure.art: A strip of film curling and burning in front of a hot lamp, a teenager's face briefly visible in the melting celluloid

choices.label: Climb to the catwalk and free the stuck sandbag

success.text: You shimmy out onto the catwalk, wrestle the jammed counterweight free and lower it hand over hand. Frankie whistles through the headset. "That's been stuck since Easter. Anybody who'll climb my catwalk is on my team."
success.art: A teenager balanced on a narrow theatre catwalk hauling on a rope line, a sandbag swinging below, a woman in a headset cheering from the stage

failure.text: The sandbag slips and drops, missing Glory by a single sequin. Glory does not scream. Glory hits a high C that cracks a mirror. Frankie gets you down safely and very firmly out. "You're banned until tomorrow. Then you're trained."
failure.art: A heavy sandbag thudding onto a stage inches from a startled drag queen in sequins, a teenager clinging to the catwalk above

arc.title: The Flying Skeleton
arc.place: The projection booth, the Glitter Box Playhouse, 2 p.m.
arc.text: Above the rewind bench, Frankie has pinned a letter from her little sister Gabi, fifteen, in Fresno: the only one in the family who writes to "Frankie." Gabi is taking the bus up Thursday for her very first visit. Frankie is building her a surprise, a plastic skeleton that flies over the seats on a wire during the Frankie Fright intro, and from the look of her she has not slept. "It has to be perfect," she says. "She's never seen me be me in front of people."
arc.art: A young woman in a headset and a lab coat on a ladder in a cramped projection booth rigging a plastic skeleton to a long wire, a handwritten letter pinned above a film rewind bench, a teenager holding the ladder

choices.label: Help her test-fly the skeleton over the empty seats

success.text: You check the pulleys and the counterweight, and the skeleton zips the length of the house and lands in seat B4 with what looks exactly like a curtsy. Frankie laughs out loud, the first time all day. "Okay. Okay! Gabi's going to lose her mind."
success.art: A plastic skeleton gliding on a wire over rows of empty red theater seats and landing neatly in one of them, a young woman in a headset laughing from the booth window beside a teenager

failure.text: The skeleton swings wide and clobbers a wall sconce. Frankie dives and catches it before it hits the floor. "Fine. It's fine! Everything is fine." Her eye is twitching. Everything is clearly not fine.
failure.art: A young woman in a headset diving to catch a tangled plastic skeleton beside a swinging wall sconce in a theater aisle, a teenager wincing nearby

choices.label: Make her sit down and eat something first

success.text: She protests twice, then eats half a cold burrito from the green-room fridge sitting on an apple box. With her mouth full, she tells you Gabi draws comics, mostly about a superhero who is suspiciously tall and fixes things. "I think it's me," Frankie says, and goes pink.
success.art: A young woman in a headset sitting on a wooden apple box eating half a burrito in a cluttered projection booth, smiling shyly as she talks, a teenager sitting across from her

failure.text: She agrees to eat, technically, by holding the burrito in her teeth while she rewires a fuse. You give up and hold the flashlight. She mumbles "thanks" around the tortilla, which is something.
failure.art: A young woman in a headset rewiring a fuse panel with a burrito clamped in her teeth, a teenager holding a flashlight for her with a resigned expression

choices.label: Rehearse the Frankie Fright intro with her, playing the heckler

success.text: You heckle from row three and Frankie Fright eats you alive, beehive and lab coat and all. She's quick, mean in the best way, and glowing by the end. "I forgot I like this part," she says. "The part where I'm not fixing anything."
success.art: A young woman in a lab coat and towering beehive wig pointing dramatically from a small stage at a teenager heckling from an empty theater's third row

failure.text: Your heckle is so weak that Frankie breaks character to give you notes, then notes on her own lines, then on the lighting, and then she's back up the ladder. The rehearsal never resumes, but now you know what she does when she's nervous.
failure.art: A young woman in a lab coat climbing back up a ladder mid-rehearsal with a clipboard, a teenager left alone in the third row of an empty theater

arc.title: She Never Went Home
arc.place: The Glitter Box fuse room, 9 a.m.
arc.text: Frankie is still in yesterday's clothes. The fuse box blew at three in the morning, the print for the second feature arrived missing its last reel, and Gabi's bus is two days out. She's trying to fix all of it at once, alone. On the workbench is Gabi's newest letter, and one line is underlined twice in Frankie's pencil: Mom asked if you're still doing this. "If Gabi sees this place falling apart," Frankie says, "that's what goes home with her."
arc.art: An exhausted young woman in a headset and rumpled clothes standing before an open fuse box with scorched fuses in a cramped theater basement, film cans stacked on a workbench beside an open letter, a teenager in the doorway

choices.label: Take over the phone hunt for the missing reel so she can nap

success.text: Three film exchanges and one very patient operator later, you find the reel in Sacramento, riding up on the afternoon bus. Frankie wakes after an hour on the costume pile and stares at your notes. "You did my job." "You let me," you say, and she doesn't argue.
success.art: A teenager on an old wall telephone scribbling notes in a theater office, a young woman asleep on a pile of costumes behind them with her headset slipping off

failure.text: Every exchange puts you on hold until closing. When Frankie wakes, she finds you asleep on the phone with the receiver on your chest, and covers you with a costume cape. She is laughing when you open your eyes. "Look at us. Two of a kind."
failure.art: A young woman draping a glittery costume cape over a teenager asleep in a chair with a telephone receiver on their chest, smiling tiredly in a cluttered theater office

choices.label: Tell her she's allowed to be tired

success.text: She sits down on an apple box all at once, like her strings were cut. She admits it: she's scared Gabi will see a mess and decide Mom was right. You tell her Gabi isn't coming to see the fuses. She's coming to see her sister. Frankie laughs, wipes her eyes on her headset cord, and nods.
success.art: A tired young woman sitting slumped on a wooden apple box beside an open fuse panel, wiping her eyes and laughing, a teenager crouched beside her

failure.text: "I'm not tired," she snaps, and sits down in the middle of the sentence. Neither of you says anything for a while. Then she hands you a fuse to hold, which in Frankie's language means stay.
failure.art: A young woman in a headset sitting abruptly on the floor of a theater basement holding out a fuse to a teenager, both silent, film cans stacked around them

choices.label: Quietly call the crew in to help without asking her

success.text: Glory arrives with coffee, Toby with gaffer tape, three neighbors with a toolbox and a casserole. Frankie is furious for exactly ten seconds. Then she cries a little into her headset and starts handing out assignments, because of course she does.
success.art: A theater basement filling with friends carrying coffee, tape rolls and a casserole dish, a young woman in a headset laughing through tears while handing out a clipboard

failure.text: The crew arrives just as Frankie gets the lights back on herself, and she feels managed. "I don't need a rescue," she says, stiff. But when everyone turns to leave, she clears her throat. "Stay anyway. There's coffee."
failure.art: A young woman in a headset standing stiffly under freshly restored lights in a theater basement as friends with coffee cups pause in the doorway

arc.title: House Lights
arc.place: The Glitter Box, the Halloween-week preview matinee, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Gabi is here: fifteen, braces, in a homemade Frankie Fright lab coat, and she runs down the aisle and hugs her sister so hard Frankie's headset flies off. Glory has decreed that the crew runs the matinee today and Frankie sits in row three like a civilian. Frankie keeps reaching for a headset that isn't there. "I'm fine," she tells you. "I'm totally fine. Who's on the fly rail?"
arc.art: A teenage girl in a homemade lab coat hugging a tall young woman in a theater aisle, a headset flying off the woman's head, rows of red seats and a waiting stage behind them

choices.label: Take her headset and run the booth yourself

success.text: You call every cue clean. The skeleton flies, lands in B4, curtsies. In row three Gabi shrieks and Frankie shrieks with her, both of them laughing like kids. Afterward Frankie hands you a headset with your name on gaffer tape, and the afternoon's worth of rigging she taught you sticks.
success.art: A plastic skeleton swooping over a delighted matinee crowd as two sisters in the third row shriek with laughter, a teenager in a headset at the booth window calling cues

failure.text: You miss the skeleton cue and it drops early into the aisle with a clatter. Frankie half rises. Gabi pulls her back down by the sleeve: "Leave it. It's funnier." Frankie sits. She stays sitting. It's the bravest thing you've ever seen her do.
failure.art: A plastic skeleton sprawled in a theater aisle while a teenage girl in a lab coat tugs her tall sister back into her seat, both laughing, a teenager wincing in the booth window

choices.label: Sit on her other side and keep her in the seat

success.text: Every time her hand drifts toward a phantom headset, you pass her the popcorn instead. By the second reel she forgets to reach. When the house lights come up, Gabi stands on her seat and announces to the whole theater, "That's my SISTER. She built all this."
success.art: A teenage girl in a homemade lab coat standing on a theater seat pointing proudly at her tall sister as house lights come up, a teenager beside them holding popcorn

failure.text: A light flickers onstage and Frankie bolts for the booth before you can grab her sleeve. Gabi just follows her up the ladder. You find them later, side by side at the booth window, Frankie explaining every cue and Gabi hanging on each word: Frankie's world, with her sister in it.
failure.art: Two sisters side by side at a projection booth window watching the stage below, the older one in a headset pointing out cues, the younger in a lab coat grinning up at her

choices.label: Bring Gabi up to the booth so Frankie can show her the magic

success.text: Frankie shows Gabi the fly rail, the fog machine, the cue sheet, and lets her pull the lever for the skeleton. It flies perfectly. Gabi whispers, "You made all of this?" and Frankie, for once in her life, just says yes.
success.art: A teenage girl in a lab coat pulling a lever in a projection booth while her tall sister in a headset watches proudly, a plastic skeleton flying over the crowd through the booth window

failure.text: Gabi pulls the wrong lever and the fog machine floods the whole house. The audience cheers like it's on purpose. Frankie stares at the fog, at her sister, at you, and then laughs until she has to sit on the floor. "Okay," she says. "Okay. It doesn't have to be perfect."
failure.art: Thick stage fog billowing over a cheering matinee audience, a young woman in a headset sitting on the projection booth floor laughing helplessly beside her sister and a teenager

reactions.tech: That's not my wiring. Somebody point me at the fuse box and stand back.
reactions.camp: Fog, cue lights, an audience screaming its head off? Honey, that's just Saturday.
reactions.cosmic: Nobody rigged a sky that big. I'd have heard about it. I'd have been asked to fix it.

name: Pearl Washington
role: Porch sentinel and retired Army radio operator
bio: Pearl Washington ran a radio set for the Women's Army Corps in 1944, came home, married Harold, and in 1959 the two of them became one of the first Black families on Crystal Street after a fight with the developer that she still describes in detail. Harold has been gone eight years. Pearl has not missed a sunset on her porch since. She keeps a logbook of every strange thing the Heartstone has ever done, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt across her knees, and a story for every house on the street. She is sharp, funny, proud, and stubborn as a mule; she refuses to see a doctor, talks to Harold out loud, and has never once been wrong about a ghost.

perk.name: Rock Salt and Scripture
perk.text: Pearl has been salting ghosts since Truman: +2 on every roll against paranormal nightmares.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin and deep laugh lines, silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab WAC field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress, pink house slippers, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt, standing tall on her porch steps at dusk with the shotgun braced on her hip, the purple glow of a giant geode in the roundabout lighting her face, ghostly shapes drifting back from a line of white salt at her feet

neutral.line: Sit down, child. Sun's going down, and I've got a story.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin and deep laugh lines, silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab WAC field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress, pink house slippers, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt, rocking in a wicker porch chair with the shotgun across her lap, porch light just coming on

happy.line: Ha! Harold, did you see that? Lord, I wish you'd seen that.
happy.art: Portrait of a 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin and deep laugh lines, silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab WAC field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress, pink house slippers, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt, slapping her knee with a big laugh, glasses sliding down her nose

scared.line: I heard that same knock in 1952. I didn't open the door then, either.
scared.art: Portrait of a 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin and deep laugh lines, silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab WAC field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress, pink house slippers, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt, peering over her glasses into the dark, one hand on the shotgun, the other on her heart

angry.line: Get off my porch before I salt you clean to Sacramento.
angry.art: Portrait of a 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin and deep laugh lines, silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab WAC field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress, pink house slippers, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt, shotgun raised to her shoulder, eyes narrowed behind gold glasses

sad.line: Everybody I served with is a photograph now.
sad.art: Portrait of a 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin and deep laugh lines, silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab WAC field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress, pink house slippers, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt, holding a framed black-and-white photo of young women in uniform beside a radio set

determined.line: Hand me my glasses and my shells. Pearl's on duty.
determined.art: Portrait of a 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin and deep laugh lines, silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab WAC field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress, pink house slippers, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt, thumbing rock-salt shells into the shotgun, jaw set, headwrap tight

meet.title: The Logbook
meet.place: Pearl Washington's porch, Crystal Street
meet.text: Mrs. Washington's porch faces the roundabout and the Heartstone in it like a front-row seat. She is in her rocker with an Army field radio in pieces on a TV tray and a logbook open on her knee, every page dated back to 1959. "Stone's humming early this year," she says without looking up. "Three days early. Sit, if you're going to sit. Help, if you're going to help. Don't stand there like a mailbox."
meet.art: A 71-year-old Black woman with deep brown skin, deep laugh lines and silver hair in a short natural crop under a marigold headwrap, gold wire-rimmed glasses, an olive-drab army field jacket with brass buttons over a floral housedress and pink slippers, rocking on a suburban porch with an old army field radio in pieces on a TV tray and a logbook open on her knee, a huge purple crystal rock glowing on the roundabout beyond, a teenager on the porch step, gold late afternoon light, medium shot

choices.label: Sit on the step and hear her ghost story all the way through

success.text: She tells you about the quarry collapse of 1952, and the singing that came up through the water that night. You don't interrupt once. When she's done she presses a coffee can of rock salt into your hands. "You listen. Most people don't. You come by every evening now, hear?"
success.art: A teenager sitting on porch steps listening to an elderly woman in a rocker, a coffee can of rock salt between them, dusk light turning purple

failure.text: You check your watch twice. She notices both times. "Come back when you've got patience," she says, and closes the logbook. Behind you, the Heartstone pulses once, brighter, as if it was listening too.
failure.art: An elderly woman closing a logbook with a disapproving look, a teenager glancing back at a giant geode glowing brighter in the roundabout

choices.label: Help her put the old field radio back together

success.text: You find the cracked tube and swap in a spare. The set warms up with a hum, and through the static comes a voice on a frequency nobody should be using, counting backward from seven. Pearl writes it down. "Well, soldier, looks like you're on my watch now."
success.art: A vintage Army field radio glowing to life on a TV tray, an elderly woman writing in a logbook, a teenager holding a vacuum tube

failure.text: The radio crackles to life with a child's laughter, far away and underwater. Pearl reaches over and switches it off without a word. "Not today," she says. "Come back tomorrow. I'll have it tuned somewhere friendlier."
failure.art: An elderly woman switching off a crackling vintage radio, her hand trembling slightly, ripples of static drawn in the air

choices.label: Volunteer to walk her salt line around the roundabout

success.text: You pour the line around the Heartstone in one steady circle while the stone hums at your back. You don't look at it. Pearl nods from her porch, the way a sergeant nods. "Steady hands. You'll do. You're with me."
success.art: A teenager pouring a careful circle of white rock salt around a giant glowing purple geode, an elderly woman watching approvingly from her porch

failure.text: A wind comes out of nowhere and blows your salt into the shape of a hand reaching for her house. Pearl sweeps it away with her slipper. "Tomorrow," she says. "And you walk it clockwise."
failure.art: Spilled rock salt on a suburban lawn shaped like a reaching hand, an elderly woman sweeping it away with a pink slipper

arc.title: Harold's Rocker
arc.place: Pearl Washington's porch, sundown
arc.text: There are two rockers on Pearl's porch. Hers, and one with a cup of coffee going cold on the seat, which nobody ever moves. She hands you the logbook before you've even sat down. "Read me last night's entry. My glasses are smudged." You look at her glasses. They are spotless. Across the roundabout, the Heartstone hums the way a refrigerator hums, and Pearl waits with her chin up, daring you to say a word about it.
arc.art: An elderly woman in a marigold headwrap and olive Army field jacket in a wicker porch rocker at sundown, an empty second rocker beside her holding a cup of coffee, a teenager on the porch steps holding an open logbook, a purple geode glowing in the roundabout beyond

choices.label: Read the entry aloud, slow and clear, in her own clipped Army style

success.text: "Oct. 24, 1986. 1900 hours. Stone humming in B-flat. Mrs. Brightwater's lawn too green for October." You read it like a dispatch, and Pearl's mouth twitches. "Harold used to read them to me like that," she says to the empty rocker. "Didn't you, you old fool." Then, to you: "Tomorrow, same time. You've got the voice for it."
success.art: A teenager reading a logbook aloud on porch steps at dusk, an elderly woman in a headwrap smiling toward an empty rocker beside her, porch light just coming on

failure.text: Her handwriting has gotten shaky, and you stumble over a word twice before you realize it says "Harold." You go quiet. Pearl takes the logbook back, gently. "It says I told Harold the stone was early. I tell him everything. Don't make that face, child. Come back tomorrow and read me the weather."
failure.art: An elderly woman taking a logbook back from a teenager on a dusky porch, shaky handwriting on the open page, an empty rocker between them

choices.label: Clean her glasses on your shirt and hand them back without a word

success.text: You polish the spotless lenses and give them back. She puts them on, squints at the page, and sighs. "Fine. The words swim. Have since August. If you tell a soul, I'll salt you." It is the first time anybody on Crystal Street has heard Pearl Washington admit to anything. She lets you read the rest.
success.art: A teenager handing a pair of gold wire-rimmed glasses back to an elderly woman in a marigold headwrap, both of them on a porch at sundown, a logbook open on her knee

failure.text: "I didn't ask you to clean them, I asked you to read." She snatches them back and reads the entry herself, nose to the page, every word a fight. You sit in the silence and feel like a mailbox. When the sun's down she says, without looking at you, "Tomorrow. And you just read."
failure.art: An elderly woman in a headwrap holding a logbook close to her nose to read on a dim porch, a teenager sitting awkwardly on the step below

choices.label: Move the coffee cup and sit in the second rocker so you can read beside her

success.text: Pearl goes very still. Then she laughs, a real one. "Harold would've liked your nerve. He sat in my mama's chair the first time he came courting and she never forgave him." She tells you the whole story, the dance hall in Oakland, the radio set, the fight with the developer, and forgets all about the glasses.
success.art: A teenager sitting in a wicker rocker holding a coffee cup on a porch at sunset, an elderly woman in an Army field jacket laughing beside them, a purple glow on the lawn

failure.text: "That's Harold's." Not angry. Just tired. You put the cup back exactly where it was, ring and all, and sit on the step. Pearl watches the stone for a long minute. "Eight years and I still pour it," she says. "Come back tomorrow. I'll pour you one of your own."
failure.art: A teenager carefully setting a coffee cup back onto an empty wicker rocker, an elderly woman in a headwrap watching a glowing geode across the street at dusk

arc.title: Sat Down Hard
arc.place: The porch steps, Crystal Street, late afternoon
arc.text: You come up the walk and find Pearl sitting on her own porch steps instead of her rocker, a coffee can of rock salt tipped over beside her and a white line spilled down the path like a broken sentence. "Got a little dizzy," she says. "Sat down hard. Nothing to it." Her hand is shaking on the railing. "And don't you dare call anybody. The minute somebody calls somebody, a nephew from Sacramento shows up with a moving van and a brochure."
arc.art: An elderly woman in a marigold headwrap sitting on porch steps clutching the railing, a tipped coffee can spilling a line of white rock salt down the front walk, a teenager hurrying up the path in late afternoon light

choices.label: Run next door for Dr. Haddad, promise or no promise

success.text: Dr. Haddad jogs over in his clinic smock with a blood pressure cuff he uses on Great Danes. "I am not a beagle, Amir." "No, Pearl, a beagle would hold still." Her pressure is high, not an emergency, but high. She glares at you the whole time, and then, when he's gone, mutters, "Thank you. Don't get used to it."
success.art: A veterinarian in a clinic smock checking an elderly woman's blood pressure on her porch with a large cuff, the woman glaring at a teenager standing nearby with arms folded

failure.text: By the time you're back with Dr. Haddad she is up in her rocker, shotgun across her knees, fit as a fiddle and furious. "False alarm, Amir." He gives you a look that says he'll keep an eye on her. Pearl gives you a look that says she'll be keeping one on you. Neither of you is wrong.
failure.art: An elderly woman sitting stiffly upright in a porch rocker with a stern expression, a veterinarian and a teenager standing on the walk below looking at each other

choices.label: Sit beside her, fetch a glass of water, and ask what she's really afraid of

success.text: She drinks the water slowly. "I fought a developer and half this street to sit on this porch. If a doctor says the wrong word, they'll put me somewhere with a nice view of a parking lot, and somebody else will sit here. Somebody who doesn't know what that stone does." She looks at you sideways. "Unless somebody does."
success.art: An elderly woman and a teenager sitting side by side on porch steps, the woman holding a glass of water, both gazing at a glowing purple geode in the roundabout

failure.text: "Afraid? I was in the Army, child." She gets herself up by the railing, inch by inch, and refuses your arm. But she doesn't send you home. The two of you sit through the sunset without a word, and at the end she says, "Same time tomorrow," which from Pearl is a whole speech.
failure.art: An elderly woman pulling herself up a porch railing at sunset while a teenager hovers ready to help, a spilled can of salt on the steps

choices.label: Offer a trade: you'll walk her salt line all week if she gets her pressure checked

success.text: Pearl narrows her eyes like she's buying a used car. "Clockwise." Clockwise. "Every night." Every night. "And you don't tell the nephew." Deal. She spits in her palm, which she says is how they did it in 1944, and you shake on it. "Thursday morning," she says. "The clinic. You drive me. No, you can't drive. You walk me."
success.art: An elderly woman in a headwrap and a teenager shaking hands on a porch, a coffee can of rock salt between them, the sun low over a cul-de-sac

failure.text: "I don't trade my health like baseball cards." She sweeps the spilled salt back into the can with the side of her hand, slow and stubborn. You help. Neither of you says anything about the deal, but you notice she writes CLINIC? in the margin of tonight's logbook page, with a question mark.
failure.art: Two pairs of hands sweeping spilled white rock salt back into a coffee can on porch steps, a logbook open nearby with a penciled note in the margin

arc.title: Relieved of Watch
arc.place: Pearl Washington's porch, Thursday at sundown
arc.text: Pearl is back from the clinic with a paper bag of pills, a new prescription for glasses and a scowl she has clearly been saving. "Blood pressure. They want me to take a pill and stop salting things at my age. I told them I'd take the pill." She sets the logbook in your lap, open to a blank page, and the old field radio on the TV tray between you. "Tonight you stand the watch and I sit. Harold," she tells the empty rocker, "we've got a relief."
arc.art: An elderly woman in a marigold headwrap and Army field jacket in a porch rocker holding a paper pharmacy bag, a teenager beside her with a logbook open on their lap, a vintage field radio on a TV tray, a purple geode glowing in the dusk

choices.label: Write tonight's logbook entry yourself, in her style, while she watches

success.text: "Oct. 30, 1986. 1900 hours. Stone humming in B-flat, then C. Watch relieved. P.W. present and accounted for." Pearl reads it over your shoulder and doesn't correct a single word, which has never happened in the history of the logbook. She taps the page. "That's how you do it. Twenty-seven years of this. Now you know how to read the stone."
success.art: A teenager writing in a weathered logbook on a porch at dusk, an elderly woman in gold glasses leaning over their shoulder with a satisfied smile, an empty rocker with a cup of coffee beside them

failure.text: You write it in your own messy hand and spell Heartstone two different ways. Pearl laughs until she has to take her glasses off. "Lord. It's terrible. It's perfect. The logbook's been too neat for twenty-seven years." She doesn't fix it. She writes underneath it, in her shaky hand: Relieved by a friend.
failure.art: An elderly woman laughing with her glasses in her hand on a porch, a logbook page with two different handwritings, a teenager grinning sheepishly

choices.label: Key the old field radio and give the sign-off she taught you, out to the dark

success.text: You key the handset. "Crystal Street watch, relieved and standing by. Over." Static. Then, faint and warm under the hiss, a man's laugh you have never heard and somehow know. Pearl closes her eyes. "That's his laugh. He always did like a proper sign-off." She takes the pill with a sip of Harold's coffee and smiles at the dark.
success.art: A teenager holding a vintage radio handset on a dusky porch, an elderly woman beside them with eyes closed and a peaceful smile, faint glowing static curling up from the radio

failure.text: You fumble the call sign and the radio squeals feedback across the cul-de-sac; every porch light on the street clicks on at once. Pearl laughs so hard she has to hold her side. "Harold would've hollered for a week." She takes the handset and says it right, then hands it back. "Try tomorrow. You've got all the tomorrows you want."
failure.art: Porch lights clicking on all around a suburban cul-de-sac at dusk, an elderly woman laughing on her porch beside a teenager holding a squealing radio handset

choices.label: Turn to the empty rocker and promise Harold, out loud, you'll mind her

success.text: "Mr. Washington, I'll walk her salt line, read her the entries and make her take the pill." Pearl looks at you for a long time. Then she pours a second cup of coffee and sets it in front of you. "He says all right. He says you'll do." It is the best thing anyone on Crystal Street has ever said to you.
success.art: A teenager speaking toward an empty wicker rocker on a porch, an elderly woman in a headwrap pouring a second cup of coffee and handing it to them, sunset glowing

failure.text: You get halfway through the promise and your voice cracks. Pearl reaches over and pats your knee. "He heard you, child. He was always a good listener, which is more than I can say for the living." She takes the pill, makes a face, and puts the logbook back in your hands. "Keep it overnight. I trust you."
failure.art: An elderly woman patting a teenager's knee on a porch at dusk, the teenager holding a logbook to their chest, an empty rocker beside them

reactions.paranormal: Ghosts? I've been salting ghosts since Truman. Hand me my shells and my reading glasses.
reactions.cosmic: That stone's been humming since '59. Whatever's under it, it's older than the developer and twice as rude.
reactions.tech: Back in my day a radio talked when you told it to. Now everything with a plug thinks it's the Lord.
reactions.slasher: A grown man with a knife chasing children? He hasn't met a seventy-one-year-old with a porch and rock salt.

name: Bea Lindqvist
bio: Bea Lindqvist skipped second and fourth grade, won the county science fair with a ghost detector built out of a Speak and Learn and a toaster, and is currently on Volume 4 of her notebook, MONSTER FACTS. Her parents are both dentists who are very busy; her teenage brothers pretend she does not exist. She lives next door, runs a treehouse lab with a periscope and a rope ladder she controls, and talks to everyone on channel nine. Bea is brilliant, bossy, fearless in the way only an eleven-year-old can be, and absolutely not going home. Her flaw is that she would rather be wrong alone than right with help, and she gets very small and quiet when someone calls her cute.

perk.name: Monster Facts Vol. 4
perk.text: Bea has cross-referenced everything: the case board shows your odds of finding each clue.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of an 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck, corduroy overalls with a walkie-talkie clipped to the bib, rainbow-striped knee socks, red rubber boots, a battered composition notebook covered in stickers, standing on a treehouse platform with one boot on the railing, walkie-talkie raised like a sword, notebook clutched to her chest, a homemade antenna sparking above her and a moonlit cul-de-sac below

neutral.line: Statistically, monsters prefer cul-de-sacs. Write that down.
neutral.art: Portrait of an 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck, corduroy overalls with a walkie-talkie clipped to the bib, rainbow-striped knee socks, red rubber boots, a battered composition notebook covered in stickers, pushing her red glasses up her nose with one finger, notebook open

happy.line: I KNEW IT. I knew it! Page forty-two was right!
happy.art: Portrait of an 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck, corduroy overalls with a walkie-talkie clipped to the bib, rainbow-striped knee socks, red rubber boots, a battered composition notebook covered in stickers, jumping in the air with the notebook held overhead, braids flying

scared.line: I'm not scared. I'm collecting data with my eyes closed.
scared.art: Portrait of an 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck, corduroy overalls with a walkie-talkie clipped to the bib, rainbow-striped knee socks, red rubber boots, a battered composition notebook covered in stickers, eyes squeezed shut behind her glasses, walkie-talkie held to her mouth

angry.line: I am not too little. You are too slow.
angry.art: Portrait of an 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck, corduroy overalls with a walkie-talkie clipped to the bib, rainbow-striped knee socks, red rubber boots, a battered composition notebook covered in stickers, hands on her hips, glaring up, cheeks pink

sad.line: Nobody ever reads my notebook. They just say it's cute.
sad.art: Portrait of an 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck, corduroy overalls with a walkie-talkie clipped to the bib, rainbow-striped knee socks, red rubber boots, a battered composition notebook covered in stickers, sitting in the treehouse doorway hugging her knees, notebook closed in her lap

determined.line: Walkie on channel nine. Over. Let's go hunting. Over.
determined.art: Portrait of an 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck, corduroy overalls with a walkie-talkie clipped to the bib, rainbow-striped knee socks, red rubber boots, a battered composition notebook covered in stickers, clicking the walkie-talkie, flashlight in the other hand, chin up

meet.title: The Treehouse Lab
meet.place: The Lindqvists' backyard treehouse, Crystal Street
meet.text: The treehouse next door has a periscope, a NO ADULTS sign and a rope ladder that is currently pulled up. A walkie-talkie dangles on a string in front of your face. It crackles. "State your name and your business. Over." Above you, a small girl in giant red glasses is aiming a homemade meter made from a colander at the Heartstone. "Also, I'm conducting science, so be quick. Over."
meet.art: An 11-year-old Swedish American girl with pale freckled skin and a gap in her front teeth, white-blonde hair in two lopsided braids, huge round red glasses, a yellow rain slicker over a blue turtleneck and corduroy overalls, leaning out of a backyard treehouse with a periscope and aiming a homemade meter built from a kitchen colander toward a glowing purple crystal rock beyond the fence, a walkie-talkie dangling on a string toward a teenager on the grass below, bright afternoon light, low angle shot

choices.label: Take her monster-facts entrance exam

success.text: "What do you put across a doorway to stop a ghost?" Salt. "What do vampires count?" Spilled seeds. "Wrong, they count anything, but I'll allow it." The ladder drops. She clips a walkie-talkie to your belt. "Channel nine. You're in. Over."
success.art: A rope ladder dropping from a treehouse, a small girl in red glasses holding out a walkie-talkie to a teenager climbing up

failure.text: You say vampires hate garlic bread. "WRONG," she announces, and the walkie goes silent. A paper airplane floats down with a study guide drawn on it in crayon. "Retake tomorrow. Over and out."
failure.art: A paper airplane covered in crayon diagrams of monsters floating down from a treehouse to a teenager below

choices.label: Climb up and help calibrate her Heartstone meter

success.text: You realize the colander is picking up the radio tower, adjust it, and the needle swings straight at the Heartstone and pins. Bea gasps. "It gets stronger at dusk. I've been wrong for a week and you fixed it in a minute. You're my lab partner now. Don't let it go to your head."
success.art: A teenager and a small girl in red glasses inside a treehouse lab, a homemade meter's needle pinned toward a glowing geode outside the window

failure.text: The meter makes a noise like a cat and explodes into a confetti of aluminum foil. Mrs. Lindqvist calls Bea in for lunch. Bea, covered in foil, does not go. "Tomorrow," she tells you darkly. "Bring better wire."
failure.art: A small girl in red glasses covered in shreds of aluminum foil in a treehouse, a smoking colander contraption, a mother calling from the back porch

choices.label: Promise she can come on every stakeout

success.text: She studies your face like a microscope slide. Then she spits in her palm and holds it out. You shake. "Binding contract," Bea says. "Also I'm in charge of the notebook. Over."
success.art: A small girl in red glasses solemnly shaking a teenager's hand from a treehouse doorway, a notebook tucked under her arm

failure.text: "You're just humoring me. Everybody humors me." The walkie clicks off. The periscope swivels away from you. You will have to prove it tomorrow.
failure.art: A treehouse periscope swiveling away from a teenager standing alone in a backyard, a silent walkie-talkie on a string

arc.title: The Symposium
arc.place: The Lindqvist treehouse lab, after school
arc.text: Bea has hung a bedsheet across the treehouse for a screen and borrowed an overhead projector from the school without, technically, asking. A hand-lettered banner says FIRST ANNUAL LINDQVIST MONSTER SYMPOSIUM, THURSDAY 7 P.M. "I mailed invitations to my parents and my brothers," she says. "Real stamps. To our own house. So they have to open them." She hands you a stack of transparencies covered in diagrams of the Heartstone. "You're my assistant. Do not touch the projector, it gets hot and I'm not allowed to get burned again."
arc.art: A cramped backyard treehouse lab with a bedsheet screen and an old overhead projector, a small blonde girl in big red glasses and a yellow slicker holding up hand-drawn transparencies of a glowing geode, a hand-lettered symposium banner, a teenager crouched under the low roof

choices.label: Go through her transparencies slide by slide and check the math

success.text: Her math is perfect. You find exactly one typo, a missing decimal on the hum frequency, and point at it. Bea looks at the slide, then at you, for a long time. "Nobody has ever found a mistake in my work before," she says, sounding thrilled. She writes your name on the credits slide, in smaller letters than hers, but there.
success.art: A teenager and a small girl in red glasses leaning over a transparency on a glowing overhead projector, the girl pointing at a circled number, sheets of diagrams scattered across the treehouse floor

failure.text: You flag a mistake that turns out not to be a mistake. Bea explains why, at length, with a pointer made from a car antenna. It takes forty minutes. At the end she says, "That was a good question, actually," in the tone of a professor, and makes you take notes for tomorrow.
failure.art: A small girl in red glasses lecturing with a car-antenna pointer in front of a bedsheet screen, a teenager sitting cross-legged taking notes in a treehouse

choices.label: Be her pretend audience and ask the questions grown-ups will ask

success.text: You put on her dad's spare reading glasses and ask, in a deep dentist voice, "And have you flossed today, young lady?" Bea laughs so hard she falls into the beanbag, then answers every follow-up you throw at her like she's on a game show. "Okay," she says, glasses crooked. "I'm ready. I'm so ready."
success.art: A teenager in oversized reading glasses pretending to be a stern grown-up in a treehouse, a small blonde girl in red glasses laughing in a beanbag chair under a hand-lettered banner

failure.text: You ask the first grown-up question that comes to mind: "Isn't this a little advanced for someone your age?" Bea's face does something small and closed. "That's what they'll say," she whispers. You take it back. She rehearses the rest anyway, quieter, and asks you to come back tomorrow with better questions.
failure.art: A small girl in red glasses hugging a stack of transparencies in a treehouse doorway, looking down, a teenager sitting nearby looking apologetic

arc.title: Margin of Error
arc.place: The treehouse lab, a rainy afternoon
arc.text: The rope ladder is down, which is never a good sign. Inside, Bea is sitting in a drift of crumpled graph paper with her meter in pieces. "The readings don't add up. If they don't add up, the whole symposium is wrong, and if it's wrong, they'll just say it was cute." Her brother Nils yelled up through the window this morning that her treehouse was "adorable." She hasn't said a word into channel nine since. "Don't help," she says. "If you help, it doesn't count."
arc.art: A small blonde girl in a yellow slicker and red glasses sitting among crumpled graph paper in a rainy treehouse, a homemade meter taken apart beside her, rain streaming down the window, a teenager poking their head up through the floor hatch

choices.label: Tell her about famous scientists who worked in pairs, and ask to be a partner, not a helper

success.text: You tell her about the Curies, and about Watson and Crick, and about Rosalind Franklin, who didn't get the credit she earned. That last one makes Bea sit up straight. "So I should share the work but make sure my name's on it." Exactly. She hands you a screwdriver. "Co-author. Second author. Don't push it."
success.art: A small girl in red glasses handing a screwdriver to a teenager inside a rainy treehouse lab, a disassembled homemade meter between them on a pile of graph paper

failure.text: You get your scientists mixed up and say Marie Curie invented the light bulb. Bea corrects you with her whole chest, which is the most like herself she's been all day. She doesn't let you help, exactly. But she lets you hold the flashlight while she rebuilds the meter, and that's a start.
failure.art: A teenager holding a flashlight over a small girl in red glasses reassembling a homemade meter by flashlight in a dim treehouse, rain on the roof

choices.label: Quietly re-run her readings yourself and find where the numbers go wrong

success.text: It isn't her math. Every reading taken after four o'clock is off by the same amount, and four o'clock is when Nils gets home and turns on his CB radio. "Interference," Bea breathes. "My data was right. My brother was wrong." She is so happy she forgets to be mad that you helped.
success.art: A teenager and a small girl in red glasses looking at a sheet of graph paper with a line of readings circled, a neighboring bedroom window visible across the yard with a big CB radio antenna on the sill

failure.text: You re-run the numbers and get a third answer that matches neither of hers. Bea stares at your page. "Now we're both wrong. Together." She says it like a discovery. You spend the rest of the afternoon wrong together, eating graham crackers, and somehow it is the best day she's had all week.
failure.art: A small girl in red glasses and a teenager sitting shoulder to shoulder in a treehouse eating graham crackers, two sheets of graph paper with different scribbled answers between them

choices.label: Climb down and tell her brother Nils exactly what he called her work

success.text: Nils is fifteen and very startled. "I didn't mean adorable like baby," he mumbles. "I meant, like, it's cool she built it. I read her notebook. Volume three. It's kind of awesome." He looks at his shoes. Up in the treehouse window, a pair of red glasses has gone perfectly round.
success.art: A teenager talking to a lanky embarrassed teenage boy on a back porch in the rain, a small girl in red glasses peering down from a treehouse window above them

failure.text: Nils just shrugs and turns his music up. When you climb back up, Bea is watching through the periscope. "You didn't have to do that," she says. Then, softer: "Nobody ever does that." She lets you sit with her while the rain comes down, which is its own kind of answer.
failure.art: A small girl in red glasses looking through a treehouse periscope in the rain, a teenager climbing back up the rope ladder, a back porch door closing below

arc.title: Questions from the Floor
arc.place: The treehouse lab, Thursday at 7 p.m.
arc.text: The treehouse holds six people if nobody breathes. At five to seven it holds you, Bea, a plate of cookies, and nine empty folding chairs she arranged on the lawn below in case of overflow. At two minutes to seven the back door opens. Both Dr. Lindqvists come out with their invitations, still in their dental smocks, and behind them, slouching, both brothers. Bea grips the projector stand. "They came," she whispers. "Oh no. They came."
arc.art: A backyard treehouse lit by an overhead projector beam at dusk, a small girl in red glasses gripping the projector stand, two parents in dental smocks and two teenage boys crossing the lawn toward a row of folding chairs holding envelopes

choices.label: Run the projector and keep the slides in perfect order so she can just talk

success.text: You swap every transparency on cue. Bea talks for twenty minutes without a single um, and when her dad asks a hard question about frequency, she answers it and then corrects his units. The applause shakes a pine cone off the roof. On the last slide, under her name, it says: and my lab partner. You learned more science this week than all of last year.
success.art: A small girl in red glasses presenting in front of a glowing bedsheet screen in a treehouse, a teenager at the overhead projector, a family applauding from folding chairs on the lawn below

failure.text: You put slide six in upside down and the Heartstone diagram projects onto Mrs. Lindqvist's smock. Everyone freezes. Then Bea says, "As you can see, the frequency affects everything it touches," and her mom laughs, a real one. It isn't perfect. It's better. They stay for every question.
failure.art: An upside-down diagram of a geode projected onto a woman's dental smock in a backyard at dusk, a small girl in red glasses grinning, family members laughing on folding chairs

choices.label: Sit on the lawn with her family and ask the first question so they'll follow

success.text: You raise your hand. Bea calls on you like a professor. Then Nils raises his hand, then the other brother, then her mom, and suddenly it is a real symposium with real questions, and Bea is answering them with her chin up and her braids flying. Afterward her dad says, "We should have been reading this notebook all along." She does not get small once.
success.art: A family seated on folding chairs on a backyard lawn with hands raised, a small girl in red glasses pointing from a treehouse platform like a professor, a teenager among the audience

failure.text: Your question comes out as "How did you get so smart?" and you hear it land wrong as soon as it's out. Bea starts to shrink. Then Nils says, loud, "Because she does the work, obviously," and she stands up straight again. The rest of the night belongs to her. You just get to watch.
failure.art: A teenage boy on a folding chair speaking up with a pointed finger, a small girl in red glasses straightening on a treehouse platform, a family gathered on a dusky lawn

reactions.creature: Creatures follow food chains. Find out what it eats and we win. Also, please let it not eat eleven-year-olds.
reactions.cosmic: The Heartstone is a crystal oscillator the size of a station wagon. I have charts. Nobody reads my charts.
reactions.tech: If it plugs in, it has a frequency. If it has a frequency, I can jam it. Over.
reactions.dream: I don't sleep on stakeouts. Sleep is for people who aren't collecting data.

name: Jesse "Moose" Kowalski
bio: Jesse Kowalski is six-foot-five, two hundred sixty pounds, and the reason half the Glimmer Falls varsity squad wears matching crimson scarves: he knits them on the bench between series, a habit his babcia taught him to keep his hands from shaking. He is bi, out to his sister and his best friend, went to homecoming with a girl last year, and has spent this whole fall working up the courage to say hi to a boy in the marching band's drumline. Moose is gentle, goofy, and the first person to step between a smaller kid and trouble. His flaw is that he swallows every conflict until it boils over, can't say no to anyone, and worries about everybody except himself.

perk.name: Big Guy Block
perk.text: Moose plants himself between you and whatever's coming: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks and a gap-toothed grin, a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, gray sweatpants, white high-tops, knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf trailing from his jacket pocket, standing like a wall in the center of a foggy football field at night, arms spread wide to shield a small crowd of kids behind him, a long crimson scarf streaming in the wind, stadium lights flaring behind his head

neutral.line: Knit two, purl two. Calms the nerves. Want to try?
neutral.art: Portrait of a huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks and a gap-toothed grin, a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, gray sweatpants, white high-tops, knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf trailing from his jacket pocket, sitting on a locker room bench, knitting needles clicking, a soft half-smile

happy.line: Group hug. That's not a question. Get in here.
happy.art: Portrait of a huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks and a gap-toothed grin, a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, gray sweatpants, white high-tops, knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf trailing from his jacket pocket, arms flung wide in a huge gap-toothed grin, mullet bouncing

scared.line: I'm big, which means I'm a big target. Stay behind me.
scared.art: Portrait of a huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks and a gap-toothed grin, a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, gray sweatpants, white high-tops, knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf trailing from his jacket pocket, eyes wide, holding his knitting needles out like tiny swords, shoulders hunched

angry.line: Nobody. Touches. My friends.
angry.art: Portrait of a huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks and a gap-toothed grin, a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, gray sweatpants, white high-tops, knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf trailing from his jacket pocket, cracking his knuckles, face red, letter jacket straining across his shoulders

sad.line: Coach says I'm too soft. Maybe soft is the point.
sad.art: Portrait of a huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks and a gap-toothed grin, a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, gray sweatpants, white high-tops, knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf trailing from his jacket pocket, sitting alone on gym bleachers with a half-knit scarf pooled in his lap

determined.line: Line up behind me. I'm the wall.
determined.art: Portrait of a huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks and a gap-toothed grin, a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, gray sweatpants, white high-tops, knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf trailing from his jacket pocket, in a three-point stance on wet grass, scarf tucked into his jacket, jaw set

meet.title: Between Sets
meet.place: The roller-rink annex, Pump Iron Gym and Aerobics
meet.text: In the corner of Pump Iron, where the weight room spills into the old roller-rink annex, the biggest teenager you have ever seen is spotting a nervous freshman on the bench press with one hand and knitting a crimson scarf with the other. Two seniors in tank tops are snickering at the needles. "Hey Grandma, knit me a cardigan." Moose's ears go red, but he just keeps counting reps out loud, gently, for the freshman.
meet.art: A huge 17-year-old Polish American boy with ruddy cheeks, a gap-toothed grin and a curly sandy-brown mullet, a crimson letter jacket with cream sleeves over a hand-knit cream cable sweater, spotting a skinny freshman on a bench press with one big hand while holding knitting needles and a half-finished crimson scarf in the other, two smirking seniors in tank tops nearby, an old roller rink visible through an archway, a teenager walking over, gym light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Sit down and ask him to teach you to knit

success.text: He lights up like a scoreboard. Knit two, purl two, and by the end of the set you've got four lumpy rows. The seniors drift away, bored. Moose bumps your shoulder with his. "You're a natural. Stick with me, okay? I mean it. I've got your back."
success.art: A huge teenage boy patiently guiding a teenager's hands on knitting needles on a gym bench, crimson yarn trailing between them

failure.text: The yarn knots into something that looks like a spiderweb and then like a spider. Moose laughs his big honking laugh, not at you. "Come back tomorrow. I'll cast on for you first. Everybody's first scarf is a monster."
failure.art: A tangled knot of crimson yarn in a teenager's lap shaped vaguely like a spider, a huge boy laughing kindly beside them

choices.label: Offer to spot him on his own heavy set

success.text: Moose loads the bar to a number you don't want to think about. You hold your breath and your grip, and on the last rep you help him rack it with a clang. He sits up beaming. "Nobody ever offers to spot me. They figure I don't need it. You're my guy now."
success.art: A teenager straining to help rack a heavy barbell over a giant boy on a bench, both grinning, plates clanging

failure.text: The bar dips toward his chest and he catches it himself, with one arm, gently, so you don't feel bad. "Maybe warm up first tomorrow," he says, rubbing your shoulder. "I'll be here. I'm always here."
failure.art: A giant teenage boy pressing a sagging barbell back up one-handed while a teenager winces above him

choices.label: Tell the seniors to knock it off

success.text: "Hey. His scarves keep your whole team warm. What have you made lately, besides noise?" The seniors mutter and leave. Moose stares at you. Then he wraps the half-finished scarf around your neck. "That's yours when it's done. You and me, okay?"
success.art: A teenager facing down two seniors in a gym, a huge boy behind them looping a half-finished crimson scarf around the teenager's neck
