failure.text: They laugh you off like a mosquito. Moose stands up, all six-foot-five of him, and they leave fast, but you feel about two inches tall. He catches up at the door. "Thanks for trying. Really. Come back tomorrow?"
failure.art: Two seniors backing away from a towering teenage boy, a smaller teenager standing at the gym door looking deflated

arc.title: Black and Gold
arc.place: The bleachers by Pump Iron's roller-rink annex, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Moose is knitting something that is not crimson. It's black with a gold stripe, the marching band's colors, and he hides it under a towel the second he sees you. Through the archway you can hear the drumline rehearsing for Friday's Halloween halftime, and one snare drummer in particular, a skinny kid named Theo Baptiste with a bleached flat-top and enormous headphones, is keeping a rhythm so tight it sounds like a clock. "It's for nobody," Moose says. "It's a, it's for my sister. She likes gold." His ears are the color of his letter jacket.
arc.art: A huge teenage boy with a curly sandy mullet and a crimson letter jacket on gym bleachers hiding black and gold knitting under a towel, a teenager sitting beside him, a marching band drumline rehearsing through an archway beyond, one slender drummer with a bleached flat-top

choices.label: Tell him gently that his sister hates gold, and ask who it's really for

success.text: Moose sags like a parade float with a slow leak. "Theo. Snare drum. He says thanks to the bus driver every single time." He shows you the scarf: there are tiny gold drumsticks knitted into the stripe. "I've said exactly one word to him. It was 'sorry,' because I stepped on his foot." He looks at you with enormous hope. "Help me say a second word."
success.art: A huge teenage boy holding up a black scarf with tiny gold drumsticks knitted into the stripe, blushing deeply, a teenager beside him grinning, a drumline blurred through an archway behind

failure.text: "She LOVES gold," he insists, much too loud, and the drumline stops dead. Theo glances over. Moose drops a needle and both of you dive for it under the bleachers. When you come back up, the drumline has moved on. "Tomorrow," Moose groans. "I'll tell you tomorrow. Probably. Maybe."
failure.art: A huge teenage boy and a teenager crawling under gym bleachers after a dropped knitting needle, a drumline in the background turning to look

choices.label: Pick up a spare set of needles and help him finish the drumstick pattern

success.text: You count stitches while he works, and between the two of you the gold drumsticks come out crisp instead of looking like french fries. Moose holds it up to the light. "It's good. It's really good." He's quiet a second. "If I give him a scarf, that's kind of saying something, right? Like, a big something."
success.art: A huge teenage boy and a teenager knitting side by side on gym bleachers, a black scarf with a crisp gold drumstick pattern stretched between them

failure.text: Your section of drumsticks comes out looking like two hot dogs. Moose laughs his big honking laugh, not at you, and leaves them in. "Nah, it's got character. He'll know a real person made it." Then he goes pale. "He'll know a real person made it."
failure.art: A black knitted scarf with a lumpy gold pattern shaped like hot dogs in a teenager's lap, a huge boy beside them laughing on gym bleachers

choices.label: Drag him to the water fountain right next to the drumline, casually

success.text: Moose drinks for eleven seconds straight. Theo, taking his headphones off, looks up at him. "You're the scarf guy. The football scarves. That's sick, man." Moose says, "Thanks," which is technically his second word. He floats back to the bleachers. "He knows I knit. He said sick. Sick is good, right? Sick is good."
success.art: A huge teenage boy bent over a gym water fountain, a slim drummer with a bleached flat-top and headphones around his neck smiling up at him, a teenager watching from nearby

failure.text: Moose gets to the fountain, sees Theo, panics, and walks straight into the roller-rink annex like he meant to go there all along. You find him sitting on a rental skate bench. "I don't know what happened," he says. "My legs went somewhere without me. Tomorrow. Tomorrow I'll be braver."
failure.art: A huge teenage boy sitting alone on a roller rink rental bench with his head in his hands, rows of skates on the wall, a teenager arriving through the archway

arc.title: The Yes Man
arc.place: The locker room at Pump Iron, after practice
arc.text: Moose has said yes to everything this week. Yes, he'll run the bake sale. Yes, he'll drive Coach's nephew to the dentist. Yes, he'll stay late Thursday for extra film, which is the exact hour the drumline has its last rehearsal before Friday, the hour he was going to give Theo the scarf. He is knitting so fast the needles are smoking. "It's fine," he says. "I can do it all. I always do it all." There's a hole in the scarf where he dropped a stitch and didn't notice.
arc.art: A huge teenage boy on a locker room bench knitting frantically, a hand-written list of chores taped inside his open locker, a black and gold scarf with a hole in it pooled in his lap, a teenager leaning against the lockers

choices.label: Make him practice saying no to you, ten times, until he means it

success.text: "Moose, will you carry my books?" "No." "Will you knit my dog a sweater?" "No. Okay, yes, what's the dog's name? No. No!" By the tenth no he is laughing and pink and standing up straight. He marches out to Coach's office. When he comes back he says, "I said no to film," like a man who has walked on the moon.
success.art: A huge teenage boy in a locker room laughing and holding up a hand in a firm stop gesture, a teenager across from him pretending to beg dramatically

failure.text: He can't do it. Every time you ask him for something, he says yes, then apologizes for saying yes, then offers you a granola bar. On the ninth try he finally says "no" to the granola bar and you both cheer anyway. It's a start. He writes the word NO on his hand in pen for tomorrow.
failure.art: A huge teenage boy in a locker room looking at the word written in ink across his palm, a teenager beside him holding a granola bar, both smiling

choices.label: Take the bake sale off his hands yourself so Thursday is free

success.text: You sweet-talk the booster moms and get the bake sale covered by Sunny's aerobics class, who are delighted. Moose stares at his list with one whole line crossed off. "You did that. For me." He looks at Thursday like it's suddenly a real day. "I can tell Coach I need the hour. I can, right?" You can.
success.art: A teenager handing a crossed-off chore list back to a huge teenage boy in a gym hallway, a table of baked goods being set up by cheerful aerobics students behind them

failure.text: The booster moms rope you into the bake sale AND a car wash. Moose finds out and says yes to helping you with both before you can stop him. You look at each other over a pile of cupcake liners. "We have the same problem," he says, horrified. "Okay. I'm saying no for both of us."
failure.art: A teenager and a huge teenage boy staring at each other over a table piled with cupcake liners and car-wash sponges in a gym lobby

choices.label: Point out the hole in the scarf and make him stop and fix it, slowly

success.text: He stops. He looks at the hole like it's a mirror. "Babcia used to say a dropped stitch means you're knitting for everybody but the scarf." He unravels back to the hole, slow, and picks it up right. Then he puts the needles down and says, very quietly, "I'm going to tell Coach no."
success.art: A huge teenage boy carefully picking up a dropped stitch in a black and gold scarf on a locker room bench, a teenager watching beside him, late light through a high window

failure.text: He unravels too far and loses the whole gold stripe. For a second it looks like he might cry. Instead he takes a deep breath, the kind his babcia taught him, and starts the stripe over. "I'm going to have to skip something to finish this," he says. "Good. Good. I'm going to skip something."
failure.art: A huge teenage boy taking a deep breath with a half-unraveled black scarf and a tangle of gold yarn in his lap, sitting on a locker room bench

arc.title: Second Word
arc.place: Outside the band room by the gym, Thursday at 5 p.m.
arc.text: Moose told Coach no. Coach said, "Huh. Okay," and that was it, and Moose had to sit down for a minute. Now he's outside the band room with the finished scarf folded in a paper bag, rocking on his heels, as the drumline packs up. Theo comes out last, headphones around his neck, and stops when he sees the size of the person blocking the door. Moose looks at you. You look at Moose. "Okay," he whispers. "Second word. Here goes."
arc.art: A huge teenage boy with a curly mullet in a crimson letter jacket holding a paper bag outside a school band room at dusk, a slim drummer with a bleached flat-top and headphones stepping out the door, a teenager hovering nearby

choices.label: Stand close, catch Theo's eye, and give Moose an opening line he can take

success.text: "Theo, Moose made something." Moose holds out the bag. Theo pulls out the scarf, finds the gold drumsticks, and goes very quiet. Then he wraps it around his neck and grins. "Are you asking me to the midnight movie at the Glitter Box tomorrow, or do I have to ask you?" Moose says, "Yes," which is his third word, and the right one. You learned how to make the room easier for somebody braver than they know.
success.art: A slim drummer with a bleached flat-top wrapping a black scarf with gold drumsticks around his neck and grinning up at a huge blushing teenage boy outside a band room, a teenager beaming nearby

failure.text: You open your mouth and say "Moose has a bag," which is not the line. Moose turns crimson and holds out the bag anyway. Theo looks inside, then up. "Did you make this? For me?" Moose nods, unable to speak. Theo puts it on. "Ask me something tomorrow," he says, smiling, "when you've got your voice back."
failure.art: A huge teenage boy holding out a paper bag with both hands, blushing, a slim drummer with a black and gold scarf draped over his shoulders smiling at him outside a band room

choices.label: Squeeze his arm and step back out of sight, so this one is all his

success.text: From around the corner you hear Moose's voice, steady and low, say more words in a row than he's said all fall. Then a laugh that isn't his. When he comes around the corner his face is shining. "He's coming to the game Friday to watch me. I'm going to watch him at halftime. He said I could hold his sticks." He hugs you off the ground.
success.art: A huge teenage boy lifting a laughing teenager off the ground in a hug in a school hallway at dusk, a slim drummer in a black and gold scarf waving from down the hall

failure.text: It goes quiet around the corner for a long time. When Moose comes back his ears are red and the bag is empty. "I just handed it to him and ran," he says. Then, from all the way down the hall, comes Theo's voice: "Hey, scarf guy! It's warm! Thank you!" Moose closes his eyes and smiles.
failure.art: A huge teenage boy leaning against a hallway wall with eyes closed and a soft smile, an empty paper bag in his hand, a teenager beside him, a drummer's silhouette at the far end of the hall

reactions.slasher: Guy with a machete? Cool. Stand behind me. I've been hit by linebackers bigger than his attitude.
reactions.creature: What if it's just scared? Big things get scared too. Trust me. ...But also, run.
reactions.camp: Sequins, smoke machines and a villain with a theme song? I'm knitting us matching capes.
reactions.cult: A bunch of people in robes telling you who to be? Hard pass. I'll knit my own robe, thanks.

name: Priya Raman
bio: Priya Raman is captain of the Glimmer Falls mathletes, a state finalist in two events, and on Friday nights the dungeon master of The Crystal Kingdoms, a homebrew campaign she has run in the library meeting room since seventh grade. Her parents expect pre-med; she wants to write game modules for a living and has three binders of graph-paper dungeons to prove it. This fall her notes have started coming true: the lich she invented, the drowned counselor, the house that eats guests. Priya is precise, competitive, a total rules lawyer and a secret softie for her players. Her flaw is perfectionism, and the fear, which she tells no one, that she imagined all of this into being.

perk.name: DM's Mercy
perk.text: Priya rules that one didn't count: reroll one failed roll each night.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, long black hair in a single braid over one shoulder with a pencil tucked behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white collared blouse, a plaid skirt with black tights and loafers, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, a binder stuffed with graph-paper maps, standing on a library table with her binder thrown open and graph-paper maps swirling around her like a storm, the gold die blazing at her throat, a shadowy dragon made of ink rising from the pages

neutral.line: Roll for initiative. No, really, it helps.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, long black hair in a single braid over one shoulder with a pencil tucked behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white collared blouse, a plaid skirt with black tights and loafers, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, a binder stuffed with graph-paper maps, seated behind a cardboard game screen, pencil poised, glasses catching the lamp light

happy.line: Natural twenty! Do you understand? NATURAL. TWENTY.
happy.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, long black hair in a single braid over one shoulder with a pencil tucked behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white collared blouse, a plaid skirt with black tights and loafers, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, a binder stuffed with graph-paper maps, throwing both arms up, a gold die tumbling in mid-air, braid flying

scared.line: I wrote this. Page sixty. I wrote this and now it's here.
scared.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, long black hair in a single braid over one shoulder with a pencil tucked behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white collared blouse, a plaid skirt with black tights and loafers, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, a binder stuffed with graph-paper maps, clutching her open binder to her chest, a drawn map on it glowing faintly

angry.line: That's not in the rules. You don't get to change the rules.
angry.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, long black hair in a single braid over one shoulder with a pencil tucked behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white collared blouse, a plaid skirt with black tights and loafers, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, a binder stuffed with graph-paper maps, pointing her pencil like a wand, eyes flashing behind gold glasses

sad.line: What if I made all of this happen just by imagining it?
sad.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, long black hair in a single braid over one shoulder with a pencil tucked behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white collared blouse, a plaid skirt with black tights and loafers, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, a binder stuffed with graph-paper maps, slumped over a library table, cheek on a pile of graph paper, the gold die in her fist

determined.line: I know how this dungeon ends. I'm the one who drew the map.
determined.art: Portrait of a 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, long black hair in a single braid over one shoulder with a pencil tucked behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white collared blouse, a plaid skirt with black tights and loafers, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, a binder stuffed with graph-paper maps, unrolling a big hand-drawn map across a table, sleeves pushed up, jaw set

meet.title: Session Zero
meet.place: The meeting room, Glimmer Falls Public Library
meet.text: The library meeting room is set for six players, with character sheets, snacks and a cardboard DM screen. Only one chair is full. Priya Raman sits behind the screen, staring at a map she drew in August: a cul-de-sac, a roundabout, a glowing stone, and in her neat handwriting, HERE THE SLEEPERS LOSE THEIR COLOR. "My players quit," she says. "Everything I wrote for them started happening. You can sit down, I guess. Everyone else is scared of my campaign."
meet.art: A 16-year-old Indian American girl with warm brown skin and thick dark brows, a long black braid over one shoulder with a pencil behind her ear, round gold-rimmed glasses, an oversized purple cardigan over a white blouse and a gold twenty-sided die on a cord around her neck, sitting alone behind a cardboard screen at a library meeting room table set for six with empty chairs and blank character sheets, staring at a hand-drawn map of a cul-de-sac with a glowing stone, a teenager pulling out a chair, warm overhead light, medium shot

choices.label: Roll up a character and play her one-player campaign

success.text: You roll a bard named Sir Vical and seduce a gelatinous cube with a sea shanty. Priya tries to keep a straight face, fails, and laughs so hard she snorts. "That's not in the rules. That's BETTER than the rules." She slides a character sheet over with your name on it. "Party of two. For real."
success.art: A teenager and a girl in a purple cardigan laughing over a tabletop game, dice scattered across a hand-drawn map, a cardboard game screen between them

failure.text: Your bard dies in round one to a ceiling mimic. At the exact moment Priya says the word ceiling, the real ceiling tile above you creaks. You both look up. Priya packs up very fast. "Session's over. Reroll tomorrow."
failure.art: Two teenagers frozen at a game table staring up at a creaking library ceiling tile, dice scattered, a character sheet with a skull drawn on it

choices.label: Compare her dungeon maps against a real town map

success.text: You lay a Glimmer Falls street map over her dungeon. The tunnels line up exactly with the storm drains under Crystal Street. Priya stares. "So I'm not causing it. I'm picking it up. Like a radio." She closes the binder. "I need a co-DM. You're hired."
success.art: A town street map and a hand-drawn dungeon map overlaid on a light table, tunnels aligning with storm drains, two teenagers leaning over them

failure.text: When you lay the maps together, the ink on hers starts to run, crawling across the paper toward the roundabout like it's late for something. Priya snatches it away. "Okay. Tomorrow. I need to think about this. Alone. No, not alone. Tomorrow."
failure.art: Black ink crawling across a hand-drawn map toward a drawn roundabout, a girl snatching the paper off a library table

choices.label: Convince her that her notes are a warning, not a curse

success.text: You tell her about the Heartstone: how it amplifies what people feel. "You didn't make the monsters. You just listen better than anyone else in this town." Priya's eyes are wet behind her glasses. She hands you the gold die. "Hold onto that. You're in my party."
success.art: A girl in a purple cardigan pressing a gold twenty-sided die into a teenager's palm across a game table, both of them smiling

failure.text: She shakes her head. "That's what a DM says to make the players feel better." She closes the screen, and for a second you see her map's roundabout glow through the cardboard. "Come back tomorrow. Maybe I'll believe you then."
failure.art: A girl closing a cardboard game screen, a faint purple glow leaking through it from the map beneath

arc.title: The Hollow Under Crystal Lake
arc.place: The library meeting room, after school
arc.text: Priya has a manila envelope addressed to Wyrm's Hoard Magazine, Open Module Contest, postmark deadline October 31. Inside is a dungeon called The Hollow Under Crystal Lake, forty typed pages, with every map hand-inked. Every page but the last. "I can't write the ending," she says. "Every ending I write is a total party kill. I keep thinking if I write the players winning and it doesn't come true, that's worse. And if I write them losing and THAT comes true..." She taps the gold die at her throat. "So I don't write anything."
arc.art: A library meeting room table covered in hand-inked graph-paper dungeon maps, a teenage girl in a purple cardigan and gold glasses holding a thick manila envelope, a gold twenty-sided die on a cord at her throat, a teenager sitting across from her

choices.label: Roll up a character and playtest her dungeon right now

success.text: You play a paladin with a fear of ducks and talk the lake guardian into a rowing contest. Priya laughs so hard she snorts, then grabs her pencil. "Wait. Wait. The guardian doesn't want to fight. It wants someone to stay and talk." She writes for ten minutes without looking up. It's not the ending yet. It's the first door to one.
success.art: A teenager acting out a character with big gestures at a tabletop game, a girl in a purple cardigan laughing and scribbling notes behind a cardboard game screen, dice rolling across a hand-drawn lake map

failure.text: Your paladin falls into the lake on turn two. Priya automatically starts to describe the drowning, then stops with her mouth open. "I keep doing that," she says. "I keep making the water win." She erases the trap and draws a rope ladder instead. "Come back tomorrow. I'll give you a better lake."
failure.art: A girl in a purple cardigan erasing part of a hand-drawn lake map, a rope ladder sketched in its place, a teenager watching with a toppled game figure in front of them

choices.label: Run the odds on her encounter tables to prove the dungeon is fair

success.text: You work it out on scratch paper: her final room gives a party of four a two percent chance of surviving. Priya stares at the number. "I'm a mathlete. How did I not see that?" Because she wasn't looking. She rebalances the tables right there. "Thirty-eight percent. That's a real fight. That's a fair fight."
success.art: A teenager and a girl in gold glasses bent over sheets of scratch paper covered in probability math, a gold twenty-sided die sitting on a stack of typed pages, library lamps glowing

failure.text: You make an arithmetic error she catches instantly, and she spends twenty minutes explaining conditional probability with a bag of dice. You're lost by minute three. But she's smiling for the first time all day. "Okay," she says, "I really like explaining things. Maybe the ending is someone explaining things."
failure.art: A girl in a purple cardigan pouring a bag of colorful dice across a library table while explaining enthusiastically, a teenager looking cheerfully overwhelmed

choices.label: Tell her to write the ending she would want to come true

success.text: "If your notes really are picking things up, then write the good one. Give the stone something better to hear." Priya goes still. Then she uncaps a fresh pen and writes, at the top of the last page: AND THE PARTY GOES HOME TOGETHER. "That's the ending. Now I have to earn it."
success.art: A teenage girl in gold glasses writing at the top of a blank typed page with a fresh pen, a stack of dungeon maps beside her, a teenager watching across a library table

failure.text: "That's magical thinking," she says, which is fair. "I'm a mathlete. I don't do magical thinking." She shoves the envelope in her bag. But the next morning, when you pass the library, you see her through the window writing furiously, and there's a sticky note on her binder that says WHAT IF THEY WIN?
failure.art: A girl in a purple cardigan seen through a library window writing intently at a table, a sticky note on her binder, early morning light

arc.title: Pre-Med
arc.place: The library reference desk, closing time
arc.text: Priya's binder is on the reference desk with a yellow sticky note in her mother's tidy handwriting: Chem tutor Saturday 9 a.m. Mathletes FIRST. Love, Amma. Her mom found the contest envelope on the kitchen table. "She wasn't mad," Priya says, which is somehow worse. "She just said, 'This is a nice hobby.' A hobby. I've been running a campaign since seventh grade." She's holding the envelope like it's evidence. "Maybe I just don't send it. It's not like anyone makes this for a living."
arc.art: A library reference desk at closing time with a stack of returned books, a teenage girl in a purple cardigan holding a manila envelope, a binder with a yellow sticky note on its cover, a teenager leaning on the counter beside her

choices.label: Dig through the library's magazine stacks for proof that people make games for a living

success.text: In a back issue of Wyrm's Hoard you find a profile: a woman in Wisconsin who writes modules full-time, with a photo of her at a desk covered in graph paper, looking exactly like Priya in twenty years. Priya reads it three times. Then she photocopies it and paperclips it to the envelope. "Exhibit A," she says.
success.art: A teenager holding up an open hobby magazine to a girl in gold glasses in the library stacks, a photo in the magazine of a woman at a desk covered in graph-paper maps

failure.text: You find a dozen issues, but every module credited is by a man with a beard. Priya looks at the bylines and laughs, short and sharp. "Great. Okay. Then somebody has to be first." She doesn't sound convinced. But she puts the envelope back in her bag instead of the trash.
failure.art: A girl in a purple cardigan flipping through a stack of old hobby magazines on a library cart, a teenager beside her, a manila envelope tucked under her arm

choices.label: Help her write down exactly what she wants to say to her mom

success.text: It takes three drafts on the back of a call slip. The final version is short: I'm good at math. I'm good at this. I want you to see me do it. Priya reads it out loud twice and her voice only shakes once. "I'll invite her to my last session. Thursday. She can see the party go home together."
success.art: A girl in gold glasses reading from a small library call slip with a determined expression, crossed-out drafts scattered on the reference desk, a teenager giving an encouraging nod

failure.text: Every draft sounds like a closing argument in a courtroom. "My client, Priya Raman, respectfully submits..." She laughs and crumples it up. "I can't write my own mom like a player character." Then she thinks about it. "Actually, maybe I just show her. Maybe I don't say anything. I just run the game."
failure.art: A girl in a purple cardigan crumpling a sheet of paper with a reluctant laugh at a library reference desk, a teenager beside her, wastebasket overflowing with drafts

choices.label: Offer to mail the envelope for her, so her mom never has to know

success.text: Priya actually hands it to you. Then she stands there with her empty hands for a whole minute, and takes it back. "No. If it wins, I want her to know it was me. And if it loses, I want her to know I tried." She looks at you. "Thanks for offering. You'd have done it, too. That's why I can't let you."
success.art: A girl in gold glasses taking a manila envelope back from a teenager's hands at a library reference desk, a thoughtful expression on her face, evening light through tall windows

failure.text: Priya says yes too fast, and you're halfway to the mailbox when her mom's station wagon pulls into the library lot. You freeze. Priya freezes. Dr. Raman, in scrubs, waves. Priya walks over, takes the envelope back from you, and says, "Amma. Can we talk in the car?" It's not the plan. It's maybe better.
failure.art: A teenager frozen on library steps holding a manila envelope, a woman in hospital scrubs waving from a station wagon in a parking lot, a girl in a purple cardigan walking toward the car

arc.title: The Party Goes Home
arc.place: The library meeting room, Thursday evening
arc.text: Priya's players came back. All five of them, plus you, plus one more chair at the end of the table where Dr. Raman sits in her hospital scrubs with a character sheet she clearly doesn't understand, holding a pencil like a scalpel. The finished module is behind the DM screen. The envelope sits beside it, stamped, unsealed. "Tonight we run the whole thing," Priya says. "Start to finish. Including the ending." Under the table, her knee is bouncing a mile a minute.
arc.art: A library meeting room table full of teenagers playing a tabletop game with character sheets and dice, a girl in a purple cardigan behind a cardboard game screen, a woman in hospital scrubs at the end of the table holding a pencil and a character sheet

choices.label: Sit next to Dr. Raman and help her play her first character ever

success.text: You show Dr. Raman how to roll. She plays a cleric, naturally, and at the climax she heals the whole party with a natural twenty and actually shouts. Priya, behind the screen, looks at her mother like she's never seen her before. At the end Dr. Raman licks the envelope herself. "Saturday," she says, "we will discuss chemistry. Tonight, my daughter is a genius."
success.art: A woman in hospital scrubs throwing her arms up in triumph over a tabletop game as a twenty-sided die lands, a girl in a purple cardigan grinning behind her game screen, teenagers cheering around the table

failure.text: Dr. Raman's cleric heals the dragon by mistake. The whole table groans. Then Priya laughs, really laughs, and rules that the dragon is so touched it joins the party. That becomes the new ending, written in pen right there. Her mom seals the envelope. "A dragon who changes its mind," she says. "Very realistic. I see it in surgery daily."
failure.art: A woman in hospital scrubs sealing a manila envelope at a library game table while a girl in a purple cardigan laughs behind a game screen, a toy dragon figure standing among the party figures

choices.label: Lead the party into the final room and solve her puzzle the way she secretly hoped someone would

success.text: The guardian of the Hollow doesn't want a fight. You remember the first playtest and offer it a seat at the table instead. Priya's pencil drops. "That's it. That's the solution. Nobody has ever found it." The party goes home together, exactly as written. Dr. Raman seals the envelope. You learned how a good story listens for the answer it was hoping for.
success.art: A teenager placing a small painted guardian figure into an empty chair drawn on a hand-inked map, a girl in a purple cardigan dropping her pencil in delight, a woman in scrubs smiling at the end of the table

failure.text: You try to sneak past the guardian and roll a one. The table goes silent. Priya looks at the die, at her mother, at you. Then she says, "The guardian sees you trying, and it lets you go home anyway, because the party tried together." She writes it in. Her mom nods slowly. "That is a very good rule."
failure.art: A twenty-sided die showing a one on a hand-drawn map, a girl in a purple cardigan writing a new line into her typed module with a pen, a woman in scrubs nodding thoughtfully

reactions.dream: Dreams are just improv with no rules lawyer. Fine. I'll be the rules lawyer.
reactions.cosmic: Elder horror from beyond space? I have literally written this. Page sixty. The weakness is on page sixty-one.
reactions.paranormal: Roll a saving throw against ghosts. I'm serious. Write down the number. It helps.
reactions.cult: A cult is just a campaign where the DM never lets anybody leave the table. That's bad DMing.

name: Lou "Lightning" Tran
bio: Lou Tran holds the high score on every cabinet at the Galaxy Zone arcade except one, and that one is killing him. His parents run the Saigon Noodle stand in the food court, and between homework and refills he has turned their dinner rush into a training regimen; he can catch a falling chopstick without looking. He keeps a coin belt of quarters for every emergency and a coffee can at home where he is saving to buy his mom a dishwasher. Lou is cocky, hilarious and an absolute menace at trash talk. His flaw is that he hates losing more than he loves winning, can't sit still for more than a minute, and hides how much he worries his family is working too hard for him.

perk.name: Extra Life
perk.text: Lou always has one more continue: reroll one failed roll each night.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove on his right hand, gray parachute pants, a coin belt bulging with quarters, white high-top sneakers, a candy necklace, leaping off an arcade cabinet with a shower of quarters fanning out of his coin belt like sparks, one gloved hand thrown forward, a pixelated monster bursting out of the glowing screen behind him

neutral.line: Got a quarter? Never mind. I've always got a quarter.
neutral.art: Portrait of a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove on his right hand, gray parachute pants, a coin belt bulging with quarters, white high-top sneakers, a candy necklace, leaning on an arcade cabinet flipping a quarter across his knuckles, screen glow on his face

happy.line: NEW HIGH SCORE. Put my initials on the moon.
happy.art: Portrait of a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove on his right hand, gray parachute pants, a coin belt bulging with quarters, white high-top sneakers, a candy necklace, pumping a gloved fist, grinning, a high score screen flashing behind him

scared.line: Game over is just a screen. Right? It's just a screen?
scared.art: Portrait of a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove on his right hand, gray parachute pants, a coin belt bulging with quarters, white high-top sneakers, a candy necklace, backing away from a cabinet, hands raised, the screen glowing red

angry.line: Nobody beats my score. Nobody touches my machine.
angry.art: Portrait of a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove on his right hand, gray parachute pants, a coin belt bulging with quarters, white high-top sneakers, a candy necklace, slamming a palm on the cabinet, eyes narrowed, lightning bolt haircut catching neon

sad.line: Mom works two shifts so I can be here. Sometimes I think I'm wasting it.
sad.art: Portrait of a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove on his right hand, gray parachute pants, a coin belt bulging with quarters, white high-top sneakers, a candy necklace, sitting on a food court bench, turning a single quarter over in his fingers

determined.line: Insert coin. Player two, get ready.
determined.art: Portrait of a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove on his right hand, gray parachute pants, a coin belt bulging with quarters, white high-top sneakers, a candy necklace, cracking his knuckles at the controls, joystick in his gloved hand, eyes locked on the screen

meet.title: Nightmare Lane
meet.place: The Galaxy Zone arcade, Starlight Mall
meet.text: In the back of the Galaxy Zone arcade there is a cabinet nobody remembers being delivered. It's called NIGHTMARE LANE, the art on the side is a suburban street at night, and the top score has belonged to the same initials since it arrived: FKR. A kid with a lightning bolt shaved into his hair is pounding the buttons, loses, and kicks the coin door. "Every machine in this place says LOU at the top," he says. "Except this one. You any good?"
meet.art: A wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a sly grin, short black hair with a lightning bolt shaved into one side, a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves, a fingerless black glove and a coin belt bulging with quarters, glaring at a shadowy arcade cabinet in the back of a neon arcade whose side panel is painted with a suburban street at night, three initials glowing on its high-score screen, a teenager beside him, magenta and blue arcade glow, medium shot

choices.label: Challenge him to one round on his favorite machine

success.text: You lose. Obviously. But you lose by only forty thousand points, which nobody ever has. Lou stares at the screen, then at you. "Okay, you got hands. You're my player two." He flips you a quarter from his belt. "Keep it. Emergencies."
success.art: Two teenagers side by side at a glowing arcade cabinet, one grinning and flipping a quarter to the other, scores flashing on screen

failure.text: Game over in twenty-eight seconds. Lou winces like he's watching a car crash. "Okay. Okay. That was... a learning experience. Come back tomorrow, I'll teach you the pattern." He's already putting another quarter in.
failure.art: A GAME OVER screen glowing red on an arcade cabinet, a boy with a lightning bolt haircut wincing beside a slumped teenager

choices.label: Take on NIGHTMARE LANE together, one hand each

success.text: You take the joystick, he takes the buttons. On the last level the screen shows a pink salon chair and a figure with shears, and you don't flinch. The score rolls past FKR's. The initials flicker and vanish. Lou is speechless for the first time in recorded history. "We're a team now. That's not up for discussion."
success.art: Two teenagers sharing the controls of an arcade cabinet, the screen showing a pixelated salon chair and a shadowy figure with shears, the old initials dissolving

failure.text: The cabinet eats your quarter, then spits it back out wrapped in a single long gray hair. The screen flashes NEXT APPOINTMENT: SOON. Lou unplugs the machine. It keeps glowing. "Tomorrow," he says, "we bring backup."
failure.art: A quarter wrapped in a long gray hair sitting in an arcade coin return, the unplugged cabinet still glowing with a sinister message

choices.label: Help his mom through the dinner rush at the noodle stand

success.text: You bus trays, refill sriracha and charm a table of mall walkers into ordering extra spring rolls. Mrs. Tran gives you a bowl on the house. Lou, slurping beside you, says, "Mom likes you more than me now. You have to be on my crew so I can keep an eye on you."
success.art: A busy food court noodle stand, a teenager carrying a tray of steaming bowls, a boy with a lightning bolt haircut grinning, a smiling woman behind the counter

failure.text: You drop a full tray of pho in front of a mall security guard. Mrs. Tran is very nice about it, which is worse. Lou pats your back. "Tomorrow you just do napkins. Napkins can't spill."
failure.art: Spilled noodle soup across a food court floor, a teenager frozen in horror, a boy patting their back

arc.title: The Coffee Can
arc.place: The Saigon Noodle stand, Starlight Mall food court, 5 p.m.
arc.text: Lou dumps a coffee can of quarters onto a food court table and counts them with the speed of a bank machine. "A hundred and eighty-four dollars and fifty cents. The dishwasher at the appliance store on Main is three forty-nine." Behind the counter his mom is up to her elbows in a sink of noodle bowls. Taped to the arcade entrance across the court is a flyer: STARLIGHT MONSTER MASH HIGH SCORE TOURNAMENT, FRIDAY 4 P.M., GRAND PRIZE $200. "Two hundred," Lou says. "Do you know what I could do with two hundred?" He's already doing the math with his fingers.
arc.art: A wiry teenage boy with a lightning bolt shaved into his hair counting a pile of quarters at a food court table, a woman washing a sink full of bowls behind a noodle stand counter, a tournament flyer taped to a neon arcade entrance across the mall

choices.label: Help him count and roll every quarter so he knows exactly what he needs

success.text: Between the two of you, the quarters are rolled in paper sleeves in ten minutes flat. You find an extra six dollars in a sock at the bottom of the can. Lou stares at it. "That's my mom's sock. She's been putting quarters in my can." He goes quiet. "She knows. She's been helping me save for her own dishwasher."
success.art: Two teenagers rolling quarters into paper coin sleeves at a food court table, a small sock full of coins tipped out of a coffee can, neon mall lights overhead

failure.text: You lose count at forty-two, then again at sixty. Lou takes over, muttering, and doesn't lose count once. "It's fine. Numbers are like enemy patterns. You just watch them long enough." But he's watching his mom's hands in the dishwater, not the quarters, and his count comes out wrong too.
failure.art: A wiry teenage boy distracted while counting quarters, glancing toward a woman washing dishes behind a food court counter, a teenager beside him with a jumbled pile of coins

choices.label: Ask him why it has to be a dishwasher, and why it has to be now

success.text: Lou flips a quarter across his knuckles three times before he answers. "Her hands crack in the winter. She puts lotion on and then goes right back in the sink. She says she's fine. She always says she's fine." He pockets the quarter. "I can't fix the shifts. I can fix the sink."
success.art: A wiry teenage boy flipping a quarter across his knuckles at a food court table, looking toward a woman at a noodle stand sink, a teenager listening beside him

failure.text: "Because I want to, that's why. Geez." He sweeps the quarters back into the can with a crash that makes three mall walkers jump. Then he sits down again. "Sorry. I just. Come to the arcade tomorrow. I play better when I'm mad, and I'm mad."
failure.art: A wiry teenage boy sweeping a pile of quarters back into a coffee can with a loud clatter, mall walkers startled nearby, a teenager sitting across the food court table

choices.label: Sneak into the arcade and scout who else signed up for the tournament

success.text: The sign-up sheet has thirty names. Most are kids Lou's beaten. One isn't: a ten-year-old named Gwen Abernathy who has been quietly setting records at the roller rink cabinet. Lou reads it twice. "A rival," he breathes, delighted. "An actual rival. Finally." He looks five years younger.
success.art: A teenager and a wiry boy with a lightning bolt haircut leaning over a clipboard sign-up sheet in a neon arcade, a small girl in a ponytail playing an arcade cabinet in the background

failure.text: The arcade manager catches you reading the sheet and assumes you want to enter. Now you're on it, in pen, right below Lou. He laughs so hard he has to sit down on a pinball machine. "Player two! For real this time! I'll train you. Come back tomorrow, you are going to need it."
failure.art: A wiry teenage boy laughing while sitting on a pinball machine, a teenager looking at their own name on a sign-up sheet held by an arcade manager

arc.title: Dinner Rush
arc.place: The Saigon Noodle stand, Wednesday at 6 p.m.
arc.text: Mr. Tran threw his back out lifting a stockpot and is home flat on a heating pad. Mrs. Tran is running the whole stand alone through the dinner rush, and the tournament qualifier started ten minutes ago, forty feet away. Lou is behind the counter in an apron, ladling broth with one hand and staring at the arcade with his whole body. "I'm not going," he says. "I'm fine. It's fine." His mom says something sharp in Vietnamese and points at the arcade. He says something back. Neither of them moves.
arc.art: A busy food court noodle stand at dinner rush, a wiry teenage boy with a lightning bolt haircut in an apron ladling broth while staring across the mall at a neon arcade, a woman behind him pointing toward it, a long line of customers

choices.label: Put on an apron, take his ladle, and push him toward the arcade

success.text: You've watched Lou work enough to fake it. Mrs. Tran shows you the bowls once, and the two of you run that line like a pit crew. Lou qualifies in fourth place and comes back running to tell you, then grabs a ladle anyway. "You can't do the spring rolls, you'll burn them." He's right. You were about to.
success.art: A teenager in an apron ladling noodle soup beside a smiling woman at a busy food court counter, a wiry boy with a lightning bolt haircut sprinting back from a neon arcade with his arms raised

failure.text: You drop the first bowl. Mrs. Tran sends you to napkins, Lou stays at the ladle, and the qualifier closes without him. Except, at nine o'clock, the arcade manager walks over for noodles and says, "Kid, I saw. Family comes first. I'm putting you in as a wildcard." Lou has to put the ladle down.
failure.art: An arcade manager handing a wildcard ticket to a wiry teenage boy in an apron across a noodle stand counter, a teenager behind him folding napkins, a woman watching with a small smile

choices.label: Tell Lou to tell his mom the real reason he wants the prize money

success.text: Lou says it in Vietnamese, fast, eyes on the broth. His mom stops ladling. She takes his face in her damp hands, says something soft, and then very firmly takes off his apron. "She says she doesn't need a dishwasher," he translates, voice thick. "She says she needs me to stop worrying so hard. And to go win."
success.art: A woman at a noodle stand gently holding her teenage son's face in her hands, the boy with a lightning bolt haircut in an apron looking down, a teenager watching from the side of the counter

failure.text: Lou won't say it. "She'll just say no." So you try, and it comes out mangled, and Mrs. Tran looks at you, then at her son, and understands perfectly anyway. She doesn't say anything. She just hands Lou his coin belt from under the counter and points at the arcade again. He goes. He keeps looking back.
failure.art: A woman handing a coin belt across a noodle stand counter to her teenage son with a lightning bolt haircut, a teenager looking awkward beside them, a neon arcade glowing across the food court

choices.label: Run messages between the stand and the arcade so he can do both at once

success.text: Fueled by two cans of Bolt Cola, you sprint the forty feet thirty times. Lou plays a round, runs back, ladles, runs back, plays. He qualifies in second, which should be impossible. Mrs. Tran gives you both bowls on the house and says something in Vietnamese that makes Lou go red. "She says we're both idiots. Nice idiots."
success.art: A teenager sprinting across a neon food court between a noodle stand and an arcade, a boy with a lightning bolt haircut mid-dash in an apron, empty soda cans on the counter

failure.text: On run twelve you collide with a mall security guard and a tray of egg rolls. Lou misses his qualifying round to help pick them up. He sits on the floor among the egg rolls and starts laughing. "Okay. Okay. I can't do everything. Turns out I can't do everything." It sounds like it's the first time he's said it.
failure.art: A wiry teenage boy sitting on a food court floor among scattered egg rolls laughing, a teenager and a mall security guard sprawled nearby

arc.title: Final Round
arc.place: The Galaxy Zone arcade, Friday at 4 p.m.
arc.text: The final is Lou against Gwen Abernathy, age ten, on the Galaxy Zone's big racing cabinet. There is a crowd. There is a banner. And at the front of the crowd, in her apron, on her break, with Mr. Tran leaning on a cane beside her, is Mrs. Tran, who has never once come into the arcade. Lou sees them and his hands freeze on the wheel. "They've never watched me play," he whispers to you. "What if I lose in front of them?" The countdown starts. Three. Two.
arc.art: A crowded neon arcade with a big racing cabinet, a wiry boy with a lightning bolt haircut and a small ten-year-old girl in a ponytail side by side at the wheels, a woman in an apron and a man with a cane watching at the front of the crowd, a teenager beside the boy

choices.label: Stand at his shoulder and call out the track pattern you learned together

success.text: "Hairpin. Boost. Shortcut by the billboard." Lou's hands unlock. He takes the final turn by a car length, and the crowd goes up like a soda can. Gwen shakes his hand like a pro. Mrs. Tran is shouting something nobody understands but everybody agrees with. The dishwasher gets delivered Monday. You learned to read a pattern under pressure, just like he does.
success.art: A wiry boy with a lightning bolt haircut throwing his arms up at a racing cabinet as the crowd erupts, a woman in an apron cheering at the front, a teenager clapping him on the shoulder, confetti in the neon light

failure.text: You call the shortcut a turn too early, and Lou loses to Gwen by a tenth of a second. The crowd groans. Lou stands there, stunned. Then his mom pushes through, grabs his face, and kisses both his cheeks in front of everybody. "She says it's the best she's ever seen anyone lose," he says, and he's laughing. "We'll put the rest on layaway. Together."
failure.art: A woman in an apron kissing her embarrassed teenage son's cheeks in a crowded arcade, a ten-year-old girl holding a trophy beside them, a teenager grinning nearby

choices.label: Tell him to stop watching the screen for one second and look at his parents

success.text: He looks. His dad gives him a thumbs-up off the cane. His mom mouths something, and his shoulders drop two inches. He plays the race loose and laughing, like he's showing them his favorite thing, and wins by a hair. Afterward he gives the two hundred dollars to his mom. She gives half back. "For more quarters," she says in English.
success.art: A wiry boy with a lightning bolt haircut glancing back from a racing cabinet at his parents in the crowd, his father giving a thumbs-up while leaning on a cane, his mother smiling, a teenager beside him

failure.text: He looks back too long and spins out on the first turn. Gwen wins easily. Lou turns around, red to the ears, and finds his dad already clapping like he won anyway. "I lost," Lou says. "You played," his mom says. He thinks about that for a long time, and then he buys Gwen a Bolt Cola.
failure.art: A wiry teenage boy turning away from a racing cabinet with a crash on its screen, his father clapping from the crowd, a small girl celebrating, a teenager patting his back

reactions.tech: If it runs on electricity I can beat it. If it runs on quarters, I already have.
reactions.slasher: Slashers have patterns. Everything has a pattern. Watch for the tell, then juke left.
reactions.creature: Big monster, slow turns. Small monster, fast turns. Either way, I'm faster. Probably.
reactions.cosmic: A monster from outer space with no hitbox? That's cheating. I'm filing a complaint.

name: Father Ignatius "Iggy" Reyes
bio: Father Iggy Reyes grew up in Daly City, played bass in garage bands through seminary, and was sent to St. Jude's in Glimmer Falls as the young priest who would 'connect with the youth.' He did not expect the youth to show up with squirt guns asking him to bless them, and he did not expect to say yes every time. His band, the Venial Sins, practices in the church basement on Thursdays; his youth group is the only one in the county where queer kids are welcomed by name. His lola told him stories about aswang, and he took notes. Iggy is warm, irreverent and a little too eager to be the cool priest; he can't keep time on bass, feuds with the monsignor, and carries guilt for a friend he couldn't help.

perk.name: Blessed Squirt Gun
perk.text: Iggy blessed the whole arsenal and didn't ask a single question: +2 on every roll against cult nightmares.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin and a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour, a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt, a studded black leather jacket pinned with safety pins, black jeans, scuffed combat boots, a red electric bass slung across his back and a neon green squirt gun tucked in his belt, standing on a crumbling mausoleum step in Pinecrest Cemetery at midnight, bass in one hand like a staff and a neon squirt gun raised in the other, a fan of holy water arcing into the moonlight, robed shadows recoiling below

neutral.line: Bless you. Also, the band practices Thursday, if you want to come.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin and a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour, a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt, a studded black leather jacket pinned with safety pins, black jeans, scuffed combat boots, a red electric bass slung across his back and a neon green squirt gun tucked in his belt, leaning in a church basement doorway, bass slung on his back, easy smile

happy.line: That's the spirit. Capital S, if you want it.
happy.art: Portrait of a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin and a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour, a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt, a studded black leather jacket pinned with safety pins, black jeans, scuffed combat boots, a red electric bass slung across his back and a neon green squirt gun tucked in his belt, laughing with a hand on his chest, pompadour bouncing

scared.line: Okay, I've read about this. I never wanted to read about this.
scared.art: Portrait of a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin and a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour, a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt, a studded black leather jacket pinned with safety pins, black jeans, scuffed combat boots, a red electric bass slung across his back and a neon green squirt gun tucked in his belt, gripping a rosary in one hand and the squirt gun in the other, eyes wide in the dark

angry.line: Not in my parish. Not on my watch. Not on Halloween.
angry.art: Portrait of a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin and a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour, a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt, a studded black leather jacket pinned with safety pins, black jeans, scuffed combat boots, a red electric bass slung across his back and a neon green squirt gun tucked in his belt, leveling the neon squirt gun, jaw tight, collar gleaming

sad.line: I became a priest to help people. Some nights I can't help anybody.
sad.art: Portrait of a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin and a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour, a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt, a studded black leather jacket pinned with safety pins, black jeans, scuffed combat boots, a red electric bass slung across his back and a neon green squirt gun tucked in his belt, sitting alone in an empty church pew, bass across his knees, head bowed

determined.line: Fill up the squirt guns. I'll square the paperwork with God later.
determined.art: Portrait of a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin and a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour, a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt, a studded black leather jacket pinned with safety pins, black jeans, scuffed combat boots, a red electric bass slung across his back and a neon green squirt gun tucked in his belt, pumping the squirt gun, bass strapped tight, standing at the church doors

meet.title: Thursday Practice
meet.place: The basement of St. Jude's
meet.text: The basement of St. Jude's smells like coffee urns and amplifier dust. A priest with a black spiked pompadour is tuning a red bass under a felt banner that says GOD IS LOVE in glitter glue, while the stone holy-water font in the corner bubbles like a pot left on the stove. "That's been doing that since Monday," Father Iggy says cheerfully. "I'm choosing to treat it as a sign. Are you here for youth group, band practice, or the other thing?" He nods at a bucket of neon squirt guns.
meet.art: A 31-year-old Filipino American priest with warm tan skin, a lopsided grin, a black spiked pompadour and a neat goatee, a white clerical collar on a black short-sleeved shirt under a studded leather jacket, tuning a red electric bass in a church basement under a felt wall hanging of glitter-glue hearts, a stone holy-water font bubbling in the corner, a bucket of neon green squirt guns at his feet, a teenager on the stairs, warm bulb light, medium shot

choices.label: Pick up a tambourine and jam with the Venial Sins

success.text: The Venial Sins blast through a three-chord version of a hymn, and you nail every tambourine hit. Iggy does a knee slide across the linoleum. "Okay, you're in the band. And you're in the other thing. Mostly the other thing."
success.art: A priest in a leather jacket doing a knee slide with a red bass across a church basement floor, a teenager shaking a tambourine, amps glowing

failure.text: The feedback shrieks through the amp and every candle in the basement goes out at once. In the dark, Iggy says, "That was either the amp or a very strong review. Come back tomorrow, we'll try it acoustic."
failure.art: A dark church basement lit only by a glowing amplifier, every candle extinguished with smoke curling up, band members frozen mid-song

choices.label: Hand him a squirt gun and ask for a blessing, no questions

success.text: He doesn't ask a single question. He fills it from the bubbling font, says a short prayer in Latin and a shorter one in Tagalog, and hands it back with a vial for backup. "Whatever you're fighting, you're not fighting it alone. I'm coming with you."
success.art: A priest filling a neon squirt gun from a bubbling stone font, a teenager holding out their hands, candle light glowing on the water

failure.text: The moment he dips the squirt gun, the font hisses and the water turns black as ink for a heartbeat before clearing. Iggy stares at it. "Okay. I need to call somebody. Come back tomorrow, and maybe stay out of the cemetery tonight."
failure.art: A stone holy-water font with dark ink-black water swirling, a priest pulling back a neon squirt gun with a startled look

choices.label: Go with him to check the founders' graves where kids heard singing

success.text: In Pinecrest, behind the founders' obelisk, the grass is pressed down in a perfect circle, and someone has left a ring of dried herbs. You don't run. Iggy squeezes your shoulder. "Most people would've bolted. I want you with me for whatever this is."
success.art: A teenager and a priest in a leather jacket standing at the edge of a circle of flattened grass in an old cemetery, a ring of dried herbs, a stone obelisk behind them

failure.text: A sound comes from inside the founders' crypt, like many people humming one note through closed lips. You're back at the church before you remember running. Iggy is right behind you. "Tomorrow," he pants. "In daylight. With the band."
failure.art: A teenager and a priest sprinting down a cemetery path away from a dark crypt, gravestones blurred, a faint glow behind the crypt door

arc.title: Return to Sender
arc.place: The basement of St. Jude's, Monday afternoon
arc.text: Father Iggy is sitting on an amp with a legal pad, and there are crumpled pages all around his combat boots. "Draft eleven," he says. "To my friend Benny. He played drums in our first band. In '78 his family threw him out for being gay, and he asked to crash in my dorm at seminary, and I said I couldn't, because I was scared of the rector." He looks at the pad. "He plays in a band in San Francisco now. He's doing great. I've never said I'm sorry. Eight years, and I keep starting with 'Dear Benny' and then nothing."
arc.art: A priest with a black spiked pompadour and studded leather jacket over a clerical collar sitting on an amplifier in a church basement with a legal pad, crumpled pages around his combat boots, a red electric bass leaning nearby, a teenager sitting on a folding chair across from him

choices.label: Read his draft and give him honest notes, even the hard ones

success.text: The draft is two pages of explaining why he did it. You tell him that, as kindly as you can. Iggy stares at the pad a long time. Then he tears off the two pages and writes one line: I was wrong, and I'm sorry, and you deserved better from me. "That's the whole letter," he says. "That's the whole thing, isn't it."
success.art: A priest in a leather jacket tearing two pages off a legal pad in a church basement, a single handwritten line on the fresh page, a teenager watching beside a glowing amplifier

failure.text: You start with the spelling, because that's easier. Iggy laughs. "You're avoiding it too. Good. I'm not alone." He folds the draft into his jacket pocket instead of the trash. "Come Thursday. If I haven't sent it, you're allowed to tell me what you really think."
failure.art: A priest with a spiked pompadour folding a handwritten letter into his leather jacket pocket in a church basement, a teenager holding a pencil and looking sheepish

choices.label: Point at the rectory phone and tell him letters are for people who can't call

success.text: Iggy dials information for San Francisco, gets the record shop where Benny works, and hangs up on the first ring. He dials again. A man's voice answers, and Iggy says, "Benny. It's Ignatius," and then, "I know. I know." You step out to give him the room. Through the door you hear, finally, two people laughing.
success.art: A priest in a leather jacket holding a rotary phone receiver to his ear in a cluttered rectory office, eyes closed, a teenager quietly stepping out through the doorway

failure.text: He dials. A machine picks up: Benny's voice, cheerful, telling callers the shop closes at six. Iggy says, "Hey, it's... never mind," and hangs up, mortified. Then he sits there. "He sounded happy," he says. "He sounded so happy." He picks up the legal pad again. "Okay. Draft twelve."
failure.art: A priest with a spiked pompadour slumped next to a rotary phone in a small rectory office, a legal pad in his lap, a teenager leaning in the doorway

choices.label: Hand him a metronome and make him play bass in time until his head clears

success.text: For twenty minutes, Iggy plays the same four notes in perfect time for possibly the first time in his life. Somewhere in there his shoulders come down. "Benny used to do this," he says. "Click his sticks at me until I stopped rushing. I always rush." He puts the bass down. "I'm rushing the letter, too. Or I'm not rushing at all. One of those."
success.art: A priest in a leather jacket playing a red electric bass in a church basement while a wind-up metronome ticks on an amplifier, a teenager tapping along on a folding chair

failure.text: Iggy cannot keep time with a metronome. He cannot keep time with you clapping. At one point he is somehow behind and ahead of the beat at the same time. He collapses on the amp laughing. "This is why Benny kept the band together. I'm a mess without a drummer." It's the first time he's smiled saying the name.
failure.art: A priest with a spiked pompadour collapsed laughing on an amplifier with a red bass across his lap, a metronome ticking beside him, a teenager clapping out a beat

arc.title: The Monsignor's Memo
arc.place: The rectory office at St. Jude's, morning
arc.text: There is a typed memo on Iggy's desk from Monsignor Kearney. The youth group's Halloween party is canceled unless "certain members of the group" stay home. Iggy reads it to you twice. "He means Raven. He means the two boys from Pinecrest Avenue. He means the kids I promised could come here as themselves." He sets it down very carefully. "In 1978, I kept my head down. I'm not doing it twice. I just don't know how to do it without losing the parish."
arc.art: A priest in a leather jacket and clerical collar standing over a desk in a wood-paneled rectory office holding a typed memo, a crucifix and a band flyer on the wall behind him, a teenager in the doorway, morning light through the window

choices.label: Help him find chapter and verse for welcoming everyone, so he walks in armed

success.text: You and Iggy pull every book off the shelf and build his case: the stranger welcomed, the lost sheep, the table where everyone eats. He writes it up on one page and walks it to the monsignor's office. He comes back an hour later, pale and grinning. "He said I'm insufferable. He said the party can stay. He said both in the same sentence."
success.art: A priest and a teenager surrounded by open books stacked on a rectory desk, the priest writing on a single sheet of paper, a reading lamp glowing

failure.text: Your case is good, but the monsignor won't read it. Iggy comes back holding the page. "He didn't say no. He said 'not now.'" He looks at the memo, then crumples it. "Fine. The party's happening. I'll answer for it. That's sort of my whole job description." It's not a win. It's a stand.
failure.art: A priest in a leather jacket crumpling a typed memo in a rectory hallway, a closed office door behind him, a teenager beside him looking determined

choices.label: Walk into the monsignor's office beside him so he isn't standing there alone

success.text: Monsignor Kearney is old, tired and not used to being told no by a man in combat boots. Iggy does it gently and doesn't back up an inch. When the monsignor looks at you, you say, "Those kids are my friends, Father." The old man is quiet. Then: "Lock up after." Outside, Iggy has to lean against the wall. "You were the reinforcements."
success.art: A young priest in a leather jacket and a teenager standing side by side in front of an elderly monsignor seated at a heavy desk, a stained-glass window glowing behind him

failure.text: The monsignor sends you to wait in the hall. Through the door you hear Iggy's voice rise, then go steady, then go quiet. He comes out with the memo torn in half. "He's writing to the bishop about me," he says. "Good. Let him. The party's on. I'm finally the kind of friend Benny needed."
failure.art: A priest in a leather jacket stepping out of a heavy wooden office door holding a memo torn in half, a teenager waiting on a hallway bench

choices.label: Suggest moving the party to the Glitter Box Playhouse, where nobody can cancel it

success.text: Glory Hallelujah picks up on the second ring and says, "Father, darling, I thought you'd never ask." The Glitter Box has a stage, a fog machine and a sign out front that says EVERYONE in glitter. Iggy hangs up laughing. "The monsignor canceled a party at St. Jude's. He didn't say anything about a party with St. Jude's."
success.art: A priest in a leather jacket laughing at a rectory phone, a teenager grinning beside him holding a flyer for a community theater Halloween party

failure.text: The Glitter Box is booked solid for the revue all week. Iggy sits back. "No, you know what? We shouldn't move. They should get to be welcome here. In the actual church." He uncaps a pen and starts writing his own memo. "Honestly, you helped. You made me say it out loud."
failure.art: A priest with a spiked pompadour writing a memo at a rectory desk with a determined expression, a teenager leaning on the desk beside him, a phone back in its cradle

arc.title: Thursday, Full Volume
arc.place: The basement of St. Jude's, Thursday night
arc.text: The youth group Halloween party is in full swing: Raven reading tarot by the coffee urn, the Pinecrest boys in matching vampire capes, squirt guns full of very holy water. The Venial Sins are setting up without a drummer. Then the side door opens and a tall man in a denim jacket walks in carrying a snare drum case. Iggy goes white, then red, then something brighter. "Benny," he says. "You came." Benny shrugs. "You said you needed somebody to keep time."
arc.art: A crowded church basement Halloween party with kids in costumes, a tarot reader by a coffee urn, a priest with a spiked pompadour holding a red bass and staring at a tall man in a denim jacket entering through a side door with a snare drum case, a teenager beside the priest

choices.label: Herd the kids toward the snack table so the two of them get a minute alone

success.text: You start an impromptu costume contest by the cookies. Across the room, Iggy and Benny talk by the stairs. Iggy says his one line, the one from draft eleven. Benny hugs him so hard his pompadour flattens. When they come back, Benny sets up his snare. "He still rushes," Benny tells you. "I'll fix it. I've got time now."
success.art: Two men hugging by a church basement staircase, one a priest in a leather jacket and one in a denim jacket, while a teenager leads costumed kids in a contest by a snack table in the foreground

failure.text: The kids won't be herded. Everybody wants to meet the drummer. So Iggy says his apology in front of thirty teenagers in costumes, cheeks burning. Benny listens to all of it. Then he says, "Took you long enough," and the whole basement cheers like it's a touchdown. Not private. Maybe better.
failure.art: A priest in a leather jacket speaking earnestly to a man in a denim jacket in the middle of a crowded church basement, costumed kids cheering all around them

choices.label: Grab the drumsticks, click them over your head, and count the band in

success.text: "One, two, one two three four!" Benny comes in on the snare, Iggy comes in on the bass, and for the first time in eight years the Venial Sins are in time. They play until the monsignor's light goes on upstairs, then play one more. Iggy shouts over the noise, "You can come to practice whenever you want." You learned the oldest trick there is: how to get a room of people moving together.
success.art: A teenager clicking drumsticks overhead in a church basement while a priest plays a red bass and a man in a denim jacket hits a snare drum, costumed kids dancing, amplifiers glowing

failure.text: You count in at a speed only a hummingbird could play. Iggy, of course, rushes it even faster. Benny bursts out laughing so hard he drops a stick, and then the whole band dissolves. They start over at Benny's pace. Iggy grins at you over the bass. "Same as it ever was. Thank God."
failure.art: A man in a denim jacket laughing with a dropped drumstick in a church basement, a priest with a red bass grinning, a teenager holding drumsticks and blushing, costumed kids laughing

reactions.cult: Robes, chanting, a guy who says he has all the answers? Amateur hour. Fill the squirt guns.
reactions.paranormal: My lola had a story for this. She also had a broom. I've got holy water and a bass. Close enough.
reactions.camp: A villain with a costume budget? Respect. I'll still bless the squirt guns, but I respect it.
reactions.dream: I believe in a God who meets you in dreams. This is not that guy. Wake up, everybody.

name: Sunny Castellanos
bio: Sunny Castellanos grew up in the Bronx, moved west with her abuela at sixteen, and has been the fastest person in Glimmer Falls on any surface ever since: track, parking lot, roller rink, or the hill down Crystal Street she is not allowed to race anymore. She has used a wheelchair since a spinal injury at nine and built her racing chair with Joey Benally's help. She is training for the 1988 Paralympics in Seoul and teaches a 6 a.m. class at Pump Iron that is pure joy: salsa, sweat and shouting. Sunny is loud, funny, competitive and generous. Her flaws are impatience and pride; she hates being helped without being asked and can't stand being called inspiring by people who won't race her.

perk.name: Sunrise Warm-up
perk.text: Sunny drags the whole crew through her dawn class whether they like it or not: +1 nerve each dawn.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin and strong shoulders, a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts, fingerless leather racing gloves, seated in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon orange wheel rims, tearing down a wet suburban street at night in the racing wheelchair, sparks flying off the orange rims, curls streaming back, a monstrous shadow falling behind and losing ground

neutral.line: Five, six, seven, eight! You're late. Warm up.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin and strong shoulders, a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts, fingerless leather racing gloves, seated in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon orange wheel rims, seated at the front of a mirrored aerobics studio, one gloved hand clapping out the count

happy.line: Wepa! You feel that? That's what alive feels like!
happy.art: Portrait of a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin and strong shoulders, a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts, fingerless leather racing gloves, seated in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon orange wheel rims, throwing both arms up mid-roll, laughing, gold hoops swinging

scared.line: Something just outran me. Nothing outruns me.
scared.art: Portrait of a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin and strong shoulders, a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts, fingerless leather racing gloves, seated in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon orange wheel rims, braking hard, gloves gripping the rims, eyes wide and searching the dark

angry.line: Ask before you push my chair. Ask before you touch anybody.
angry.art: Portrait of a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin and strong shoulders, a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts, fingerless leather racing gloves, seated in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon orange wheel rims, turning her chair sharply to face someone, eyebrows down, finger raised

sad.line: Everybody wants to call me inspiring. Nobody wants to race me.
sad.art: Portrait of a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin and strong shoulders, a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts, fingerless leather racing gloves, seated in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon orange wheel rims, alone on an empty track at dusk, gloves in her lap, looking at the finish line

determined.line: Brakes off. Watch me go.
determined.art: Portrait of a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin and strong shoulders, a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts, fingerless leather racing gloves, seated in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon orange wheel rims, leaning forward low in the racing chair, gloved hands on the rims, headband tight

meet.title: Empty Class
meet.place: The aerobics studio, Pump Iron Gym and Aerobics
meet.text: Sunny Castellanos's 4 p.m. aerobics class usually has twenty people in it. Today it has a boom box, a mirrored wall and Sunny, in an orange headband, glaring at a VHS box someone left on the bench: VONDA VELOUR'S BURN TO THE BONE. "They all bought this tape," she says. "They say they can't stop doing it. They say it's fun." She spins her chair to face you. "You. You want to sweat or you want to talk?"
meet.art: A 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with golden-brown skin, strong shoulders and a big mane of dark curls held back by an orange terry headband, gold hoop earrings, a teal high-cut leotard over orange bike shorts and fingerless leather racing gloves, sitting in a low sleek racing wheelchair with neon-orange rims in an empty mirrored aerobics studio, glaring at a lurid aerobics videotape box on a bench beside a boombox, a teenager in the doorway, afternoon window light, medium shot

choices.label: Lace up rink skates and race her around the roller annex

success.text: She laps you twice. You never stop skating. When you finally cross the line, Sunny is waiting with a towel and a grin. "You're slow, but you don't quit. I can work with that. You're with me."
success.art: A woman in a racing wheelchair lapping a wobbling teenager on roller skates around an old roller rink, colored lights spinning overhead

failure.text: You wipe out on the first turn, spectacularly, into a stack of rental skates. Sunny circles back, offers a hand and waits until you take it. "Tomorrow we start with braking. Braking is not optional."
failure.art: A teenager sprawled in a pile of rental roller skates, a woman in a racing wheelchair holding out a gloved hand

choices.label: Do her entire class, start to finish, just the two of you

success.text: Forty minutes of salsa, punches and shouting, and you do not stop. At the end you're both laughing and dripping. Sunny pops the Vonda tape out of its box and drops it in the trash. "That's what exercise is supposed to feel like. Joy. You're on my crew."
success.art: A teenager and a woman in a racing wheelchair laughing and drenched in sweat in a mirrored studio, a videotape tossed into a trash can

failure.text: You make it eleven minutes before you lie down on the floor and become one with the carpet. Sunny rolls over with a cup of water. "Not bad for a first day. Come back tomorrow. I'll go easy. I won't go easy."
failure.art: A teenager collapsed flat on an aerobics studio floor, a woman in a wheelchair holding out a paper cup of water, boom box still playing

choices.label: Ask what exactly her students said about the tape

success.text: She tells you: they do the tape at midnight, every midnight, and the woman on the screen counts them down and won't let them stop. "Mrs. Esposito's seventy. She cried in the parking lot." Sunny cracks her knuckles. "I'm not losing my people to a tape. You in?"
success.art: A woman in a racing wheelchair holding up a lurid aerobics videotape, her face serious, a teenager listening in a mirrored studio

failure.text: "Don't look at me like that. I don't need a pep talk." She thinks you're pitying her, and her chair is already turning away. "Come back when you want to sweat, not talk." The VHS box on the bench seems to smile.
failure.art: A woman in a wheelchair turning away from a teenager in an empty studio, a videotape box on a bench with a smiling aerobics star on the cover

arc.title: Two Seconds
arc.place: The high-school track behind Pump Iron, 6:45 a.m.
arc.text: After her dawn class, Sunny hands you a stopwatch and a clipboard. "Seoul wants a qualifying time by December. I'm two seconds off. Two."
