She circles the track in her racing chair, gloves slapping the rims, while the fog lifts off the empty bleachers. On the third lap she brakes in front of you, breathing hard, and glares at the number. "Don't tell me it's good. Tell me what's wrong with it."
arc.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims braking hard on a foggy high-school track at dawn, a teenager holding a stopwatch and a clipboard beside empty bleachers

choices.label: Study her turns and tell her the honest truth

success.text: You noticed she sits up on the curves, like she's checking behind her. "Huh," Sunny says. "I do that. I've done that since the Bronx." She tucks low on the next lap and the stopwatch drops a full second. She points at you. "Same time tomorrow, coach."
success.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims tucked low into a curve on a foggy track, a teenager pumping a fist with a stopwatch, gold morning light

failure.text: You tell her she looks great, and she looks at you like you just called her inspiring. "Great doesn't get me to Seoul." She does six more laps alone, angry and fast, and the time doesn't move. At least now you know: she wants the truth, not a cheer.
failure.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims circling a track alone with her jaw set, a sheepish teenager sitting on the bleachers holding a stopwatch

choices.label: Grab a bike from the rack and pace her on the outside lane

success.text: You pedal like your life depends on it, and for one lap Sunny actually has someone to chase. She passes you on the last turn, laughing out loud. The stopwatch says a second faster. "That's it. I race better annoyed. Be annoying more often."
success.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims overtaking a teenager on a bicycle on the outside lane of a track at sunrise, both of them laughing

failure.text: You pedal hard into the first turn and the borrowed bike's chain jumps off. You coast, tragically, onto the infield grass. Sunny laps you, circles back and helps you put the chain on. "Tomorrow you get a better bike. I'm not losing my rabbit."
failure.art: A teenager crouched over a bicycle with a slipped chain on the infield grass of a track, a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims holding the bike steady

choices.label: Ask her what Seoul would really mean to her

success.text: She's quiet for a whole lap. Then: "My abuela came here with two suitcases and me. She cleans the bank at night. If I go to Seoul, she sees me on TV, fast, in a uniform with my name on it, and nobody calls me brave for getting out of bed." She sniffs, hard. "Allergies. Time me."
success.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims pausing on a misty track and looking toward the bleachers, a teenager beside her listening with a stopwatch held loosely

failure.text: "It would mean I'm going to Seoul. Obviously." She shuts the question down and spins off for another lap. But when she comes back, she hands you her water bottle to hold, which, you are beginning to understand, is Sunny for thanks for asking.
failure.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims handing a water bottle to a teenager on a foggy track with her eyes on the lane, already turning away

arc.title: The Sugar Tin
arc.place: The back office at Pump Iron, 5 p.m.
arc.text: Sunny is truing a front wheel of her racing chair in the gym's back office and not looking at you. Before Halloween, an official from Sacramento will time a run down the closed Crystal Street hill: her qualifying shot. "My abuela won't come," she says. "She's never watched me race. Not once since I was nine." Taped to the desk is a photo of a little girl on a bike at the top of a Bronx hill, and a woman behind her, smiling. "She's the one who let go of the seat."
arc.art: A cramped gym office with a racing wheelchair wheel clamped to a desk, a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims holding a spoke wrench, an old snapshot of a girl on a bicycle taped beside her

choices.label: Offer to go with her to talk to her abuela tonight

success.text: Abuela Mercedes feeds you arroz con gandules first, because that is the law. Then Sunny says it, and her abuela answers in Spanish, too fast for anyone but Sunny: she has never stopped seeing the hill. Sunny holds her hands. "I'm not nine. I'm fast. Come see." Abuela doesn't say yes. She doesn't say no.
success.art: An elderly Puerto Rican woman and a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims holding hands across a kitchen table covered in dishes of rice and beans, a teenager at the end of the table

failure.text: You mean to help, and instead you explain Sunny to her own abuela, which goes over like a dropped plate. "Ay, I know my granddaughter," Abuela Mercedes says, and serves you more rice anyway. Outside, Sunny laughs at you, then says quietly, "I'll tell her myself. You reminded me I have to."
failure.art: An elderly Puerto Rican woman spooning more rice onto a blushing teenager's plate in a small kitchen, a woman in an orange headband hiding a grin

choices.label: Help her write down what she can't say out loud

success.text: You sit on a stack of gym mats and she dictates while you write. It's mostly yelling at first, then it isn't. The last line is hers alone: Abuela, you didn't let go. You let me fly. She folds it into the sugar tin on her abuela's counter before she can chicken out.
success.art: A folded handwritten letter being tucked into a dented sugar tin on a kitchen counter, a woman in an orange headband and fingerless gloves doing the tucking

failure.text: Every draft turns into a list of her personal records. "She doesn't care about my splits," Sunny groans, and balls up page five. She keeps one line from the wreckage, though, and tapes it inside her racing glove: You let me fly. She'll find the rest of the words on the hill.
failure.art: Crumpled pages of handwritten drafts scattered across gym mats, a woman in an orange headband taping a scrap of paper inside a leather racing glove

choices.label: Tell her she's been fast without an audience for years

success.text: "You've been fast without anyone at the finish line for thirteen years," you say. Sunny weighs that like a coach weighs a split. "I don't need her there," she says. "I want her there. That's different. That's allowed." She cranks the wheel nut tight. "Okay. I'll want it out loud."
success.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims tightening a wheel nut with a wrench and a small determined smile, a teenager leaning in the office doorway

failure.text: It comes out colder than you meant. Sunny goes still. "I know I don't need her. I'm not asking about need." The wrench clinks on the desk. After a long minute she pushes a spare headband across to you, a truce. "You're right that I'll race either way. That's the part that scares me."
failure.art: A woman in an orange headband sliding a spare orange terry headband across a cluttered desk toward a teenager, a wrench lying between them

arc.title: The Hill
arc.place: The top of the Crystal Street hill, early morning
arc.text: Somebody convinced the HOA to close the Crystal Street hill for twenty minutes, and that somebody was Sunny, yelling. The race official from Sacramento waits at the bottom by the Heartstone with a stopwatch. Halfway down, a small figure in a church coat and a hand-knit scarf holds a cowbell: Abuela Mercedes, who has not watched a race in thirteen years. Sunny pulls on her gloves at the top and looks at you. "Ready?"
arc.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims at the top of a steep suburban hill at dawn, a small elderly woman in a church coat holding a cowbell halfway down, a glowing purple geode in a roundabout at the bottom

choices.label: Race her down the hill for real, holding back nothing

success.text: You go flat out, and Sunny still flies past at the bend, sparks off the orange rims, the cowbell clanging like a fire alarm. The official stops the watch and stares. Under the time. Abuela Mercedes is crying and ringing the bell at once. Sunny circles back to you, grinning. "You actually raced me. Nobody races me."
success.art: a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims flying past a running teenager on a steep suburban hill, sparks off the rims, an elderly woman ringing a cowbell with both hands

failure.text: You take the bend too fast and tumble onto the HOA president's prize lawn, which is fine, mostly. Sunny glances back once to see you wave, then flies. She misses the time by a hair. Abuela is ringing the bell anyway, and Sunny laughs into the wind. "Sacramento in December. She already said she's coming."
failure.art: A teenager sprawled laughing on a manicured suburban lawn, a woman in a racing wheelchair speeding downhill past them, an elderly woman ringing a cowbell

choices.label: Stand halfway down with her abuela and ring the second bell

success.text: Abuela Mercedes grips your arm when Sunny pushes off. Then she lets go and rings that cowbell like she's calling the whole Bronx home. Sunny passes so close you feel the wind, whooping. Under the time. At the bottom she spins around and yells up the hill, "Did you see? Did you see?" Abuela did.
success.art: An elderly Puerto Rican woman and a teenager ringing cowbells on a suburban curb as a woman in an orange headband in a low racing wheelchair with orange rims rockets past them downhill, curls streaming

failure.text: Abuela's grip is iron, and she covers her eyes when Sunny pushes off. You miss your cue on the bell completely. Sunny finishes two-tenths off the time. But when Abuela uncovers her eyes, the first thing she sees is her granddaughter at the bottom, safe and laughing, and she rings the bell for a full minute.
failure.art: An elderly woman in a church coat peeking between her fingers at a hill, a teenager beside her holding a silent cowbell, a racing wheelchair at the bottom of the street

choices.label: Do one last check of her wheels with her before the start

success.text: You find a front tire a few pounds low and pump it while she counts down from ten, out loud, refusing to rush. The run is perfect. The official holds up the watch: under. From the bottom of the hill Sunny flings her headband up at you. "Pit crew! Joey's gonna be so jealous."
success.art: A teenager kneeling with a bicycle pump at the front wheel of a racing wheelchair at the top of a hill, the woman in the chair counting down on gloved fingers

failure.text: You fumble the valve cap and it bounces into a storm drain, and Sunny's start is three minutes late while you both hunt for it. She runs anyway, furious, then joyful, then fast, and misses by a breath. Her abuela is hugging her at the bottom. "December," Sunny says into her shoulder. "You'll come?" "I'll come."
failure.art: A tiny valve cap bouncing toward a curbside storm drain, a teenager diving after it, a woman in a racing wheelchair glaring at a stopwatch

reactions.tech: A tape that makes you exercise forever? Please. I AM the tape. Mine just lets you stop.
reactions.slasher: Slashers walk slow on purpose. I don't walk. Let's see him keep up.
reactions.cult: Matching sweatbands and chanting at dawn? That's my 6 a.m. class with worse music.

name: Wade Whitfield
bio: Wade Whitfield is repeating his senior year, works the crusher at Rusty's Junkyard, and lives about half the time in his black van, which has a wizard airbrushed on the side and a cassette deck that only plays one tape. His dad left when he was ten; he drives his little sister to school every morning and threatens anyone who looks at her funny. Everybody in Glimmer Falls thinks Wade is a burnout. Nobody knows about the spiral notebook in his glove box full of poems about the moon, the quarry and his mom working nights. Wade is loyal to the bone, funnier than people expect, and braver than he should be. His flaws: he hides every soft thing behind noise, procrastinates everything, and drives like a maniac.

perk.name: Glovebox Sonnet
perk.text: Every morning Wade reads the crew one poem from the notebook and dares anyone to laugh: +1 nerve each dawn.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of an 18-year-old white guy with a scruffy jaw and sleepy blue eyes, a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in metal band patches over a black tee, ripped acid-wash jeans, a studded leather wristband, black work boots, a spiral notebook sticking out of his back pocket, standing on the roof of his black van in a junkyard at night with one boot on the luggage rack, a tire iron raised like a sword, the airbrushed wizard on the van glowing in red headlights, car wrecks stacked like a castle behind him

neutral.line: Van's got half a tank and a full cassette. Get in.
neutral.art: Portrait of an 18-year-old white guy with a scruffy jaw and sleepy blue eyes, a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in metal band patches over a black tee, ripped acid-wash jeans, a studded leather wristband, black work boots, a spiral notebook sticking out of his back pocket, leaning against the side of a black van, arms crossed, mullet in the breeze

happy.line: Duuude. That ruled. That absolutely ruled.
happy.art: Portrait of an 18-year-old white guy with a scruffy jaw and sleepy blue eyes, a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in metal band patches over a black tee, ripped acid-wash jeans, a studded leather wristband, black work boots, a spiral notebook sticking out of his back pocket, throwing the devil horns with both hands, head banging, grinning wide

scared.line: Nope. Nope. That's like, a real one, man.
scared.art: Portrait of an 18-year-old white guy with a scruffy jaw and sleepy blue eyes, a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in metal band patches over a black tee, ripped acid-wash jeans, a studded leather wristband, black work boots, a spiral notebook sticking out of his back pocket, pressed flat against the van door, eyes huge, clutching the spiral notebook

angry.line: Mess with my friends and you're going in the crusher.
angry.art: Portrait of an 18-year-old white guy with a scruffy jaw and sleepy blue eyes, a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in metal band patches over a black tee, ripped acid-wash jeans, a studded leather wristband, black work boots, a spiral notebook sticking out of his back pocket, gripping a tire iron, jaw clenched, junkyard lights behind him

sad.line: 'The moon is a quarter nobody spends.' ...Forget I said that.
sad.art: Portrait of an 18-year-old white guy with a scruffy jaw and sleepy blue eyes, a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in metal band patches over a black tee, ripped acid-wash jeans, a studded leather wristband, black work boots, a spiral notebook sticking out of his back pocket, sitting in the open van door reading from the spiral notebook, shoulders slumped

determined.line: Crank it to eleven. We're going in.
determined.art: Portrait of an 18-year-old white guy with a scruffy jaw and sleepy blue eyes, a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in metal band patches over a black tee, ripped acid-wash jeans, a studded leather wristband, black work boots, a spiral notebook sticking out of his back pocket, hand on the van's cassette deck, cranking the volume, staring through the windshield

meet.title: The Van Won't Start
meet.place: The back lot, Rusty's Junkyard
meet.text: In the back lot of Rusty's, a black van with a wizard airbrushed on the side is making a noise like a dying cow. A guy with a feathered mullet is kicking the tire and swearing creatively. When he yanks open the glove box for a wrench, a spiral notebook falls out at your feet and flops open. The page says, in careful pencil: the quarry keeps the moon like a coin / nobody in this town ever spends. Wade freezes. "That's... my sister's."
meet.art: An 18-year-old with a scruffy jaw, sleepy blue eyes and a long feathered dirty-blond mullet, a sleeveless faded denim vest covered in band patches over a black tee and ripped acid-wash jeans, frozen mid-kick beside a black van with a wizard airbrushed on its side in a junkyard back lot, a spiral notebook lying open on the gravel at a teenager's feet, gray afternoon light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Hand back the notebook and tell him the poem is good

success.text: "The coin line is really good," you say, and you mean it. Wade turns brick red. Then he grins, slowly, like a sunrise. "Nobody's ever read one. Okay. Okay, you're cool. You're riding with me from now on."
success.art: A guy with a mullet taking a spiral notebook from a teenager, blushing and grinning, the black van behind them in golden afternoon light

failure.text: You mean to say it's good, but you snort a little at the word 'moon' and he snatches the notebook back. "Whatever. It's my sister's." He's not mad, exactly; he's embarrassed. "Come back tomorrow. I'll... think about it."
failure.art: A guy with a mullet shoving a spiral notebook into his vest, avoiding eye contact, a teenager wincing beside a black van

choices.label: Help him push-start the van down the junk hill

success.text: You both shove, the van rolls, Wade pops the clutch and the engine roars to life with a blast of heavy metal from the tape deck. He leans out the window, hand up for a high five. "Get in, slowpoke. You're crew now."
success.art: A black van roaring down a gravel hill in a junkyard, a guy with a mullet leaning out the window for a high five, a teenager running alongside

failure.text: The van rolls, does not start, and keeps rolling, straight into the car maze. It takes an hour to find it again, wedged between a hearse and an ice cream truck. Wade sighs. "Tomorrow. With Joey. Joey knows vans."
failure.art: A black van wedged between a hearse and an ice cream truck deep in a junkyard car maze, two figures staring at it in dismay

choices.label: Fix the jammed cassette deck while he works on the engine

success.text: You unspool the tape with a pencil, and when the deck clicks back to life the whole junkyard echoes with a guitar solo. Somewhere in the car maze, every stray dog howls along. Wade nods slowly. "Respect. You get to pick the tape. Sometimes. You're in."
success.art: A teenager in the passenger seat of a van fixing a cassette deck with a pencil, a guy with a mullet nodding in approval, dogs howling in the distance

failure.text: The tape snaps. It was the only tape. Wade stares at the two shiny ends for a long moment. "That was my dad's." He breathes out. "It's okay. It's okay. Come back tomorrow, man, I need a minute."
failure.art: A guy with a mullet holding a snapped cassette tape in both hands, two loose ends of tape fluttering, the van door hanging open

arc.title: The Coin Line
arc.place: The roof of the van, Rusty's Junkyard, sunset
arc.text: Wade hauls you up the van's ladder to the roof, where he has a lawn chair, a cooler of Bolt Cola and the spiral notebook on his knee like a live grenade. Below you, the junkyard goes orange. He pulls a crumpled flyer out of his vest: OPEN MIC NITE, ALL WELCOME. It has been torn in half and taped back together. "I'm not doing it," he says. "Obviously. I just want somebody to tell me if the poems are, like, poems."
arc.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest sitting in a lawn chair on the roof of a black van in a junkyard at sunset, a spiral notebook on his knee, a teenager climbing up the ladder

choices.label: Ask him to read you one out loud, the scariest one

success.text: He reads the one about his mom's night shift at the hospital laundry, the town lights 'going out one by one like nobody's waiting up.' His voice shakes on the last line and then doesn't. You don't say anything for a second, and that's the right thing. "Yeah," Wade says softly. "Yeah, okay."
success.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest reading from a spiral notebook on a van roof against an orange sunset, a teenager sitting cross-legged beside him listening

failure.text: He gets two lines in and the junkyard dog starts howling along, and you laugh at the dog, and he slams the notebook shut. "See? See? That's what happens." It takes a whole Bolt Cola to calm him down. He doesn't read again, but he doesn't throw the flyer away, either.
failure.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest clutching a closed spiral notebook on a van roof, a stray dog howling up at them from the gravel below, a teenager covering their mouth

choices.label: Ask if you can read the notebook quietly, to yourself

success.text: He hands it over like a kidney. You read for twenty minutes while he pretends to fix the antenna. The poems are messy and good: the quarry, the moon, his sister asleep in the passenger seat. You hand it back with three pages dog-eared. "Those three," you say. He looks at the dog-ears for a long time.
success.art: A teenager reading a spiral notebook on a van roof at dusk while a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest fiddles with a bent antenna and sneaks glances over

failure.text: You read too slowly, and Wade can't stand it. Every time you turn a page he says "that one's dumb" until you've barely read anything. Finally he takes it back and tucks it in his vest. "Sorry. It's like, my skin's in there. Tomorrow. Maybe."
failure.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest tucking a spiral notebook into his vest on a van roof, a teenager holding up empty hands, the junkyard dark below

choices.label: Dare him to write a new one right now, about the sunset

success.text: "Fine," he says. "Ten minutes." He writes like he's defusing a bomb. What comes out is four lines about a junkyard at sunset where 'every wreck gets one more ride.' He reads it out loud before he can stop himself, then looks shocked. "I just did that. Out loud. Dude."
success.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest hunched over a spiral notebook scribbling fast on a van roof, a teenager holding up a wristwatch, stacked car wrecks glowing orange

failure.text: Ten minutes later he has drawn a wizard, a skull, a better wizard, and written zero words. "It's not a vending machine, man," he groans, but he's laughing. You learn that his poems don't come on command. They come at three in the morning in the van, when the whole town is asleep.
failure.art: A spiral notebook page covered in doodles of wizards and skulls, a mullet-haired guy laughing beside it on a van roof at dusk

arc.title: The Crusher
arc.place: The car crusher, Rusty's Junkyard, end of shift
arc.text: You find Wade at the crusher controls with the spiral notebook lying on the dashboard of a doomed station wagon. His little sister Tiff found it this morning and read a poem out loud at breakfast, the one about Dad leaving, in front of their mom. "She didn't mean anything. She's ten. She thought it was a song." His mom didn't say a word; she just went to work. Wade's hand hovers over the big red lever. "Better if it's gone."
arc.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest in the cab of a junkyard car crusher with his hand over a red lever, a spiral notebook visible on the dashboard of a rusted station wagon in the crusher bed

choices.label: Climb into the wagon and grab the notebook off the dash

success.text: You're in and out of the station wagon before he can argue, notebook clutched to your chest. Wade lets go of the lever and sags against the cab. "You're insane," he says. Then, smaller: "Thanks. I wasn't gonna. I don't think I was gonna."
success.art: A teenager scrambling out of a rusted station wagon window clutching a spiral notebook, a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest slumped against the crusher cab in relief

failure.text: The wagon door is rusted shut and you end up stuck halfway through the window, legs kicking, until Wade shuts the crusher down and pulls you out by the belt loops. He fetches the notebook himself, laughing despite everything. "Okay. Okay. Nobody's getting crushed today."
failure.art: A teenager stuck halfway through a station wagon window with legs kicking, a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest hauling them out by the belt loops, both laughing

choices.label: Ask what his mom actually did after breakfast

success.text: "She didn't say anything. She just held my face for a second and left for work." He hears it as he says it. You don't have to point it out. He takes his hand off the lever. "She left a note on the fridge," he admits. "It said keep writing, baby. I thought she meant homework."
success.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest sitting in the crusher cab staring at a small note held in his hand, a teenager leaning on the cab door, sunset behind the junk piles

failure.text: It's the wrong moment, and he shuts down hard. "Doesn't matter what she did." But he does climb out of the cab, and he does take the notebook off the dash, and he puts it in his vest pocket, over his heart, where he thinks nobody notices. Everybody notices.
failure.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest climbing down from a crusher cab and sliding a spiral notebook into his vest pocket, a teenager watching from beside a rusted wagon

choices.label: Trade him the most embarrassing thing you ever wrote

success.text: You recite the worst thing you've ever written, every terrible rhyme. Wade laughs so hard he has to hold onto the lever housing for balance. "Okay, okay, mine are way better than that." He grabs the notebook off the dash. "Way better. Not even close."
success.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest doubled over laughing in a crusher cab, a teenager reciting with dramatic arm gestures, a spiral notebook in his hand

failure.text: You start your confession and chicken out halfway. Wade raises an eyebrow. "See? It's hard." Somehow that's the thing that helps. He climbs out, gets the notebook, and sits on the wagon's hood next to you. "Nobody should have to read their skin out loud by accident."
failure.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest and a teenager sitting side by side on the hood of a rusted station wagon at dusk, a spiral notebook resting between them

arc.title: Headlights
arc.place: The back lot, Rusty's Junkyard, after dark
arc.text: Wade did the thing nobody expected: he called a reading himself. Not at the Glitter Box. Here, on his own turf. The van is parked with its headlights on a stack of car hoods like a stage, the crew is sitting on tailgates, and his mom took the night off. Tiff is in the front row with a flashlight, very serious. Wade climbs onto the van roof with the notebook, looks out at everyone, then at you. "If I freeze, do something."
arc.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest standing on the roof of a black van in a junkyard at night holding a spiral notebook, headlights blazing across a stack of car hoods, friends on tailgates and a small girl with a flashlight in front

choices.label: Clap first and loudest before he even starts

success.text: You clap like he just won a world title, and the crew catches it, then Tiff, then his mom. Wade laughs into the notebook and starts reading over the noise. The quarry. The moon like a coin. His mom's night shift. When he finishes, his mom is on her feet, and he climbs down and hugs her, notebook and all.
success.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest hugging a tired woman in a hospital laundry uniform beside a black van at night, a spiral notebook squashed between them, friends cheering on tailgates

failure.text: You start clapping way too early, during his first line, and the whole crew follows your lead, so the opening gets drowned out. Wade stops, laughs, and starts over. "Thanks, I think." He's less scared after that. The second time through, his voice is steady and loud, and his mom mouths the words back.
failure.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest grinning and holding up a hand for quiet on a van roof, a crowd of friends on tailgates mid-applause in the headlights

choices.label: Hit the cassette deck for a guitar intro if he freezes

success.text: He freezes on the first line, exactly like he said. You slam play and the van's one tape screams a guitar solo across the junkyard. Wade throws the horns, the crew howls, and when the solo ends he reads into the quiet like a frontman. "That," he says after, "was the most metal thing that ever happened in this town."
success.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest throwing devil horns on a van roof in blazing headlights, a teenager leaning into the open van door pressing the cassette deck, friends howling

failure.text: You hit the button and the tape eats itself with a sad warble. Silence. Then Tiff says, very loud, "Just READ IT, Wade." Everyone laughs, Wade too, and he does. His voice cracks on the moon line and he keeps going anyway, which turns out to be the bravest part.
failure.art: A small girl with a flashlight shouting up at a guy with a mullet on a van roof, loops of cassette tape spilling out of a van dashboard

choices.label: Climb up first and read something of your own

success.text: You climb onto the van roof and read four shaky lines you wrote last night. The crew cheers like you're the headliner. When you hand the roof over, Wade is grinning. "Okay, the opener was good. Watch this." He reads his best, and afterward he tells you the trick: "Somebody has to go first. That's all bravery is, man."
success.art: A teenager reading from a folded sheet on a van roof in blazing headlights, a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest waiting at the ladder with his notebook and a proud grin

failure.text: Your lines come out mumbled and too fast, and you lose your place. Nobody laughs. Wade climbs up beside you and finishes your last line, perfectly, from memory, because he was listening. Then he reads his. When his mom hugs him afterward, he's still holding your page, too.
failure.art: a guy with a feathered dirty-blond mullet in a patched denim vest and a teenager standing together on a van roof in headlights, the guy reading from a crumpled page in the teenager's hand

reactions.cult: Satanic panic? Dude, I just like the guitar solos. The robes are new, though.
reactions.cosmic: Giant eye in the sky, tentacles, end of the world? That's every album in my van, man.
reactions.creature: It's got claws and it lives in the junk? I've worked here three years, man. That's my turf.

name: Zelda Fishbein
role: Former scream queen, video store clerk
bio: From 1951 to 1959 Zelda Fishbein screamed her way through eleven pictures, including Brides of the Atom and The Thing from Crystal Springs, and walked away from the movies when the studio wanted her to become Zelda Fisher and fix her nose. She kept her name and her nose. Now she works the counter at Rewind Video, judges your rentals out loud, and lives in a little house by the creek with Ruth, her 'roommate' of thirty years, who makes the best rugelach in the county. Zelda knows exactly how every monster movie ends, and why. She is tough, nosy, hilarious and sentimental; her flaw is that she spoils every ending, never lets anyone take care of her, and still quietly mourns the scream they kept and the name they cut.

perk.name: Final Girl Rules
perk.text: Zelda has outlived forty movie slashers and taught you every rule: +2 on every roll against slasher nightmares.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store staff vest over a black mock-neck sweater, a string of pearls, a black pencil skirt, holding a VHS tape like a dagger, posed in the classic scream: one hand at her cheek, mouth wide, cat-eye glasses flashing, her other hand jabbing a VHS tape straight at a looming masked shadow, a wall of lurid horror tape boxes glowing behind her

neutral.line: That one? The babysitter lives. Don't tell anybody I told you.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store staff vest over a black mock-neck sweater, a string of pearls, a black pencil skirt, holding a VHS tape like a dagger, leaning on a video store counter beside a stack of returns, one eyebrow arched

happy.line: Kiddo, that was a scream worthy of a close-up.
happy.art: Portrait of a 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store staff vest over a black mock-neck sweater, a string of pearls, a black pencil skirt, holding a VHS tape like a dagger, laughing with a hand on her pearls, red lipstick bright, eyes crinkled

scared.line: In the picture, this is where the music gets quiet. I hate when it gets quiet.
scared.art: Portrait of a 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store staff vest over a black mock-neck sweater, a string of pearls, a black pencil skirt, holding a VHS tape like a dagger, peering over the top of her cat-eye glasses into a dark aisle, clutching the counter

angry.line: I screamed for a living. Don't make me do it for free.
angry.art: Portrait of a 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store staff vest over a black mock-neck sweater, a string of pearls, a black pencil skirt, holding a VHS tape like a dagger, slapping a VHS tape down on the counter, eyes narrowed behind cat-eye glasses

sad.line: They kept my scream and cut my name. It's in forty movies and nobody knows it's me.
sad.art: Portrait of a 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store staff vest over a black mock-neck sweater, a string of pearls, a black pencil skirt, holding a VHS tape like a dagger, holding an old black-and-white publicity photo of a young screaming starlet

determined.line: Never split up, never go in the basement, and never say you'll be right back.
determined.art: Portrait of a 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store staff vest over a black mock-neck sweater, a string of pearls, a black pencil skirt, holding a VHS tape like a dagger, pulling on driving gloves, a VHS tape tucked under her arm, chin raised

meet.title: The Night-Drop Slot
meet.place: The counter, Rewind Video
meet.text: Behind the counter at Rewind Video, under a poster for a 1954 picture called Brides of the Atom, a woman with a silver-streaked bouffant is eyeing the night-drop slot. It has been growling since yesterday. "Every morning there's a tape in there that nobody rented," Zelda Fishbein says, "and every tape has a new ending." She looks at your hands. "Before you ask, no, you can't rent the adults-only aisle. And yes, I'm going to judge whatever you pick."
meet.art: A 63-year-old Jewish woman with olive skin and deep laugh lines, a dramatic silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, a red video store vest over a black mock-neck sweater and a string of pearls, leaning on a cluttered rental counter beneath an old painted monster-movie advertisement and eyeing a metal night-drop slot in the wall with its flap rattling, a teenager at the counter, warm store light, medium shot

choices.label: Take her challenge and name how a classic monster movie ends

success.text: "The scientist's daughter climbs the tower and talks to it. Nobody shoots." Zelda takes off her glasses. "Nobody your age knows that one. I was the daughter." She slides an employee discount card across the counter. "You're with me now, kiddo."
success.art: A woman in cat-eye glasses sliding a card across a video store counter to a teenager, an old black-and-white movie still on the wall behind her

failure.text: You guess wrong. Zelda clutches her pearls like you've insulted her mother. She hands you a tape with a sticky note: WATCH THIS. THEN COME BACK. "Tomorrow. And you rewind it before you return it."
failure.art: A woman in a bouffant handing a teenager a VHS tape with a sticky note on it across a counter, a disappointed look on her face

choices.label: Ask about the poster and the pictures she made

success.text: Her whole face lights up. Twenty minutes later you know about the rubber atom suit, the director who drank, and the scream she recorded once and heard in forty movies after. "Nobody asks anymore." She pats your hand. "Come by any time. I mean it. I'll come by too, if there's trouble."
success.art: A woman in cat-eye glasses telling a story with big hand gestures across a video store counter, a teenager laughing, an old painted movie advertisement above them

failure.text: "I don't sign autographs for gawkers," she says, and turns away to sort returns. Then, more softly: "Sorry, kid. Bad morning. Come back tomorrow and ask me again."
failure.art: A woman in a bouffant turning away to sort a stack of videotapes, a teenager standing awkwardly at the counter

choices.label: Reach into the growling night-drop slot for today's tape

success.text: Your arm goes in up to the elbow and comes out with a warm tape labeled with tomorrow's date. Zelda puts it in the counter VCR. It shows the Heartstone at night with a crowd around it. She ejects it, grim. "Final girls don't go it alone. Neither do I. I'm coming with you."
success.art: A teenager pulling a VHS tape out of a metal night-drop slot, a woman in cat-eye glasses watching a small counter TV showing a glowing geode at night

failure.text: The slot snaps shut on your fingers like a mouth. When you yank free, there's a perfect ring of tiny teeth marks on your knuckles. Zelda hands you a bandage. "Rule six: don't put your hand in anything. Come back tomorrow."
failure.art: A metal night-drop slot snapping shut, a teenager clutching their hand, a woman in cat-eye glasses holding out a bandage

arc.title: Zelda Fisher
arc.place: The counter, Rewind Video, opening time
arc.text: A box of re-release tapes arrived this morning: BRIDES OF THE ATOM, remastered for home video. Zelda has one in her hand, and her red fingernail is on the back of the box, under the cast list, where it says Zelda Fisher. "Thirty-two years," she says, "and they still couldn't spell it." She is smiling. She is very much not fine. There are forty-eight copies.
arc.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest at a cluttered video store counter holding up a videotape box and tapping the cast list with a red fingernail, a carton of identical tapes open beside her

choices.label: Get the label maker and fix all forty-eight boxes with her

success.text: Forty-eight little black labels, one by one: ZELDA FISHBEIN. She does the first; you do the next forty-seven while she pretends to sort returns and supervises every single one. When you finish, she lines them up on the New Releases wall. "Now that," she says, "is a picture worth renting."
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest admiring a long row of videotape boxes on a store shelf, each with a small black label on the back, a teenager holding a label maker

failure.text: The label maker jams on copy six and prints FISHBEINFISHBEINFISHB on one long strip. Zelda laughs so hard she has to sit on the step stool. "Leave it," she wheezes, and sticks the whole strip across one box. "That one's mine. I'm keeping that one."
failure.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest laughing on a step stool behind a video store counter, a long curling strip of label tape dangling from a jammed label maker in a teenager's hands

choices.label: Help her write a furious letter to the distributor

success.text: She dictates; you type on the store's ancient typewriter. It is a masterpiece of politeness with knives in it. She signs it with a flourish, the whole name, and seals the envelope with a kiss of red lipstick. "They kept my scream for thirty years. They can have my name with it."
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest pressing a red lipstick kiss onto a sealed envelope at a video store counter, a teenager at an old typewriter beside her

failure.text: Her first draft is perfect. Her second gets angrier. By the fifth she's teary and calling it allergies, and the letter just says MY NAME IS ZELDA FISHBEIN in capitals. "Mail that one," she says. "It's the only true one."
failure.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest dabbing her eyes behind cat-eye glasses, a pile of crumpled letters by an old typewriter, one sheet in capital letters held up by a teenager

choices.label: Ask her why she walked away when the studio asked her to change

success.text: "Because my grandmother came over on a boat with that nose and that name and nothing else," Zelda says. "They wanted a girl who could be anybody. I wanted to be somebody." She shrugs, as if it cost her nothing, and you can see exactly what it cost. "Best bad decision I ever made, kiddo."
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest leaning on the counter with her chin raised and a faint proud smile, an old black-and-white publicity photo of a young starlet pinned behind her

failure.text: "Ancient history," she snaps, and goes to rewind tapes that are already rewound. You let her. Ten minutes later she slides you a rugelach from a tin under the counter without a word, which you are learning is how Zelda apologizes, and how she says thank you.
failure.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest sliding a small pastry across a video store counter toward a teenager while pointedly looking the other way

arc.title: My Roommate
arc.place: The back room, Rewind Video, lunch hour
arc.text: Ruth came by at noon with a tin of rugelach and a thermos, kissed Zelda's cheek over the counter, quick, and a customer asked who that was. "My roommate," Zelda said, the way she has said it for thirty years. Now she's in the back room among the busted VCRs, eating rugelach too fast. "Friday is thirty years," she says, not looking at you. "We met on a picture. She did my makeup. And I still introduce her like she splits the gas bill."
arc.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest sitting among stacks of broken VCRs in a cramped stockroom, an open tin of pastries on her lap, a teenager in the doorway

choices.label: Ask her what she wishes she had said

success.text: Zelda takes off her glasses and wipes them for a long time. "I'd say: this is Ruth. She did my face for eleven pictures and she's been doing my heart for thirty years. Leave a tip." She laughs at herself, wet-eyed. "Listen to me. Sixty-three and still rehearsing."
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest polishing her cat-eye glasses with a handkerchief and laughing through tears in a stockroom, a teenager smiling beside the VCR stacks

failure.text: "What I wish? I wish people minded their own business." She means the customer, not you, but the door is shut for now. Still, as you leave, you see her take a photo off the corkboard, a young Ruth holding a powder puff at the edge of a film set, and tuck it into her purse.
failure.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest slipping an old photograph of a young makeup artist with a powder puff into her purse, a corkboard of snapshots behind her

choices.label: Help her plan a thirtieth-anniversary surprise for Ruth

success.text: You plan it on the back of a late-fee slip: Friday, after close, the store TV, the picture where they met, and every rugelach in the county. Zelda reads it twice. "A private screening." She tucks the slip into her vest pocket. "Or maybe not so private. Maybe the kids should come."
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest reading a scribbled plan on a small pink slip with a widening smile, a teenager pointing at it, a television on a cart behind them

failure.text: Your plans get bigger and bigger until there's a band, a cake shaped like an atom and a banner, and Zelda puts her hand over yours. "Kiddo. Ruth hates fuss. Ruth hates fuss almost as much as she loves me." You did learn the important part: it's Friday, and it matters.
failure.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest resting a hand over a teenager's pencil on a crowded sketch of a giant atom-shaped cake, her eyebrow raised, VCR stacks around them

choices.label: Tell her the crew would cheer for them, loud

success.text: "You don't know that," Zelda says. "I do," you say, and you name every single person on the crew. She listens with her arms crossed. Then she uncrosses them. "A whole crew of meshuggeners." She almost smiles. "I might hold you to that."
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest uncrossing her arms with a reluctant smile in a cluttered stockroom, a teenager counting names off on their fingers

failure.text: You say it with so much conviction it comes out like a speech, and Zelda arches an eyebrow. "Thank you, Senator." Then she sobers. "It's not you kids I worry about. It's thirty years of habit." But she writes FRIDAY on the back of her hand in pen.
failure.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest writing a word on the back of her hand with a ballpoint pen, a teenager standing awkwardly mid-gesture in a stockroom

arc.title: Coming Attractions
arc.place: Rewind Video, the Halloween-week matinee
arc.text: Folding chairs between the aisles, the big TV on a cart, and the newly relabeled BRIDES OF THE ATOM in the VCR. The store is full: the crew, Toby with his camcorder, a dozen regulars, and Ruth in the back row with a tin on her lap. Zelda stands up front in her red vest and pearls to introduce the picture, and you can see the index cards shaking in her hands. She looks at you. Then she looks at Ruth.
arc.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest standing in front of a television on a cart holding index cards, folding chairs packed between video store aisles, a silver-haired woman with a pastry tin in the back row

choices.label: Hold up a hand-lettered sign from the front row: WE LOVE YOU, ZELDA

success.text: She reads your sign, laughs out loud and tosses the index cards over her shoulder. "My name is Zelda Fishbein. I screamed in eleven pictures and they cut my name from every one." She points to the back row. "And that is Ruth. She did my face for all eleven. Thirty years on Friday." The crew is on its feet before she finishes.
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest flinging index cards over her shoulder and pointing to the back row of a packed video store, a teenager in front holding up a hand-lettered sign, the crowd rising

failure.text: Your sign is upside down. Zelda notices, of course, and the whole room turns to look at you. In the laughter, something in her loosens. "Kiddo, it's upside down. Like my whole life." Then she says it anyway: her name, every letter, and Ruth's, and thirty years. The applause rattles the tape racks.
failure.art: A teenager holding an upside-down sign in a packed video store, a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest laughing at the front, the audience turning in their folding chairs

choices.label: Ask her to teach the whole room her famous scream

success.text: Zelda's eyes go bright. She teaches the store: breath from the belly, hand at the cheek, and forty people scream at once, so loud the night-drop slot rattles. Then, flushed and triumphant, she says her name into the quiet, all of it, and holds out a hand. Ruth comes up to take it. "Thirty years," Zelda says. "Applaud, you animals."
success.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest holding hands with a silver-haired woman at the front of a video store, a room full of people in folding chairs with hands at their cheeks mid-scream

failure.text: Your scream comes out a squeak. Zelda laughs, kindly. "My first take sounded exactly like that." Then she does the real one, the one in forty movies, and the room goes silent with awe. "That's me," she says. "Zelda Fishbein." She nods to the back row. "And that's my Ruth."
failure.art: a woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red video store vest mid-scream with one hand at her cheek in front of a television, a stunned audience in folding chairs, a teenager in the front row covering a grin

choices.label: Slip into the back row and sit with Ruth

success.text: Ruth squeezes your hand. "She's going to chicken out," she whispers. "She always does. I don't mind." Up front, Zelda sees the two of you together and something in her face decides. "Before the picture," she says, "I want to introduce the love of my life." Ruth's tin of rugelach hits the floor. Everybody cheers.
success.art: A silver-haired woman in the back row of a packed video store dropping a pastry tin in surprise, a teenager beside her grinning, a woman in cat-eye glasses pointing at her from the front

failure.text: You sit down too hard and the folding chair folds, loudly, with you in it. Ruth helps you up, giggling, and Zelda, at the front, cracks up so hard the nerves go out of her. "That's Ruth," she says, pointing, "helping that one up. She's been helping me up for thirty years." It isn't the speech she rehearsed. It's better.
failure.art: A teenager tangled in a collapsed folding chair at the back of a video store, a silver-haired woman helping them up, a woman in cat-eye glasses laughing at the front

reactions.slasher: Never split up. Never say 'I'll be right back.' I said it in 1953 and they cut me out of reel two.
reactions.creature: I spent a summer in a rubber suit next to one of these. Talk to it. They always want to be talked to.
reactions.camp: Camp? Darling, I invented camp. I just did it in black and white.
reactions.paranormal: Ghosts are just extras who never got their names in the credits. Believe me.

name: Kevin "Kev" Park
role: Paperboy with a map of every secret
bio: Kevin Park throws the Glimmer Falls Gazette onto ninety-one porches every morning by 6 a.m. from a red BMX with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes. His parents run Park's Cleaners on Main, so he also knows whose suits came in with mud on the cuffs. He knows which dogs bite, which porch lights stay on all night, who gets weird mail, and that nobody, ever, delivers to number 13. Kev considers himself a businessman, not a kid, and sells information for candy at reasonable rates. He is fast, funny, endlessly curious and braver on a bike than on foot. His flaw is that he cannot keep a secret to save his life, and he talks fastest when he is scared.

perk.name: Paper Route Tips
perk.text: Kev splits his tips with his business partners, as is only fair: +2 quarters each dawn.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack slung across a blue hooded sweatshirt, cuffed jeans with bandaged knees, red high-tops, riding a red BMX bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes, popping a wheelie on the red BMX down a moonlit cul-de-sac, one hand flinging a rolled newspaper like a missile, the sack of papers flying open behind him, every porch light on the street snapping on at once

neutral.line: Number nine gets the Gazette, eleven gets the weird mail, and nobody gets thirteen.
neutral.art: Portrait of a skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack slung across a blue hooded sweatshirt, cuffed jeans with bandaged knees, red high-tops, riding a red BMX bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes, straddling his BMX at the curb, rolling a newspaper with one hand

happy.line: Tip day! Somebody gave me a whole dollar!
happy.art: Portrait of a skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack slung across a blue hooded sweatshirt, cuffed jeans with bandaged knees, red high-tops, riding a red BMX bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes, holding a crumpled dollar bill over his head, gap-toothed grin, cap askew

scared.line: Thirteen's porch light just came on. Nobody lives at thirteen.
scared.art: Portrait of a skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack slung across a blue hooded sweatshirt, cuffed jeans with bandaged knees, red high-tops, riding a red BMX bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes, clutching his handlebars, eyes huge, staring at something off to one side

angry.line: Hey! I'm not a kid, I'm a businessman.
angry.art: Portrait of a skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack slung across a blue hooded sweatshirt, cuffed jeans with bandaged knees, red high-tops, riding a red BMX bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes, arms crossed over his newspaper sack, scowling up, cap pulled low

sad.line: Everybody on my route knows my name. Nobody at school does.
sad.art: Portrait of a skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack slung across a blue hooded sweatshirt, cuffed jeans with bandaged knees, red high-tops, riding a red BMX bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes, sitting on a curb with his bike on its side, picking at a bandage on his knee

determined.line: I know a shortcut. I always know a shortcut.
determined.art: Portrait of a skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack slung across a blue hooded sweatshirt, cuffed jeans with bandaged knees, red high-tops, riding a red BMX bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes, crouched low on the BMX pedals, cap turned forward, eyes narrowed down the street

meet.title: Number Thirteen
meet.place: The end of the cul-de-sac, Crystal Street
meet.text: A red BMX is lying on its side at the curb in front of 13 Crystal Street, the model home nobody ever bought. Its owner, a skinny kid in a backwards cap, is standing as far from the lawn as physics allows. Half his newspapers have blown across the perfect grass to the perfect porch. "I don't go on that lawn," Kev Park says. "Nobody goes on that lawn. Mr. Pruitt's dog went on that lawn in 1984 and now it only barks backward."
meet.art: A skinny 12-year-old Korean American boy with a big gap-toothed grin, a black bowl cut under a backwards red baseball cap, a canvas newspaper sack across a blue hooded sweatshirt and bandaged knees, standing well back on the sidewalk in front of an immaculate pastel model home, his red bike with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes lying at the curb and newspapers scattered across the flawless striped lawn, a teenager stepping onto the grass, early morning light, wide shot

choices.label: Walk onto the lawn at 13 and gather his papers

success.text: The grass is soft as carpet and the front curtains twitch, but you gather every paper and walk, not run, back to the curb. Kev stares at you like you just landed on the moon. "You're my business partner now. Fifty-fifty. Okay, sixty-forty. Okay, fifty-fifty."
success.art: A teenager walking calmly off a perfect lawn with an armful of newspapers, curtains twitching in the model home behind them, a boy on the sidewalk gaping

failure.text: You reach the third paper and the sprinklers come on with a hiss like a breath. The front door clicks open an inch. You run. Kev is already halfway down the street. "Come back tomorrow!" he yells over his shoulder. "From a DISTANCE!"
failure.art: A teenager fleeing across a perfect lawn as sprinklers hiss on and the front door of a model home creaks open, a boy on a BMX pedaling away

choices.label: Offer him a deal: help with the route for one good secret

success.text: You finish his route together in record time. As promised, he leans in close. "Number 7. The new family. Their lights come on all at the same second every night, every room. Like one guy flips one switch." He shakes your hand like a banker. "Pleasure doing business. Partners."
success.art: A boy on a BMX and a teenager on foot tossing newspapers onto suburban porches, the boy leaning in to whisper, a pristine house glowing in the background

failure.text: Kev is a better negotiator than you. By the end of the route you have somehow paid him a quarter for the privilege of helping him. "Come back tomorrow," he says brightly. "I'll give you the friends-and-family rate."
failure.art: A grinning boy on a BMX pocketing a quarter from a bewildered teenager on a suburban sidewalk at dawn

choices.label: Race him to finish the rest of the route before 6 a.m.

success.text: You sprint, he pedals, and every paper lands on the right porch at 5:58. Kev skids to a stop, breathless and delighted. "Nobody's ever kept up with me. You're hired. You're crew. You're both."
success.art: A boy on a red BMX and a teenager running side by side down a suburban street at dawn, newspapers flying onto porches

failure.text: You throw a paper through Mrs. Abernathy's screen door. She comes out in curlers. Kev pedals away so fast his playing cards scream. You get the lecture alone. Tomorrow, he'll owe you one.
failure.art: An angry woman in curlers and a bathrobe holding a newspaper at a torn screen door, a teenager standing guilty on the porch, a BMX speeding away

arc.title: The Scoop
arc.place: Kev's front steps, Crystal Street, after his route
arc.text: Kev is on his porch steps with a stack of Gazettes, a pencil behind his ear and a flyer from the paper: YOUNG REPORTERS CONTEST, WIN $25 AND A BYLINE ON THE KIDS' PAGE. "I deliver ninety-one papers a day and my name has never been in one," he says. "I know everything on this route. Everything. I just need the big story." He flips open a notebook labeled ROUTE BOOK, TOP SECRET, underlined three times. "So. Who do we interview first?"
arc.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack sitting on suburban porch steps with a stack of newspapers, waving a flyer and a battered notebook at a teenager, a red BMX on the lawn

choices.label: Suggest he interview Pearl Washington about her war years

success.text: Pearl gives you both lemonade and two hours on being a radio operator in 1944. Kev fills nine pages and forgets to talk the entire time, which may be a personal record. Walking home he says, stunned, "She asked me questions back. About me. Like I was a real reporter."
success.art: An elderly Black woman in a porch rocker telling a story with her hands, a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack scribbling furiously in a notebook, a teenager holding two glasses of lemonade

failure.text: Kev knocks too loudly, three times, and Pearl comes to the door mid-nap in curlers and a mood. Kev drops his notebook in the azaleas. Pearl relents and laughs. "Come back with better questions, Mr. Reporter. And knock like a person."
failure.art: An elderly woman in curlers at a screen door with arms folded, a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack digging a notebook out of an azalea bush, a teenager wincing on the steps

choices.label: Help him stake out number 13 for the big scoop

success.text: You hide behind the hedge across from 13 with a thermos and binoculars for an hour. At exactly 4:13, every curtain in the model home closes by itself. Kev writes it all down, hands shaking, then looks at you. "Nobody'll believe it. A real reporter needs a story people can check." He underlines that twice.
success.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack and a teenager crouched behind a hedge with binoculars, across the street an immaculate model home with every curtain drawn shut

failure.text: Kev talks the whole stakeout, nonstop, in a whisper that is not a whisper. At 4:13 the porch light at 13 clicks on and you both bolt for three blocks. Panting, Kev says, "Okay. Maybe the big story isn't the haunted house. Maybe it's... I don't know yet."
failure.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack and a teenager sprinting down a suburban sidewalk, a single porch light glowing on a too-perfect house behind them

choices.label: Ask to see what is really in the top-secret route book

success.text: It's amazing and a little alarming: every dog's name, every porch light, who gets letters from far away and who gets seed catalogs. Kev beams. Then you ask, "Do they know you write it down?" and he goes quiet. "Is that bad? I never told anybody. Okay. I told everybody some of it."
success.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack holding open a notebook crammed with tiny handwriting and hand-drawn maps of a cul-de-sac, a teenager leaning in to read it

failure.text: Kev snatches it back. "Top secret means top secret." Then, because he cannot help himself, he tells you seven things from it anyway in under a minute, and catches himself, horrified. "I gotta stop doing that. Don't tell anybody I do that."
failure.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack clutching a notebook to his chest with a horrified expression, hand over his mouth, a teenager on the porch steps trying to hold in a laugh

arc.title: Off the Record
arc.place: The bus bench at the end of Crystal Street, late afternoon
arc.text: Kev skids up on his BMX, pale and talking at top speed. Collecting at the Gaines house, he saw Mr. Gaines's kitchen table: a library literacy-program workbook, a brand-new library card, and Mr. Gaines's big, careful handwriting copying out the alphabet. Mr. Gaines, who coached Little League for twenty years, is learning to read. "It's the biggest story on the route," Kev says. "It's an amazing story. It'd win." He already has a headline. He also looks like he might throw up.
arc.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack skidding his red BMX to a stop beside a bus bench at the end of a cul-de-sac, a teenager sitting there, late afternoon shadows long

choices.label: Walk with him to the Gaines house and ask Mr. Gaines what he wants

success.text: Mr. Gaines listens to Kev's stammered confession on the porch and is quiet a long time. "Fifty-eight years I hid it," he says. "You're the first one who asked instead of told." Not in the paper, he says. Not yet. Then he hands Kev the workbook. "You can quiz me Thursdays, though. Reporter."
success.art: A gray-haired man on a porch handing a reading workbook to a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack, a teenager standing on the step below, warm porch light

failure.text: Kev panics on the porch and blurts out everything he saw, all at once. Mr. Gaines goes stiff, then sighs. "Well. Now you know." He asks Kev to keep it to himself, and Kev promises with his whole face. Walking back, Kev is quiet for once. "That was the hardest promise I ever made."
failure.art: A gray-haired man in a doorway with a heavy sigh, a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack with both hands raised in a frantic promise, a teenager behind him on the walk

choices.label: Tell him what real reporters do with a source's secret

success.text: You tell him about protecting sources, the kind of thing reporters in movies go to jail over. Kev listens with his whole body. "So a real reporter would kill the story." He tears the headline page out of the route book and folds it into his pocket. "Then I'll find a better one. One nobody gets hurt by."
success.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack tearing a page out of a notebook on a bus bench and folding it into his pocket, a teenager beside him nodding

failure.text: You tangle yourself up explaining, and Kev pounces on every loophole. "What if I change his name? What if I say 'a local man'?" Then he answers himself. "Everybody'd know. It's a cul-de-sac." He slumps on the bench. "Being a businessman was easier."
failure.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack slumped dramatically on a bus bench with his cap over his eyes, a teenager beside him mid-explanation with both hands spread

choices.label: Say nothing and let him work it out out loud

success.text: You sit on the bench and say nothing, which is the hardest thing in the world next to Kev. He talks for nine minutes straight, argues both sides, loses to himself twice, and finally crosses out the headline. "I'm not telling. I'm not." He looks amazed. "I've never not told before."
success.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack crossing out a headline in a notebook with a firm pencil stroke on a bus bench, a teenager sitting quietly beside him

failure.text: The silence gets to you and you jump in at minute four, and Kev hops onto your idea like a train. Then he climbs back off. "No. If you tell me what to do, it's just a deal. I gotta pick it." He crosses out the headline himself, slowly, and you both watch the pencil.
failure.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack slowly drawing a pencil line through a word in a notebook, a teenager beside him on a bench watching the pencil

arc.title: Ninety-One Porches
arc.place: Kev's front steps, Crystal Street, deadline day
arc.text: The contest deadline is five o'clock, and Kev has a new story: NINETY-ONE PORCHES, the people on his route, written with every single one's permission. Pearl's war. Mrs. Abernathy's prize roses. Mr. Gaines, who said Kev could print that he 'started a new chapter this year,' which Kev considers an excellent pun. It's four handwritten pages, and he has to type it. He's on the steps with his mom's typewriter and a face full of terror. "What if it's boring? What if nobody at school even reads the kids' page?"
arc.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack on porch steps beside a heavy typewriter and four handwritten pages, a kitchen clock visible through the screen door, a teenager arriving at a run

choices.label: Type it up together, fast, and beat the five o'clock deadline

success.text: You read, Kev types, two fingers flying. At 4:51 you jog beside his BMX all the way to the Gazette office, and the editor reads page one right there at the desk. "Kid, this is good." On the way home Kev rides down Crystal Street yelling every neighbor's name, and every porch yells back.
success.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack riding a red BMX down a cul-de-sac with one fist in the air, neighbors waving from their porches, a teenager jogging alongside

failure.text: The typewriter ribbon runs out on page three. You finish it in Kev's neatest handwriting and reach the Gazette at 5:02. The editor sighs, looks at Kev's face, and takes it anyway. "Next time, early." It runs the week after, small, as an honorable mention, with his name right on top.
failure.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack handing a half-typed, half-handwritten story across a newspaper office counter to a weary editor, a wall clock reading just past five

choices.label: Have him read it to his parents at the cleaners first

success.text: Mr. and Mrs. Park stop pressing shirts to listen. Kev reads all four pages without speeding up once. When he finishes, his dad takes the story without a word and tapes it in the front window of Park's Cleaners, facing Main Street, where everyone can see. His mom fixes his cap. Kev is silent the whole way home, which has never happened.
success.art: A Korean American man taping handwritten pages to the front window of a dry cleaner's shop, a woman straightening a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack's cap, a teenager watching from the sidewalk

failure.text: Kev reads so fast nobody can follow, and a steam press hisses through the best part. His dad asks him to start over. The second time, slower, his mom laughs at the right joke, and his dad nods once, which for Mr. Park is a standing ovation. "Mail it," he says. "Then come back and fold."
failure.art: a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack reading pages aloud in a dry cleaner's shop through a cloud of steam from a pressing machine, his parents listening behind the counter

choices.label: Help him deliver a carbon copy to every porch in the story

success.text: You walk the whole route a second time in one afternoon, a carbon copy for every porch. People come out. Pearl reads hers on the step and wipes her eyes. Mr. Gaines reads his slowly, out loud, every word, and gives Kev a whole dollar. "Best paper I ever got," he says.
success.art: A gray-haired man on a porch reading a page aloud with careful concentration, a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack holding a canvas sack of papers and beaming, a teenager behind him

failure.text: Your legs give out at porch sixty, and Kev finishes the last thirty-one alone while you lie on Pearl's lawn. He comes back at dusk, wrecked and glowing. "Mr. Gaines read his out loud," he says. "Every word. By himself."
failure.art: A teenager lying flat on a front lawn at dusk, a skinny boy with a black bowl cut under a backwards red cap and a canvas newspaper sack standing over them with an empty sack and a huge gap-toothed grin

reactions.paranormal: I KNEW number thirteen was haunted. I've been charging extra for that info since 1984.
reactions.creature: I know every dog on this street. That is NOT one of the dogs on this street.
reactions.tech: A computer that knows everybody's business? That's my job. I'm calling my union.

name: Raven
bio: Raven reads tarot for a quarter on the steps of the Ashworth mausoleum in Pinecrest Cemetery, dresses entirely in velvet from the St. Jude's rummage sale, and knows the name and story on every grave older than 1900. In 1986 there aren't many words for someone who is neither a boy nor a girl, so Raven just says, "Call me Raven, no pronoun needed," and waits to see who listens; the crew learns to say they, and it means more to Raven than they will ever admit. They are dry, dramatic, aloof until they decide you are worth it, and secretly obsessed with cheesy creature features and cartoon bears. Their flaw is that they test everyone before they trust them, and they would rather tell your fortune than talk about their own.

perk.name: The Spread
perk.text: Raven lays out the cards each morning and reads where the truth is hiding: the case board shows your odds of finding each clue.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of an olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings, a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, a long black skirt over chunky buckled boots, silver rings on every finger, holding a fanned tarot deck, standing atop a mossy mausoleum under a full moon, frock coat billowing, a spread of glowing tarot cards whirling in the air around them, a crow on one shoulder and the cemetery fog parting below

neutral.line: Pick a card. Don't tell me. I already know.
neutral.art: Portrait of an olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings, a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, a long black skirt over chunky buckled boots, silver rings on every finger, holding a fanned tarot deck, seated on a mausoleum step shuffling the tarot deck, one eyebrow raised

happy.line: The Sun, upright. Don't make it weird. I'm smiling.
happy.art: Portrait of an olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings, a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, a long black skirt over chunky buckled boots, silver rings on every finger, holding a fanned tarot deck, a small reluctant smile, holding up a single golden tarot card

scared.line: Death means change. It means change. Please mean change.
scared.art: Portrait of an olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings, a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, a long black skirt over chunky buckled boots, silver rings on every finger, holding a fanned tarot deck, staring at a single card in their hand, face pale beneath the eyeliner

angry.line: Say my name right or don't say it at all.
angry.art: Portrait of an olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings, a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, a long black skirt over chunky buckled boots, silver rings on every finger, holding a fanned tarot deck, eyes narrowed, slapping a card face-down on the stone, rings glinting

sad.line: Everybody wants their fortune told. Nobody asks how I'm doing.
sad.art: Portrait of an olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings, a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, a long black skirt over chunky buckled boots, silver rings on every finger, holding a fanned tarot deck, hugging their knees on a mausoleum step, cards scattered at their feet

determined.line: The cards are dealt. Now we play them.
determined.art: Portrait of an olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings, a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, a long black skirt over chunky buckled boots, silver rings on every finger, holding a fanned tarot deck, sweeping a hand across a spread of cards, coat flaring, chin lifted

meet.title: The Tower
meet.place: The Ashworth mausoleum, Pinecrest Cemetery
meet.text: On the steps of the oldest mausoleum in Pinecrest sits someone in plum velvet with a deck of tarot cards and a hand-lettered sign: FORTUNES 25 CENTS, TRUTH EXTRA. A crow on the roof watches you. They flip a card before you even sit down: a tower struck by lightning. "Huh," they say. "That's yours. That's bad." When you ask their name, they say, "Raven. No pronoun needed." Then they wait, the way people wait who have been disappointed before.
meet.art: An olive-skinned 16-year-old with sharp cheekbones and dark watchful eyes, a teased black bob with a long asymmetrical fringe, winged black eyeliner, dark plum lipstick, silver crescent-moon earrings and a thrifted plum velvet frock coat over a black lace shirt, sitting on the steps of an old stone mausoleum with a tarot spread laid out and one painted tarot face turned up, a small cardboard square propped beside them, a crow perched on the roof above, a teenager sitting down across from them, overcast afternoon light, medium shot

choices.label: Pay your quarter and let them finish the reading

success.text: Tower, then the Star, then the Six of Cups. "Something falls," Raven says, "and then you get help from people you didn't expect. Kids. Old friends." They study you. "The cards say I'm one of them. I hate when the cards are right." They fall in beside you.
success.art: Three tarot cards laid out on a mausoleum step, a teenager and a goth teen in velvet leaning over them, a crow watching from above

failure.text: A cold wind lifts every card off the step and scatters them across the graves. Raven watches them go without moving. "The cards say come back tomorrow," they say. "Also help me find the Hanged Man. He's under a cherub somewhere."
failure.art: Tarot cards blowing across a foggy cemetery between gravestones, a goth teen in velvet watching calmly from a mausoleum step

choices.label: Say their name right and ask how they're doing
