success.text: "Nice to meet you, Raven. How are you doing today?" There is a very long pause. The crow caws. Raven looks down at the cards so you don't see their face. "Nobody ever asks the reader." They tuck the Tower back in the deck. "Okay. I'll come with you. Somebody has to keep you alive."
success.art: A goth teen in velvet looking down at a tarot deck to hide a smile, a teenager sitting beside them on the mausoleum steps, a crow cawing above

failure.text: You start the sentence three different ways and trip over every one. Raven rolls their eyes, but not unkindly. "It's a new word for an old thing. Practice. Come back tomorrow and try again." They flip you a card for luck: the Fool.
failure.art: A goth teen in velvet flicking a single tarot card to an embarrassed teenager, a faint smile on their face, mausoleum stones behind them

choices.label: Follow the crow into the founders' row

success.text: The crow leads you to a cracked headstone from 1859 with no name, only a carved sprig of rosemary. Raven kneels and touches it. "Every grave here has a name but this one. Somebody wanted her forgotten." They stand, coat swirling. "Fine. I'm in. We find out who."
success.art: A teenager and a goth teen in velvet kneeling at a weathered unnamed headstone carved with a sprig of rosemary, a crow perched on top, fog curling

failure.text: The crow leads you in a circle and then up onto a stone angel, which turns its head. It definitely turns its head. Raven drags you out the cemetery gate by your sleeve. "New rule: tomorrow, in daylight, and we don't follow birds."
failure.art: A stone cemetery angel with its head turned toward the viewer, a crow on its wing, two teenagers fleeing toward a wrought-iron gate

arc.title: Read the Reader
arc.place: The Ashworth mausoleum steps, Pinecrest Cemetery, dusk
arc.text: Raven is on the Ashworth mausoleum steps at dusk, the crow on the roof, the cemetery gone violet. Above the door, beside eleven bronze name plaques, is a twelfth space: bare stone and four old screw holes. "Somebody got taken down," Raven says. "I've sat under that blank for two years." Then, instead of dealing your fortune, they hold out the deck. "I've never read my own. Bad luck. So you do it. Three cards. Don't make it weird."
arc.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat holding out a tarot deck on the steps of a stone mausoleum at violet dusk, a row of bronze plaques above the door with one bare space, a crow on the roof

choices.label: Draw three cards for them and lay them out carefully

success.text: The Page of Cups, the Star, the Six of Pentacles. Raven reads them slowly. "Something tender I'm hiding. Hope. Somebody giving me something I didn't ask for." They look up at the blank space over the door. "I always felt like this was my spot. I never asked why." They pocket the Star.
success.art: Three tarot cards laid in a neat row on a mossy mausoleum step, a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat studying them, a teenager kneeling beside them

failure.text: You fumble the deck and cards scatter down the steps. Raven goes very still, and you think you've ruined it, but they pick up the three that landed face up. "The cards pick themselves when you're clumsy. House rule." The Star is one of them. They pocket it without explaining.
failure.art: Tarot cards scattered down mossy mausoleum steps, a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat calmly picking up three face-up cards, a teenager wincing

choices.label: Skip the cards and ask how they are really doing

success.text: Raven stares at you. Then, because you asked, they tell you: school is fine, home is complicated, and their mother still uses a name that was never theirs. "She's not mean. She just doesn't have a word for me. Hardly anybody does." They tap the blank stone over the door. "Somebody here didn't get a word either."
success.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat reaching up to touch a bare patch of stone beside a row of bronze plaques on a mausoleum, a teenager listening on the steps

failure.text: "I'm fine," Raven says, in the voice of someone who isn't, and starts dealing your cards instead, fast, like a shield. But when you leave, they say to your back, quietly, "Ask again tomorrow. I might answer."
failure.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat dealing tarot cards rapidly onto a mausoleum step with eyes down, a teenager walking away through cemetery fog and glancing back

choices.label: Suggest a creature-feature break on your battery TV

success.text: On a battery TV balanced on a gravestone, a man in a rubber lizard suit stomps a model city. Raven laughs, a real laugh, sudden and loud, then covers their mouth. Halfway through they say, eyes on the screen, "The monster's always just lonely. Have you noticed? Every time." The crow caws in agreement.
success.art: A small battery television balanced on a gravestone showing a rubber lizard monster, a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat laughing behind a ringed hand, a teenager beside them, a crow overhead

failure.text: The battery TV gets two channels: a farm report and static. Raven watches the static with great dignity. "Cosmic horror," they say. You both crack up. It isn't the feature, but it's the first time you've ever heard Raven laugh.
failure.art: A small television full of static propped on a gravestone at dusk, a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat and a teenager staring at it solemnly, then cracking up

arc.title: The Twelfth Name
arc.place: The records room under St. Jude's
arc.text: Father Iggy unlocked the basement, said "the 1890s are in the gray boxes," and went upstairs to tune his bass. Raven has the Ashworth file open on a folding table: a burial record for Sam Ashworth, 1811 to 1894, beekeeper, and a letter from a nephew asking for the plaque to be removed 'to spare the family name.' Under it, in older ink, the priest's own note: Sam lived as neither son nor daughter, kept the best bees in the county, and was loved. Raven's hands are very still on the page. "There was somebody," they say. "Right here. The whole time."
arc.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat bent over an open archive box under a bare bulb in a church basement, holding a yellowed handwritten letter, a teenager beside them, dusty gray boxes stacked high

choices.label: Copy every word by hand before the box goes back

success.text: You copy it all onto loose-leaf while Raven reads the letter four more times. When you hand over the pages, they fold them into the inside pocket of the velvet coat, over their heart. "Eighty-three years," they say. "Sam got to be old. Sam got to keep bees." They sound like someone breathing out for the first time in a long while.
success.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat folding handwritten loose-leaf pages into the inside pocket of a velvet coat, a teenager with a pencil at a folding table in a church basement

failure.text: The fluorescent tube dies and you lose half a page in the dark. When Father Iggy fixes it, you've copied the bee part twice and missed the priest's note. Raven memorizes it instead, mouthing it over and over. "I know every grave in this place by heart," they say. "I can memorize one more true thing."
failure.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat mouthing words with eyes closed in a dim church basement, a priest on a stepladder replacing a fluorescent tube, a teenager holding a flashlight

choices.label: Ask Raven what they would tell their mother about Sam

success.text: "That I'm not new," Raven says slowly. "That I'm not a phase from a record store. There was a Sam in 1850, and the town knew, and the bees didn't care." They look up. "I think I want to tell her. Not ask. Tell." They sound terrified and sure at once, like a card drawn upright.
success.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat looking up from an old letter with a fierce, frightened resolve under a bare bulb, a teenager across the folding table

failure.text: "Leave my mother out of this," Raven says, too fast, and shuts the box lid. Then they apologize to the box, of all things. After a while they say, "She'd call Sam eccentric. She says that about me." It hurts to hear, and it's still the most they've ever told you.
failure.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat resting both hands on a closed archive box with head bowed, a teenager sitting quietly across the folding table

choices.label: Run upstairs and ask Father Iggy if the old plaque survived

success.text: Iggy puts down his bass and leads you to a crate in the bell tower marked MISC BRONZE. Under three dented candlesticks is a small green plaque: SAM ASHWORTH, BEEKEEPER, BELOVED. Raven holds it in both hands. "Can we put it back?" Iggy grins. "It's a church. Putting things back is our whole deal."
success.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat holding a small tarnished bronze plaque in both hands in a dusty bell tower, a priest with a bass guitar strap grinning, a teenager beside an open crate

failure.text: You and Iggy search the bell tower for an hour, and the crate marked MISC BRONZE is full of doorknobs. Raven is quiet on the walk back, then says, "Fine. Then I'll make one myself. In chalk, if I have to. Sam gets a name."
failure.art: An open crate of old brass doorknobs in a dusty bell tower, a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat with arms folded and jaw set, a priest scratching his head

arc.title: No Pronoun Needed
arc.place: The Ashworth mausoleum, Pinecrest Cemetery, late afternoon
arc.text: Raven asked their mother to meet them at the cemetery, and she came, in her good coat, holding her purse like a shield. Above the mausoleum door the twelfth space has a name in it again: Sam Ashworth, beekeeper, beloved. Raven stands under it in plum velvet, the deck in their pocket, not using it. "I'll do the talking," they told you on the way. "You stand where I can see you."
arc.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat standing beneath a row of mausoleum name plaques in golden afternoon light, facing a woman in a good wool coat clutching a purse, a teenager a few steps behind

choices.label: Stand right where they can see you, and stay

success.text: Raven tells their mother about Sam: the bees, the eighty-three years, the priest who wrote it down. Then they tell her about themself. Their mother is quiet a long time, looking up at the name. "Sam," she says. Then, carefully, like a word in a new language: "Raven. My Raven." Raven turns to you, eyeliner running, with the smallest, most stunned smile.
success.art: A woman in a wool coat cupping the cheek of a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat beneath a mausoleum plaque, the teen's eyeliner running as they smile, a teenager standing steady nearby

failure.text: Your nerve wobbles and you drift toward the gate, and Raven loses sight of you mid-sentence. They falter. But their mother steps closer and asks, "Who was Sam?" and Raven has to answer. It's slow. She uses the old name once and corrects herself, red-faced. "I'll practice," she says. "Teach me." Raven looks to the gate and nods: you came back.
failure.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat and a woman in a wool coat talking quietly beside a mausoleum, a teenager walking back in through a wrought-iron cemetery gate

choices.label: Press the tarot deck into their hands for something to hold

success.text: Raven shuffles while they talk, which keeps their hands from shaking. Halfway through, their mother reaches out and cuts the deck, the way she must have watched Raven do it a thousand times. The top card is the Sun. "Raven," she says, testing it. "That's what you want?" "That's who I am." Their mother nods. "Then that's what I'll say."
success.art: A woman in a wool coat cutting a tarot deck held by a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat, the top card a golden sun, a mausoleum behind them in late light

failure.text: The deck slips and bursts across the grass. Raven's mother kneels in her good coat to help gather it, and somewhere in that, on her knees in the cemetery beside her kid, she listens. She gets the word wrong twice and right once, and Raven counts the once. "It's a start," they tell you later. "The cards say it's a start."
failure.art: A woman in a wool coat kneeling in cemetery grass gathering tarot cards beside a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat, a teenager reaching for a card in the grass

choices.label: Tell their mother how the whole crew learned to say they

success.text: You tell her about the crew: Kev correcting himself mid-sentence, Wade practicing out loud in the van, Bea writing it into her monster notebook. Raven's mother laughs despite herself. "A paperboy and a metalhead manage it," she says, "and I can't?" She turns to her child. "Raven. Okay. Raven." The crow on the roof caws, very satisfied.
success.art: A woman in a wool coat laughing beside a mausoleum, a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat beaming at her, a teenager mid-story with animated hands, a crow on the roof

failure.text: You get nervous and tell the story too long, with far too much about Wade's van. Raven's mother looks bewildered. But Raven laughs, and the laugh does what your story couldn't: their mother sees how happy they are with these people. "I'll try," she says. "I'm going to get it wrong." "Everybody does at first," Raven says. "Then they don't."
failure.art: a goth teen with a teased black bob, winged eyeliner and a plum velvet frock coat laughing with a hand over their mouth, a bewildered woman in a wool coat glancing between them and a rambling teenager beside a mausoleum

reactions.creature: A real creature feature? I've trained every Saturday of my life for this. The monster's always just lonely.
reactions.cult: Matching robes, chanting, candles? Amateurs. Also, they stole my entire look.
reactions.paranormal: Ghosts are just people with unfinished business. Pull up a gravestone. Let's hear it.
reactions.cosmic: The cards didn't mention tentacles. I'm filing a complaint with the Major Arcana.

name: Coach Tammy Jo Pruitt
role: Softball coach and last line of defense
bio: Tammy Jo Pruitt pitched fast-pitch softball for a Tulsa barnstorming team in the sixties, struck out a minor-league home-run king at a county fair, and has coached the Glimmer Falls High Lady Prospectors to four league titles. She is six feet tall, built like a refrigerator, and has never lost a fight with a parent, a referee or a monster. Her office door is always open after school, and every kid in town knows it is the safe room: no questions, cold orange slices, a couch. She is loud, blunt, warm under all the gravel and a terrible cook who insists on bringing casseroles anyway. Her flaw is that she would rather run through a wall than talk about a feeling, and she takes every kid's trouble home with her at night.

perk.name: Coach's Got You
perk.text: Tammy Jo steps between you and it, every time: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard, a green and gold coach's windbreaker, gray sweatpants, cleats, an aluminum softball bat over one shoulder and a clipboard under her arm, planted on a pitcher's mound under blazing stadium lights in a wind-up stance, aluminum bat cocked like a battle axe, whistle flying, a swarm of shadowy monsters pouring over the outfield fence toward her

neutral.line: Eyes up, chin up, hustle up. That's three ups.
neutral.art: Portrait of a tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard, a green and gold coach's windbreaker, gray sweatpants, cleats, an aluminum softball bat over one shoulder and a clipboard under her arm, standing at a dugout fence with her clipboard, whistle in her teeth

happy.line: THAT'S what I'm talking about! Somebody get this kid an orange slice!
happy.art: Portrait of a tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard, a green and gold coach's windbreaker, gray sweatpants, cleats, an aluminum softball bat over one shoulder and a clipboard under her arm, fist pumping with a huge grin, cap pushed back, whistle swinging

scared.line: I'm not scared. I'm strategically reassessing at a dead sprint.
scared.art: Portrait of a tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard, a green and gold coach's windbreaker, gray sweatpants, cleats, an aluminum softball bat over one shoulder and a clipboard under her arm, mid-backpedal, bat held crosswise, eyes wide under the cap brim

angry.line: You do not come into my school and scare my kids. Batter up.
angry.art: Portrait of a tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard, a green and gold coach's windbreaker, gray sweatpants, cleats, an aluminum softball bat over one shoulder and a clipboard under her arm, gripping the aluminum bat with both hands, face red, squint deadly

sad.line: Twenty years of kids. I don't always know if I helped.
sad.art: Portrait of a tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard, a green and gold coach's windbreaker, gray sweatpants, cleats, an aluminum softball bat over one shoulder and a clipboard under her arm, alone on an empty bench in a dim locker room, cap in her hands

determined.line: Bases loaded, bottom of the ninth. Let's win it.
determined.art: Portrait of a tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard, a green and gold coach's windbreaker, gray sweatpants, cleats, an aluminum softball bat over one shoulder and a clipboard under her arm, tightening her batting glove, cap pulled low, staring down the field

meet.title: Stakeout at the Equipment Shed
meet.place: The softball field, Glimmer Falls High
meet.text: Coach Pruitt is sitting in a lawn chair behind the dugout with a thermos, a pair of binoculars and an aluminum bat across her knees, watching the equipment shed. "Something's been taking my softballs," she says without lowering the binoculars. "Forty-two of 'em. Leaves the door locked and a trail of what I sincerely hope is gravy." She finally looks at you. "You got business here, or you want to make yourself useful?"
meet.art: A tall, broad 45-year-old white woman with a sunburned freckled face and a fierce squint, a red-blonde perm under a green ball cap, a silver whistle on a lanyard and a green and gold coach's windbreaker, sitting in a lawn chair behind a softball dugout with binoculars raised, a thermos at her feet and an aluminum bat across her knees, a padlocked equipment shed across the field with a trail of brown goo leading to its door, a teenager walking up, late afternoon sun, medium wide shot

choices.label: Grab a helmet and take a few swings off her fastball

success.text: Her first pitch you never see. Her second you foul off. Her third you crack right up the middle and she has to duck. Coach whoops so loud the crows leave. "Now THAT'S a ballplayer. You're on my team. Not the softball team. The other team."
success.art: A teenager in a batting helmet connecting with a softball, a tall coach ducking on the pitcher's mound and laughing, crows scattering

failure.text: Three pitches, three swings, three misses, and you're pretty sure the third one was a changeup out of spite. Coach hands you a helmet with your name taped on it. "Tomorrow, 3:15. We'll fix that swing."
failure.art: A teenager swinging and missing as a softball smacks into a backstop, a coach on the mound shaking her head with a grin

choices.label: Pull up a bucket and join her stakeout

success.text: At four-thirty a cafeteria lunch tray slides out from under the shed door by itself, loaded with softballs, and scoots off toward the school kitchen. You don't scream. Coach writes it on her clipboard. "Kid, you kept your cool. You're with me now. We're following that tray."
success.art: A cafeteria lunch tray loaded with softballs sliding by itself across a ball field, a coach and a teenager crouched behind a dugout watching

failure.text: You doze off on your bucket. When you wake, the shed door is open, your shoelaces are tied together, and there's gravy on your shoes. Coach is furious, at the shed. "Come back tomorrow, and bring coffee."
failure.art: A teenager waking up on an overturned bucket with their shoelaces tied together, an open equipment shed and a trail of gravy, a coach glaring at the shed

choices.label: Tell her straight what has been happening on Crystal Street

success.text: She listens to the whole thing without blinking, then nods once. "I've been coaching for twenty years. When a kid tells me something's wrong, something's wrong." She stands and shoulders the bat. "Okay. Coach is in."
success.art: A tall coach standing up from a lawn chair and shouldering an aluminum bat, a teenager beside her, the late sun behind the dugout

failure.text: "Kid, I believe you believe it." She squints at you, worried now, which is worse than disbelief. "Come back tomorrow with something I can see. Then I'm all yours." She hands you an orange slice for the road.
failure.art: A coach holding out an orange slice to a teenager with a worried look, a ball field behind them

arc.title: The Letter From Tulsa
arc.place: Coach Pruitt's office, Glimmer Falls High, 3:30 p.m.
arc.text: The safe room smells like orange peels and liniment. Coach Pruitt sits at her desk, ignoring her own tuna casserole, turning an unopened envelope over and over in hands the size of catcher's mitts. The corner is stamped with a cartoon tornado holding a softball: the Tulsa Tornadettes, twentieth reunion. "Junk mail," she says, drops it in the trash, and fishes it right back out. Pinned above her desk is a faded snapshot of two young women in matching jerseys, one of them laughing so hard she's bent double.
arc.art: A tall broad-shouldered woman softball coach in a green windbreaker at a cluttered school office desk, turning a sealed envelope in her big hands, a faded snapshot of two young women in matching jerseys pinned above her, a casserole dish and orange slices on the desk, afternoon light through blinds

choices.label: Ask who the laughing catcher in the photo is

success.text: "Darlene Voss. Dee. Best catcher in three states, and the only person alive who could call my pitches before I knew 'em." Coach looks at the photo a long time. "I left the team in '66 for a coaching job. Didn't say goodbye. Couldn't figure out how." She sets the envelope on the desk face up, which feels like a start.
success.art: A big woman softball coach holding a faded snapshot of two young women in matching jerseys close to her face, an envelope face up on the desk in front of her, a teenager listening from a worn office couch

failure.text: "Teammate," Coach says, in the voice she uses to end parent-teacher conferences, and she offers you casserole to change the subject. You eat it. It is very bad. But when you leave, the envelope is pinned to the corkboard next to the photo instead of sitting in the trash.
failure.art: A teenager bravely eating a forkful of gray tuna casserole in a coach's office, a corkboard behind them with an envelope freshly pinned beside an old team snapshot, a big coach watching with crossed arms

choices.label: Offer to open the envelope so she doesn't have to

success.text: You slit it with her clipboard pen and read it out loud: a reunion dinner in Tulsa, Thanksgiving weekend, and a postcard tucked inside in blocky handwriting. I'll be there if you will. Still calling your pitches. Dee. Coach takes the postcard and holds it by the edges, like it might bruise.
success.art: A teenager reading a postcard aloud in a school coach's office, a torn envelope with a cartoon tornado stamp on the desk, a big woman coach reaching out with both hands to take the postcard very gently

failure.text: Your hands shake and the envelope tears straight through the postcard inside. Coach tapes it back together with white athletic tape, very gently, and reads it to herself, turned away from you. "Thanks, kid," she says, gruff. "Go on home. I've got it from here."
failure.art: A big woman softball coach at her desk carefully mending a torn postcard with strips of white athletic tape, her back half turned, a teenager hovering awkwardly by the office door

choices.label: Ask her to hit you grounders so she can think without talking

success.text: Out on the diamond she hits grounders at you hard and fast, and somewhere around the fortieth she starts talking: Dee's terrible jokes, the county fair, a team bus breaking down outside Amarillo in a hailstorm. "Funny," she says, leaning on her fungo bat. "Didn't know I remembered all that."
success.art: A teenager scooping up a hard grounder on a dusty high school softball diamond at golden hour, a tall coach in a green windbreaker swinging a long fungo bat at home plate, a bucket of softballs beside her

failure.text: A grounder takes a bad hop off a pebble and catches you in the shin. Coach is beside you in a heartbeat with an ice pack and an orange slice, fussing like a mother hen, and the reunion never comes up again. Still, she walks you to the gate and says, "Same time tomorrow."
failure.art: A teenager sitting in the infield dirt holding an ice pack to their shin, a big softball coach kneeling beside them offering an orange slice with a worried frown, a softball rolling away

arc.title: Forty Cents a Minute
arc.place: Coach Pruitt's office, after practice
arc.text: Coach Pruitt has dragged the athletic department's phone, cord and all, into her office and shut the door. A phone number is written on her palm in ballpoint. "Long distance is forty cents a minute," she says, "so I figure I oughta know what I'm saying first." She dials anyway. Somewhere in Oklahoma a woman says hello, and Coach Pruitt, who has stared down every referee in the county, slams the receiver down so fast the bell dings.
arc.art: A tall softball coach in a green windbreaker frozen beside a beige office telephone she has just slammed down, a phone number inked on her palm, the long coiled cord stretched across the room from the door, a teenager on the couch wide-eyed

choices.label: Help her write out what she wants to say, like a game plan

success.text: You draw it as a play sheet. Leadoff: I'm sorry. Second base: I missed you. Third: I was scared of saying goodbye, so I didn't. Home: come to the reunion. Coach stares at the clipboard. "That's just feelings in a batting order." But she copies it onto an index card and tucks it inside her cap.
success.art: A coach's clipboard with a hand-drawn baseball diamond and short phrases written at each base, a big woman in a ball cap holding it with a stunned expression, a teenager beside her pointing at home plate

failure.text: Every draft comes out sounding like a press release from the athletic director. Coach crumples the fifth one and sinks it in the wastebasket from across the room. "See, this is why I coach softball," she sighs. "You can't strike out a feeling." She thanks you anyway, and means it.
failure.art: A big woman coach tossing a crumpled sheet of paper into an overflowing office wastebasket full of crumpled drafts, a teenager holding a pencil and a blank legal pad

choices.label: Tell her about a friend you let drift away

success.text: You tell her about a friend you stopped calling and never really knew why. Coach listens the way she listens to every kid who lands on her couch: completely. Then she says, very quietly, "Okay. If you can say that out loud, I can say it to Dee." She doesn't dial yet, but she leaves the phone in the middle of her desk.
success.art: A teenager talking softly on a worn office couch, a big softball coach leaning forward on a folding chair listening with her whole body, a beige telephone sitting in the middle of the desk between them

failure.text: You start the story and lose your nerve halfway, and the silence gets heavy enough to sit on. Coach clears her throat, hands you an orange slice and talks about the batting cage for ten minutes. It isn't a disaster. When you leave, she's looking at the phone.
failure.art: A teenager and a big softball coach sitting in awkward silence in a small office, each holding an orange slice, a beige telephone on the desk between them in a pool of lamplight

choices.label: Dial the number yourself and put the receiver in her hand

success.text: You dial, it rings, and you push the receiver into her hand before she can bolt. "Dee? It's Tammy Jo." A long pause, then a laugh comes down the line so loud you can hear it across the room. Coach turns toward the window, shoulders shaking, and waves you out the door. She talks for forty minutes and pays every cent.
success.art: A big softball coach turned toward a window at dusk clutching a corded phone receiver to her ear, shoulders shaking with laughter and tears, a teenager tiptoeing out the office door with a grin

failure.text: The number on her palm has smudged, and you get a very confused man at a bait shop in Broken Arrow. Coach takes the phone and apologizes to him for five minutes, and by the end they're both laughing too hard for her to be scared. "Tomorrow," she says, hanging up. "I'll call her tomorrow."
failure.art: A big woman coach laughing helplessly into a corded office phone, her palm smeared with ballpoint ink, a teenager covering their face with both hands in embarrassment

arc.title: Bottom of the Ninth
arc.place: The softball field, Glimmer Falls High, dusk
arc.text: Coach Pruitt is waiting at home plate with a pocket cassette recorder and a softball older than you, signed in faded ink: County Fair 1964, you owe me a soda, D. "Dee asked for something real before she books a flight," Coach says. "On tape. So I can't hang up on it." She clips the recorder to her collar, opens her mouth, and closes it again. Around you, the field lights buzz on one bank at a time.
arc.art: A tall softball coach in a green windbreaker standing at home plate on an empty high school field at dusk, a small cassette recorder clipped to her collar and a yellowed signed softball in her hand, stadium lights flickering on behind her

choices.label: Put on the catcher's gear and catch while she talks

success.text: You squat behind the plate and she pitches, and between every pitch she says one true thing into the recorder: I was proud of you. I was scared. I missed you every single season. The last pitch pops into your mitt like a firecracker. Coach clicks the tape off and says, rough as gravel, "Best I ever threw." Some of her stubborn nerve rubs off on you.
success.art: A teenager in oversized catcher's gear crouched behind home plate catching a fastball under field lights, a tall coach in mid-follow-through on the mound, a cassette recorder glowing red on her collar

failure.text: Her fastball is still a fastball, and the third one knocks you onto your back in a puff of chalk. Coach drops to her knees beside you, frantic, and in the middle of fussing it all comes out at once: "I'm done losing people because I'm too scared to talk." The recorder on her collar gets every word.
failure.art: A teenager in catcher's gear flat on their back in a cloud of chalk dust behind home plate, a big coach kneeling over them in panic, a cassette recorder still clipped and glowing on her collar

choices.label: Interview her like a sportscaster so she only has to answer

success.text: "Coach Pruitt, Tulsa wants to know: what do you say to your old catcher?" She snorts, then answers like it's a postgame show, and then she stops performing and just talks, ten minutes straight. When it's done she labels the tape in block capitals, FOR DEE, and hugs you hard enough to lift your sneakers off the grass.
success.art: A teenager holding a cassette recorder out like a sportscaster's microphone at home plate, a big softball coach answering with her eyes shining, field lights glowing against a purple dusk sky

failure.text: Your sportscaster voice is so bad that she laughs until she has to sit down in the dirt, and most of the tape is Coach Pruitt wheezing. She seals it in an envelope anyway. "Dee'll get it," she says, wiping her eyes. "Dee always got the joke before I did."
failure.art: A big softball coach sitting in the infield dirt doubled over laughing, a teenager with a cassette recorder looking sheepish, an addressed envelope and a yellowed softball on the ground between them

choices.label: Walk out to center field and give her the infield to herself

success.text: You sit in center field with your back to her. Across the dark grass you can hear her voice, low and steady, going on for a long time. When she jogs out to you, her eyes are red and she's grinning. "Said it. All of it. Didn't even need a play sheet." She drops an arm around your shoulders. "Thanks for playing outfield, kid."
success.art: A teenager sitting alone in the center field grass at night with their back to the infield, far away a tall coach speaking into a tiny recorder under the field lights, moths circling the lamps

failure.text: The sprinklers come on while you're sitting in center field. You sprint for the dugout soaked, and Coach is laughing so hard she forgets to be scared, and somewhere in the laughing she says all the true things into the tape. You get a towel, an orange slice and a casserole for your trouble.
failure.art: A drenched teenager sprinting across a softball outfield at night through arcs of sprinkler water, a big coach in the dugout laughing and holding out a towel, field lights sparkling in the spray

reactions.slasher: A big lug in a hockey mask? I've coached JV boys' baseball. Get in line.
reactions.creature: Big, slimy and fast. Good. I respect an opponent with hustle.
reactions.paranormal: Ghosts don't scare me. Ghosts don't call the athletic director.
reactions.camp: Sequins, a cape and a theme song? Fine. Somebody hold my whistle.

name: Dr. Amir Haddad
bio: Dr. Amir Haddad grew up in Dearborn, Michigan, the son of a Beirut tailor, and left a big Sacramento animal hospital after he refused to put down a dog that just needed time. Now he runs the Haddad Animal Clinic out of his garage on Crystal Street, charges what people can pay, and keeps meticulous case files on the strangest patients in California: a two-headed garter snake, a cat that glows faintly in the dark, a possum that talks in its sleep. He cooks enormous dinners for neighbors and is far too curious for his own good. His flaws: he avoids every fight with the homeowners' association, works until he falls asleep at the exam table, and is gentler with animals than with his own grief.

perk.name: Field Dressing
perk.text: Amir patches you up between scares, steady as a surgeon: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a 39-year-old Lebanese American man with olive skin and warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache, wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head, a teal scrub shirt under a white lab coat with pockets full of pens and dog biscuits, a stethoscope around his neck, khakis, a calico cat draped over one shoulder, standing in a glowing open garage at night with a medical bag in one hand and a flashlight in the other, lab coat flaring, a crowd of strange glowing animals gathered protectively around his feet as something enormous looms in the street beyond

neutral.line: Hold the flashlight steady. She bites, but only when she's scared.
neutral.art: Portrait of a 39-year-old Lebanese American man with olive skin and warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache, wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head, a teal scrub shirt under a white lab coat with pockets full of pens and dog biscuits, a stethoscope around his neck, khakis, a calico cat draped over one shoulder, leaning over a steel exam table in a converted garage, stethoscope in hand

happy.line: Look at that! Healthy as a horse. A very small, glowing horse.
happy.art: Portrait of a 39-year-old Lebanese American man with olive skin and warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache, wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head, a teal scrub shirt under a white lab coat with pockets full of pens and dog biscuits, a stethoscope around his neck, khakis, a calico cat draped over one shoulder, beaming and holding up a tiny glowing animal in cupped hands, mustache lifted in a grin

scared.line: I have seen a lot of animals. That is not an animal.
scared.art: Portrait of a 39-year-old Lebanese American man with olive skin and warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache, wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head, a teal scrub shirt under a white lab coat with pockets full of pens and dog biscuits, a stethoscope around his neck, khakis, a calico cat draped over one shoulder, backing against a garage wall, the calico cat hissing on his shoulder, glasses slipping

angry.line: Whoever hurt this creature will answer to me.
angry.art: Portrait of a 39-year-old Lebanese American man with olive skin and warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache, wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head, a teal scrub shirt under a white lab coat with pockets full of pens and dog biscuits, a stethoscope around his neck, khakis, a calico cat draped over one shoulder, cradling a bandaged animal, eyes hard, jaw set beneath the mustache

sad.line: I can mend a broken wing. I couldn't mend my father's heart.
sad.art: Portrait of a 39-year-old Lebanese American man with olive skin and warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache, wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head, a teal scrub shirt under a white lab coat with pockets full of pens and dog biscuits, a stethoscope around his neck, khakis, a calico cat draped over one shoulder, sitting on an overturned crate in the garage at night, holding an old tailor's measuring tape

determined.line: Gloves on. Let's see what we're dealing with.
determined.art: Portrait of a 39-year-old Lebanese American man with olive skin and warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache, wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head, a teal scrub shirt under a white lab coat with pockets full of pens and dog biscuits, a stethoscope around his neck, khakis, a calico cat draped over one shoulder, snapping on latex gloves, glasses pulled down, medical bag open beside him

meet.title: The Crystal Possum
meet.place: The Haddad Animal Clinic, a garage on Crystal Street
meet.text: Dr. Haddad's garage door is rolled up, and inside, under a hanging shop light, a man in a lab coat is bent over a wire cage. In it is a possum, and sprouting from its fur along its spine are tiny purple crystals, glittering like rock candy. "Found her under the roundabout this morning," Dr. Haddad says. "Third one this month. She's frightened, and she's very sick, and I don't have enough hands." A calico cat on his shoulder stares at you, unimpressed.
meet.art: A 39-year-old Lebanese American veterinarian with olive skin, warm brown eyes, a thick salt-and-pepper mustache and wavy black hair going gray at the temples, wire glasses pushed up on his head and a white lab coat over a teal scrub shirt, bent over a wire cage in a converted garage clinic under a hanging shop light, inside it a frightened possum with tiny purple crystals sprouting along its spine, a calico cat draped over his shoulder, a teenager pulling on gloves, warm work light, medium shot

choices.label: Glove up and hold the patient steady for the exam

success.text: You hold her gently while he works the crystals loose with tweezers, one by one, and she stops shaking under your hands. Dr. Haddad sits back and exhales. "You have good hands, and better nerve. I could use you. Out there, too, I think."
success.art: A teenager in oversized latex gloves gently holding a possum on an exam table while a veterinarian removes small purple crystals with tweezers

failure.text: She twists free and bites your thumb, not hard, but enough. Dr. Haddad cleans it, bandages it, and sends you home with a first-aid kit and an apology. "She's scared, not mean. Come back tomorrow. She'll remember you were kind."
failure.art: A veterinarian bandaging a teenager's thumb in a garage clinic, a possum glaring from its cage

choices.label: Read his case files and look for the pattern

success.text: You pin every strange case on his street map. Every single one was found within a block of the Heartstone, and they've doubled every Halloween week since 1981. Dr. Haddad takes off his glasses. "Then it isn't the animals that are sick. It's the street. We should look into this together."
success.art: A street map pinned on a garage wall with clustered red pins around a central roundabout, a teenager and a veterinarian studying it under a shop light

failure.text: The folders slide off the shelf and scatter across the floor. As you gather them, the calico cat fluffs to twice her size and hisses at an empty corner of the garage, steady and unblinking. Dr. Haddad turns off the light. "Tomorrow. Let's do this tomorrow."
failure.art: Case files scattered across a garage floor, a calico cat puffed up and hissing at a dark empty corner, a veterinarian reaching for a light switch

choices.label: Calm the possum by singing to her very softly

success.text: You sing the only lullaby you know all the words to, which is the theme from a cartoon about bears. The possum's ears relax. The cat purrs. Dr. Haddad laughs, quietly, so as not to break the spell. "Bedside manner. You can't teach that. Stay. Please."
success.art: A teenager singing softly beside a wire cage where a crystal-furred possum dozes, a veterinarian smiling and a calico cat purring on the counter

failure.text: Your voice cracks on the high note. The possum plays dead, deeply and theatrically. Dr. Haddad checks her pulse, then pats your shoulder. "She's fine. She's just a critic. Come back tomorrow and try a lower key."
failure.art: A possum dramatically playing dead in a cage with its tongue out, a teenager wincing, a veterinarian checking the animal with a stethoscope

arc.title: Notice of Violation
arc.place: The Haddad Animal Clinic garage, 5 p.m.
arc.text: A pink notice is taped to Dr. Haddad's garage door: COMMERCIAL USE OF A RESIDENTIAL GARAGE. HEARING THURSDAY. By order of the Crystal Street Homeowners' Association. Dr. Haddad is pretending it isn't there. He's stirring a pot of lentil soup big enough to bathe in and telling the two-headed garter snake about his day. "It's a misunderstanding," he says. "I'll close for a while. Nobody needs a fuss." Behind him, a wall of cages watches you, every patient in them with nowhere else to go.
arc.art: A gentle veterinarian in a lab coat and glasses stirring a huge pot of soup on a hot plate in a garage clinic, a bright pink official notice taped to the open garage door behind him, cages of odd animals including a two-headed snake and a faintly glowing cat

choices.label: Read the clinic logbooks and count how many neighbors he has helped

success.text: You go through three years of logbooks: two hundred and twelve patients, most of them from Crystal Street, a third of them never billed. You read the total out loud. Dr. Haddad stops stirring. "I didn't realize it was so many," he says. Then, more quietly, "Neither will they, unless someone tells them."
success.art: A teenager at a garage workbench surrounded by stacks of handwritten logbooks, tallying on a notepad, a veterinarian holding a soup ladle frozen mid-stir behind them, a calico cat sprawled across an open ledger

failure.text: The logbooks are in four handwritings, two languages and one coffee stain shaped like Ohio, and you lose count twice. Dr. Haddad takes the book from you gently and closes it. "It doesn't matter how many," he says, but he keeps his hand flat on the cover for a long while.
failure.art: A veterinarian resting his palm on a closed, coffee-stained logbook in a cluttered garage clinic, a teenager surrounded by spilled papers on the floor, a calico cat batting at a loose page

choices.label: Ask him why he won't fight it

success.text: He ladles you a bowl before he answers. "My father had a tailor shop in Beirut, then another in Dearborn. Whenever a landlord shouted, he bowed and said, we are guests here." He sets the ladle down. "I've lived on this street eight years, and I still feel like a guest."
success.art: A veterinarian and a teenager sharing steaming bowls of lentil soup on overturned crates in a garage clinic at sunset, an old framed photo of a tailor at a sewing machine hanging on the pegboard

failure.text: "Who said anything about fighting?" he says brightly, and changes the subject to the possum's recovery, then to cardamom, then to the cat. You never get back to the notice. But when you leave, he's standing alone in the driveway, reading it again.
failure.art: A veterinarian in a lab coat standing in a suburban driveway at dusk reading a pink notice on his garage door, a pot of soup steaming on a workbench behind him

choices.label: Read the notice aloud to the patients in a pompous little judge voice

success.text: You read the notice in the voice of a tiny, pompous judge, and the calico cat sneezes on the word "residential" exactly on cue. Dr. Haddad laughs until he has to take his glasses off. "Okay," he says, wiping his eyes. "Okay. Maybe it's a little absurd."
success.art: A teenager holding up a pink official notice and orating dramatically to a row of animal cages, a calico cat mid-sneeze, a veterinarian behind them laughing with his glasses in his hand

failure.text: The joke lands wrong. The possum hides, the cat leaves, and Dr. Haddad smiles the polite smile of a man being careful. "They get anxious when the door is shut," he says. You help him feed everyone in silence, which turns out to be its own kind of help.
failure.art: A teenager and a veterinarian quietly filling food dishes along a row of cages in a dim garage clinic, a possum hiding under a folded towel, a pink notice on the garage door

arc.title: The Suit in the Closet
arc.place: Dr. Haddad's spare room, behind the clinic, after dark
arc.text: Dr. Haddad has fallen asleep at the exam table again, and while you're looking for a blanket you find the garment bag at the back of the closet. Inside is a charcoal suit, hand-stitched, with a slip of paper pinned to the lapel in Arabic and English: For Amir, for the day you need to stand up. Baba. The sleeves are basted, never finished. When you turn around, Dr. Haddad is awake in the doorway with the cat in his arms, watching you hold his father's unfinished work.
arc.art: A teenager in a small lamplit spare room holding up a charcoal hand-stitched suit jacket from an open garment bag, a handwritten note pinned to its lapel, a veterinarian in a rumpled lab coat in the doorway holding a calico cat

choices.label: Apologize, and ask him to tell you about his father

success.text: He sits on the edge of the bed and tells you: a tailor who sang while he hemmed, who started this suit the year Amir walked out of the big hospital rather than put down a dog that only needed time. "He said a man should own one suit he isn't afraid to argue in," Amir says, and laughs, wet-eyed. "I think he'd say Thursday counts."
success.art: A veterinarian sitting on the edge of a narrow bed holding a charcoal suit jacket across his knees, smiling with wet eyes, a teenager sitting on the floor listening, a calico cat curled on the jacket

failure.text: Your apology tumbles out too fast and he waves it away too quickly, and then you're both standing there, embarrassed and kind. He zips the bag closed. "Another time," he says. But he hangs it on the outside of the closet door, where he'll see it every morning.
failure.art: A veterinarian hanging a zipped garment bag on the outside of a closet door in a small lamplit room, a teenager standing awkwardly nearby with their hands in their pockets

choices.label: Offer to help him finish the basted sleeves tonight

success.text: He threads the needle; you hold the sleeve steady under the shop light, the same way you held the crystal possum still. He sews slowly, humming a song his father used to hum, and when the last stitch is in he holds the jacket up against himself. It fits. For a second he looks exactly like the man in the photo on his wall.
success.art: A veterinarian sewing a charcoal suit sleeve by hand under a hanging garage shop light while a teenager holds the fabric steady, a spool of gray thread on the exam table, a calico cat watching closely

failure.text: You prick your finger, he pricks his, and the calico cat steals the spool and runs it under the couch. By midnight the sleeves are still basted, and the two of you are laughing helplessly on the floor in a web of gray thread. "Baba would be appalled," Amir says, delighted.
failure.art: A veterinarian and a teenager sprawled laughing on a garage floor tangled in loops of gray thread, a calico cat darting under a couch with a spool in its mouth, a half-sewn suit jacket draped over a chair

choices.label: Tell him his father made it for exactly this week

success.text: "For the day you need to stand up," you read back to him. "The hearing is Thursday." Amir is quiet for a long time. Then he takes the suit, holds it up to the light and says, "He always did have impeccable timing." He hangs it on the exam-room door like a flag.
success.art: A veterinarian holding a charcoal suit up to a bare hanging bulb in a garage clinic, the handwritten note fluttering on its lapel, a teenager beside him, animal cages glowing softly in the background

failure.text: It comes out sounding like an order, and he flinches the way he flinches at HOA letters. "Please," he says softly. "Not tonight." You leave the garment bag on the bed and let yourself out. In the morning, you notice, it's been unzipped.
failure.art: A garment bag lying unzipped on a neatly made narrow bed in morning light, a charcoal suit sleeve spilling out, a calico cat asleep on top of it

arc.title: The Thursday Hearing
arc.place: The Crystal Street clubhouse, 7 p.m.
arc.text: The clubhouse smells like burnt coffee and carpet shampoo. Mr. Merriweather presides from a folding table beneath a framed map of the street, and Dr. Haddad stands at the microphone in his father's charcoal suit, holding a stack of case files in both hands. Behind him, a surprising number of folding chairs are filled with neighbors who came on their own, some holding cat carriers, one holding a very calm iguana. "Dr. Haddad," says Mr. Merriweather, "you have three minutes." Amir looks back at you.
arc.art: A veterinarian in a charcoal hand-tailored suit at a microphone stand in a wood-paneled suburban clubhouse, clutching a stack of folders, a man in a golf sweater at a folding table facing him, neighbors in folding chairs behind holding pet carriers and one iguana

choices.label: Hand him the logbook and the case map, open to the right pages

success.text: Page by page he reads the record into the minutes: two hundred and twelve patients, the dog that lived, the cat that glows, the possum that came back from the roundabout. Then, steady: "I am not a guest on this street. I am a neighbor." The board drops the violation, the iguana's owner applauds, and Mr. Merriweather sighs and moves on to hedge heights. You walk out knowing how to build a case from evidence, the Haddad way.
success.art: A veterinarian in a charcoal suit reading confidently from an open logbook at a clubhouse microphone, a teenager beside him holding up a street map covered in pins, neighbors applauding, an iguana on a shoulder

failure.text: You hand him the wrong folder, and he ends up reading the possum's sleep-talk transcripts into the record. The room laughs, then softens, and then a dozen neighbors stand one after another to say what he did for their animals. The violation is tabled for a year, not dropped. Amir walks out in his father's suit, a little dazed, completely surrounded.
failure.art: A veterinarian in a charcoal suit stepping out of a clubhouse at night surrounded by smiling neighbors holding cats, dogs and pet carriers, a teenager trailing behind clutching a mixed-up stack of folders

choices.label: Ask everyone whose animal he ever treated to stand up

success.text: You climb onto a folding chair and ask anyone whose animal Dr. Haddad has treated to stand. Chairs scrape. Nearly the whole room rises, carriers and leashes and all. Amir looks out at them with one hand on his father's lapel and says only, "Thank you. I'm staying." The vote isn't close.
success.art: A teenager standing on a folding chair in a wood-paneled clubhouse, nearly every neighbor rising to their feet holding leashes and pet carriers, a veterinarian in a charcoal suit at the microphone with his hand on his lapel

failure.text: Your chair wobbles, folds and drops you in a clatter of metal. In the silence, Amir walks over, helps you up and, still holding your elbow, speaks to the board without notes for five plain minutes. It isn't polished. It's him. The violation is tabled instead of dropped, and he calls it a win.
failure.art: A veterinarian in a charcoal suit helping a teenager up from a collapsed folding chair in a clubhouse aisle, turning to address a board table, neighbors leaning forward in their seats

choices.label: Sit in the front row and keep your eyes on him

success.text: He finds your face in the front row and holds onto it. His voice shakes for the first sentence and never again. He talks about his father the tailor, about guests and neighbors, about a street that brings him its strange, frightened animals because it trusts him. When he finishes, the room is quiet, then loud. The notice is withdrawn.
success.art: A veterinarian in a charcoal suit speaking with quiet confidence at a clubhouse microphone, a teenager in the front row meeting his gaze, rows of neighbors with pets listening intently under fluorescent lights

failure.text: Halfway through, his voice catches on the word Baba and he can't go on. The board waits. Then Pearl Washington, in the back row, starts clapping, slow and stubborn, and the whole room joins her. They table the matter. Amir sits down beside you, shaking, and whispers, "I said it. I actually said it."
failure.art: An elderly woman in a church hat clapping from the back row of a clubhouse meeting, the whole room joining in, a veterinarian in a charcoal suit sitting down shakily beside a teenager in the front row

reactions.creature: Nobody shoot it. Nobody poke it. I want a heart rate and a stool sample.
reactions.cosmic: Every animal on the street left at sundown. Animals know. That's never a good sign.
reactions.paranormal: My teta would hang a blue eye over the door for this. I'll get the tape.

name: Chip Merriweather
bio: Charles "Chip" Merriweather III is class president, captain of the debate team, organizer of every fundraiser at Glimmer Falls High and the son of the homeowners' association president, who sold half the houses on Crystal Street. He has a perfect GPA, a perfect side part and a smile for every photo. He has also known since junior high that he likes boys, and he has rehearsed saying so a hundred times to the bathroom mirror and never gotten past the first word. Chip is genuinely kind, sharp as a tack, a gifted organizer and a dork who makes terrible puns when he is nervous. His flaw is that he has spent so long being who everyone needs that he lies smoothly by reflex, and he is terrified of disappointing his father.

perk.name: Bake Sale Treasurer
perk.text: Chip runs every fundraiser in town and always rounds in the crew's favor: +1 quarter each dawn.
