neutral.line: Hi! Chip Merriweather, class president. Can I count on your vote? I mean, your help?
neutral.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old white boy with a clean-cut handsome face and a dimpled, nervous smile, neatly side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt with the collar popped under a navy blazer with a small gold pin, khaki chinos, penny loafers, a clipboard of petitions held to his chest, holding the clipboard, dimpled campaign smile, school lockers behind him

happy.line: Ha! That's great. That's really great. Sorry, I'm just... happy.
happy.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old white boy with a clean-cut handsome face and a dimpled, nervous smile, neatly side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt with the collar popped under a navy blazer with a small gold pin, khaki chinos, penny loafers, a clipboard of petitions held to his chest, laughing with his head ducked, cheeks pink, a real smile for once

scared.line: If anyone finds out... about the, um, monster. If anyone finds out about the monster.
scared.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old white boy with a clean-cut handsome face and a dimpled, nervous smile, neatly side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt with the collar popped under a navy blazer with a small gold pin, khaki chinos, penny loafers, a clipboard of petitions held to his chest, clutching the clipboard to his chest, eyes darting, a bead of sweat at his temple

angry.line: I've smiled through every single thing in this town. I'm done smiling.
angry.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old white boy with a clean-cut handsome face and a dimpled, nervous smile, neatly side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt with the collar popped under a navy blazer with a small gold pin, khaki chinos, penny loafers, a clipboard of petitions held to his chest, jaw tight, clipboard lowered, blazer shrugged off one shoulder

sad.line: Everybody likes the version of me on the campaign poster.
sad.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old white boy with a clean-cut handsome face and a dimpled, nervous smile, neatly side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt with the collar popped under a navy blazer with a small gold pin, khaki chinos, penny loafers, a clipboard of petitions held to his chest, sitting alone in an empty classroom beneath his own smiling campaign sign

determined.line: I'm done being careful. Let's do this for real.
determined.art: Portrait of a 17-year-old white boy with a clean-cut handsome face and a dimpled, nervous smile, neatly side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt with the collar popped under a navy blazer with a small gold pin, khaki chinos, penny loafers, a clipboard of petitions held to his chest, loosening his tie, rolling up his oxford sleeves, eyes steady

meet.title: The Homecoming Spread
meet.place: The yearbook office, Glimmer Falls High
meet.text: The yearbook office smells of rubber cement and darkroom chemicals. Chip Merriweather, class president, is redoing the homecoming spread alone at four in the afternoon, because every photo keeps coming out of the developer with gray faces. When you knock he jumps, and a flyer slides out of his binder onto the floor between you: the Glitter Box's Saturday midnight double feature. He goes pale. "That's, um. That's for a civics project. On local... theatre."
meet.art: A 17-year-old white boy with a clean-cut handsome face and a nervous dimpled smile, neatly side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt with the collar popped under a navy blazer with a small gold pin, frozen beside a desk in a cluttered high school yearbook office, photo proofs pinned to a corkboard behind him with several faces drained gray, a folded theater flyer lying on the floor between him and a teenager, red darkroom light from a half-open door, medium shot

choices.label: Hand back the flyer like it is nothing and ask about the photos

success.text: You pass him the flyer without a second look. "Midnight shows are the best ones. So, why are your photos gray?" His shoulders drop an inch, like he's set down something heavy. You fix the spread together until the custodian kicks you out. "Hey," Chip says at the door. "Thanks. For... the help. Can I help you with whatever you're doing? I'd like that."
success.art: A teenager handing a flyer back to a relieved preppy boy in a yearbook office, both bent over photo proofs, late afternoon light through the blinds

failure.text: You hand it back too carefully, and he hears something you didn't mean. His smile snaps back into place, bright and empty. "Student council meeting. Totally forgot. You should come back tomorrow, though. I'm here every day. Every single day."
failure.art: A preppy boy flashing a bright, brittle smile while hurriedly stuffing papers into his binder, a teenager in the doorway of a yearbook office

choices.label: Help him work out why the photos keep turning gray

success.text: Under the red light you see it: the gray always starts at the hair and creeps down, like a dye job in reverse, and only on kids whose parents were in the 1961 PTA. Chip stares. "My mom was PTA secretary." He takes a breath. "Okay. I'm in. Whatever this is, I want to help fix it."
success.art: Two teenagers in a red-lit darkroom examining a dripping photo where a student's hair is turning gray from the roots down

failure.text: A face in the developing tray smiles at you. It is not a face that was in the photograph. Chip drops the tongs. You both stand very still until the red light buzzes out. "Tomorrow," Chip whispers. "In the regular light. Please."
failure.art: A face smiling up from a darkroom developing tray under red light, two teenagers frozen in shock, a pair of tongs falling

choices.label: Pocket the flyer and claim it when his father appears at the door

success.text: "Chipper, the HOA dinner," says a tall man in a golf sweater from the doorway. You tuck the flyer in your own jacket and ask Chip loudly about the homecoming fundraiser. His father nods and leaves. Chip looks at you like you've pulled him out of the quarry lake. "I owe you," he says. "Let me pay it back. I'm with you."
success.art: A tall man in a golf sweater in a yearbook office doorway, a teenager casually tucking a flyer into their jacket, a preppy boy staring at them in quiet gratitude

failure.text: Mr. Merriweather looks at the flyer sticking out of your pocket, then at you, and decides you are a bad influence. You are shown out with great politeness. Through the window, Chip mouths sorry. Come back tomorrow, when his father is at the office.
failure.art: A tall man in a golf sweater politely escorting a teenager out of a school office, a preppy boy behind him mouthing an apology through the window

arc.title: The Hypothetical
arc.place: The yearbook office, Glimmer Falls High, 4 p.m.
arc.text: Chip is supposed to be laying out the Halloween spread. Instead he's arranging and rearranging the same six photos while he talks, very fast, about a hypothetical. "Say there's a guy. Totally hypothetical guy. And he's, um, different from what everybody expects, and now he has a group of friends, a crew, and he doesn't know if they'd still..." He trails off and makes a pun about cropping. It is not a good pun. He is looking very hard at the light table instead of at you.
arc.art: A preppy teen boy with a perfect side part and a navy sweater fidgeting with photographs on a glowing light table in a cramped yearbook office, drying racks of prints and a red darkroom bulb behind him, a teenager leaning in the doorway

choices.label: Answer the hypothetical, carefully, as a hypothetical

success.text: "Hypothetically," you say, "that guy's crew would have his back. Whatever it was. Whenever he wanted to say it, or if he never did." Chip nods too many times. "Cool. Good. Great answer. For the hypothetical." He goes back to the layout, but his hands have stopped shaking.
success.art: A preppy teen boy at a yearbook light table exhaling with relief, his hands resting still on a spread of photos, a teenager beside him with a reassuring half-smile, warm late-afternoon light

failure.text: You start to answer and Chip panics and talks over you about the bake-sale budget for two solid minutes. When he runs out of breath he looks mortified. "Sorry. Forget I asked." You tell him you won't forget, in a good way, and he almost smiles.
failure.art: A flustered preppy teen boy waving a bake-sale ledger and talking rapidly in a yearbook office, a teenager trying to get a word in, photographs scattered across a light table

choices.label: Answer his terrible pun with a worse one

success.text: "Don't worry," you say. "I'm sure that guy will develop just fine." Chip makes a noise like a kettle and laughs so hard he has to sit on the floor between the drying racks. When he gets up, he's lighter somehow. "You're the worst," he says, delighted. "Okay. I'll think about the hypothetical."
success.art: A preppy teen boy sitting on a darkroom floor between hanging drying racks of photographs, doubled over laughing under a red safelight, a teenager grinning smugly above him

failure.text: Your pun is so bad it takes Chip ten full seconds to get it, and by then the moment has slipped away. He laughs politely, then for real. "That was awful." He puts the photos away, but he walks out with you, which he has never done before.
failure.art: A preppy teen boy and a teenager walking side by side down an empty high school hallway lined with lockers at dusk, the boy carrying a binder and laughing

choices.label: Say nothing about it and quietly help with the layout

success.text: You start pasting down photos beside him and leave the hypothetical alone. The quiet gets comfortable. Twenty minutes later, staring at a picture of the Glitter Box marquee, Chip says, "Thanks for not making it a thing." Then, almost too softly to hear: "It is a thing. Just not yet."
success.art: Two teenagers side by side at a glowing light table pasting photographs onto a yearbook layout, one photo showing a sparkling theatre marquee, rubber cement jars and scissors between them

failure.text: Rubber cement gets everywhere, including Chip's perfect side part. He stares at himself in the darkroom mirror, hair sticking up like a punk rocker's, and for one second he looks horrified, and then he looks kind of thrilled. "Don't tell anyone," he says, grinning. "About the hair."
failure.art: A preppy teen boy staring into a darkroom mirror with his hair glued up into wild spikes, his reflection grinning, a teenager behind him holding a dripping glue brush in dismay

arc.title: The Harvest Ball Arrangement
arc.place: The student council room, Glimmer Falls High, lunch
arc.text: Chip's father has called the school office twice this morning. The message, which Chip reads to you in a perfectly cheerful voice, is that Chip will escort the HOA treasurer's daughter, Missy Albright, to the Crystal Street Harvest Ball on Thursday, and the Glimmer Falls Gazette photographer will be there. "Which is great!" Chip says. "Missy's great. Everything is great." He snaps his pencil in half without looking at it. You recognize the smile: it's the one from all his campaign flyers.
arc.art: A preppy teen boy in a navy sweater smiling too brightly while holding a pink office message slip, a snapped pencil in his other hand, student council banners and a ballot box behind him, a teenager across the table watching with concern

choices.label: Tell him gently that he doesn't have to do the smile with you

success.text: The smile slips, then falls off completely. Chip puts his face in his hands. "I lie so well," he says through his fingers. "I'm so good at it. I don't even notice I'm doing it until it's done." You sit with him until the bell. When he looks up, he says, "I'm going to tell you something. Not today. Soon. On purpose."
success.art: A preppy teen boy with his face buried in his hands at a student council table, a teenager sitting close beside him in quiet support, a snapped pencil and a pink message slip on the tabletop

failure.text: "What smile?" he says, smiling, and you both hear how fake it sounds. He laughs once, unhappily, and apologizes. "Reflex. Twenty years of it." "You're seventeen," you point out. "Exactly," he says. It doesn't fix anything, but it's honest.
failure.art: A preppy teen boy laughing ruefully across a student council table, his campaign flyer pinned to the bulletin board behind him showing the same bright smile, a teenager raising an eyebrow

choices.label: Find Missy Albright and see what she actually wants

success.text: Missy Albright, it turns out, is in the band room hiding from her own mother. "I'd rather go with Yvonne from flute section," she blurts, then turns crimson. You promise her secret is safe and say nothing about anybody else's. When you tell Chip that Missy wants out of the date as badly as he does, he laughs so hard he cries. "A conspiracy. Oh, thank goodness."
success.art: A blushing teen girl clutching a clarinet case in a cluttered high school band room, a teenager crouched beside a music stand listening kindly, rows of folding chairs and a tuba in the background

failure.text: Missy is sweet and thrilled about the ball, and she wants to know Chip's favorite color for the boutonniere. You come back with a list of her questions. Chip reads it and sags. "She's nice. That makes it worse." Then, firmly: "I'm going to be honest with her. Not about everything. About not wanting to pretend."
failure.art: A preppy teen boy reading a handwritten list on notebook paper with a pained expression, a teenager beside him shrugging, a flyer for a harvest ball tacked to the wall

choices.label: Offer to invent an airtight excuse to get him out of the ball

success.text: You draft a masterpiece: a debate tournament, an emergency student-council audit and a possible case of mono. Chip reads it and laughs, then hands it back. "It's perfect," he says. "I'm not going to use it. I am so tired of perfect excuses." He sounds surprised to hear himself say it.
success.art: A preppy teen boy laughing and handing back a sheet of notebook paper covered in elaborate scribbled excuses, a teenager holding a pen with a conspiratorial look, a student council gavel on the table

failure.text: The excuse falls apart before you finish writing it, because Chip keeps fact-checking it. "No, Dad knows the debate schedule. No, I can't have mono, I gave blood Tuesday." Finally he puts the pen down. "I can't even lie well about lying anymore." Somehow, he looks relieved.
failure.art: A notebook page crowded with crossed-out excuses on a student council table, a preppy teen boy setting down his pen with a tired, relieved half-smile, a teenager slumped in the chair opposite

arc.title: Item One on the Agenda
arc.place: The yearbook office, Glimmer Falls High, after school
arc.text: Chip has called a meeting. There is a printed agenda, a tray of bake-sale brownies and a chair for every member of the crew, and he's standing at the light table in his best sweater, pale as paper. Item one reads: Chip has something to say. "I wanted to do this myself," he says, "before anybody guesses, or finds out some other way, or my dad decides who I'm allowed to be." He takes a breath. "I'm gay. I like boys. I've known since seventh grade, and you're the first people I've ever said it to."
arc.art: A preppy teen boy in his best navy sweater standing nervously at a glowing light table in a yearbook office, a stack of printed agendas and a tray of brownies beside him, a circle of mismatched folding chairs filled with friends of many ages facing him

choices.label: Be the first one out of your chair to hug him

success.text: You're across the room before he finishes exhaling, and then the whole crew is there, a pileup of arms around Chip Merriweather and his best sweater. Someone knocks the brownies off the table. Nobody cares. From inside the hug, Chip says, muffled and shaky and laughing, "Okay. Okay. Item two is brownies, I guess."
success.art: A preppy teen boy laughing through happy tears in the middle of a big group hug of mismatched teenagers and adults in a yearbook office, a tray of brownies upside down on the floor

failure.text: You stand up so fast your chair crashes over, and Chip flinches, then sees your face and bursts out laughing. You hug him anyway, a little awkwardly, the chair still on the floor, and the crew piles on. "I had a whole plan for if this went badly," he says into your shoulder. "I never planned for this."
failure.art: A teenager hugging a laughing preppy teen boy beside a toppled folding chair in a yearbook office, the rest of a mismatched crew rushing in from every side to join the hug

choices.label: Thank him for trusting you, and ask what he needs from the crew

success.text: "Thank you for telling us," you say. "What do you need?" Chip blinks; he has an answer prepared for everything except that. "Same as always. Except I'd like to stop lying to you guys. And come to the midnight show at the Glitter Box with you, out loud." He squares his shoulders. "My dad, I'll tell when I'm ready. That part's mine." Watching him, you learn how much a few honest words can do in a room.
success.art: A preppy teen boy standing taller at a yearbook light table, smiling with damp eyes and squared shoulders, friends leaning forward from a circle of folding chairs, one holding a midnight movie flyer

failure.text: Your voice cracks halfway through "thank you," and you have to start over twice. By the third try Chip is laughing and wiping his eyes. "You're nervous? I'm the one who just came out." He grabs both your hands. "Thank you. Honestly. That's the nicest thing anybody has ever stammered at me."
failure.art: A preppy teen boy laughing and wiping his eyes while holding both of a flustered teenager's hands in a yearbook office, the crew grinning from their folding chairs around them

choices.label: Grab a pen and fill in the rest of the agenda with him

success.text: Item two: brownies. Item three: Chip picks the next midnight movie. Item four: the crew goes to the Harvest Ball as a group, in whatever they want to wear. Item five, in Chip's own handwriting: Tell Dad when I'm ready, and not one minute before. He looks at the finished agenda for a long time. "Motion carries," he whispers. "Unanimous."
success.art: A printed meeting agenda on a glowing light table filled in with handwriting in several colors of pen, a preppy teen boy holding it up proudly, a raised forest of hands from the crew voting yes

failure.text: Your handwriting is so bad that item three appears to read "Chip picks the next mutiny." Chip reads it out loud with total seriousness, and the crew loses it. He laughs until he has to sit down. "Motion carries," he gasps. "I'll lead the mutiny. I'm extremely organized."
failure.art: A preppy teen boy sitting on a yearbook office floor laughing and clutching a messy handwritten agenda, a circle of friends cracking up in their folding chairs around him

reactions.cult: Matching robes, chanting and total conformity? I've sat through HOA dinners. I've read these minutes.
reactions.camp: Oh no. This one has a fabulous sense of theme. I hate how much I admire it.
reactions.dream: A nightmare that digs up your secrets. Great. Everybody stay calm. Especially me.

name: Joey Benally
bio: Joey Benally's family moved from Shiprock, New Mexico, to Glimmer Falls when his mom took a nursing job at County General, and he has hated the fog every day since. He works after school in the garage at Rusty's Junkyard, where he can make anything with an engine run, and he is rebuilding a 1968 pickup to drive home to his grandmother's every summer. He helped Sunny Castellanos build her racing chair out of bicycle parts and stubbornness. Joey is dry, practical and allergic to nonsense; he has a dozen rational explanations for every haunting and is annoyed every time they don't work. His flaw is that he would rather fix everything himself than ask for help, and he trusts machines faster than people.

perk.name: Jump Start
perk.text: Joey gets it running on the second try, every time: reroll one failed daytime roll each day.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm, serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal, oil-stained canvas work pants, scuffed work boots, his grandfather's silver wristwatch, a socket wrench in one hand and a red shop rag in his back pocket, standing on the hood of a rumbling old pickup truck in a junkyard at night, headlights blazing, one hand raised with a socket wrench and the other holding a set of jumper cables crackling with blue sparks, wrecked cars stacked into walls behind him

neutral.line: It's not haunted. It's a bad starter. ...Probably a bad starter.
neutral.art: Portrait of a lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm, serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal, oil-stained canvas work pants, scuffed work boots, his grandfather's silver wristwatch, a socket wrench in one hand and a red shop rag in his back pocket, leaning on the open hood of a pickup, wiping his hands on the red rag

happy.line: Hear that? That's a V8 that hasn't run since Nixon.
happy.art: Portrait of a lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm, serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal, oil-stained canvas work pants, scuffed work boots, his grandfather's silver wristwatch, a socket wrench in one hand and a red shop rag in his back pocket, a rare grin, head cocked toward a roaring engine, wrench raised

scared.line: Okay. That's not the engine knocking.
scared.art: Portrait of a lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm, serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal, oil-stained canvas work pants, scuffed work boots, his grandfather's silver wristwatch, a socket wrench in one hand and a red shop rag in his back pocket, frozen under a junkyard floodlight, wrench held tight, eyes fixed on the car maze

angry.line: Don't touch my tools. Don't touch my truck. Don't touch my friends.
angry.art: Portrait of a lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm, serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal, oil-stained canvas work pants, scuffed work boots, his grandfather's silver wristwatch, a socket wrench in one hand and a red shop rag in his back pocket, stepping forward with the socket wrench, jaw set, ponytail swinging

sad.line: My grandma's a thousand miles away and I still hear her telling me to eat.
sad.art: Portrait of a lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm, serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal, oil-stained canvas work pants, scuffed work boots, his grandfather's silver wristwatch, a socket wrench in one hand and a red shop rag in his back pocket, sitting on the tailgate of the pickup at dusk, turning the silver watch on his wrist

determined.line: Give me ten minutes and a wrench. We're getting out of here.
determined.art: Portrait of a lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm, serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal, oil-stained canvas work pants, scuffed work boots, his grandfather's silver wristwatch, a socket wrench in one hand and a red shop rag in his back pocket, sliding under a car on a creeper, flashlight in his teeth

meet.title: Under the Pickup
meet.place: Joey's garage, Rusty's Junkyard
meet.text: In the cinderblock garage at the edge of Rusty's, a pair of work boots sticks out from under a 1968 pickup. A radio is playing the farm report. Behind the garage, the car maze creaks and settles like it is breathing, and you could swear the rows were in a different order when you walked in. "If you're here to tell me the junkyard moves at night," says a voice from under the truck, "I've heard it. It's ground settling. Hand me the 9/16."
meet.art: A lean 17-year-old Diné young man with brown skin and a calm serious face, black hair pulled back in a low ponytail, a grease smudge across one cheekbone, a rust-orange work shirt with rolled sleeves over a gray thermal and his grandfather's silver wristwatch, rolling out on a creeper from under a 1968 pickup on jacks in a cinderblock junkyard garage, holding out an open hand for a wrench, a teenager kneeling by an open toolbox, rows of stacked wrecks through the bay door, warm work light, medium shot

choices.label: Find the right wrench and keep handing tools without being asked

success.text: 9/16, then the ratchet, then the flashlight before he asks for it. Joey rolls out on the creeper and looks at you for a long second. "Most people hand me a hammer and hope. You can stick around." Coming from Joey, that's a parade.
success.art: A young mechanic rolling out from under a pickup on a creeper and taking a socket wrench from a teenager, a toolbox open between them

failure.text: You hand him a 10mm. He looks at it. He looks at you. He slides back under the truck. "Come back tomorrow when you know a 9/16 from a 10mm. There's a chart on the wall."
failure.art: A young mechanic holding up the wrong wrench with a deadpan stare from under a pickup, a teenager wincing beside a toolbox

choices.label: Help him jump-start the pickup off a junked car

success.text: You hold the cables steady, he turns the key, and the old V8 coughs and roars to life for the first time in years. Joey slaps the hood, almost smiling. "Okay. You're useful and you don't flinch. You can ride shotgun."
success.art: A teenager holding jumper cables between a junked car and a roaring old pickup, a young mechanic leaning out of the driver's seat to slap the hood

failure.text: Sparks jump, and the moment they do, every junked car in the maze honks its horn at once, a long rusty chorus. Joey kills the battery. In the silence, he says flatly, "Ground settling. Come back tomorrow."
failure.art: Rows of rusted wrecked cars in a junkyard with headlights flaring on all at once, a young mechanic and a teenager frozen beside a sparking battery

choices.label: Ask him the right question about the car maze

success.text: "Not whether it moves," you say. "Which way it moves." Joey pauses, then rolls out and draws on the dusty floor with a rag: the rows always shift toward Crystal Street, every night this week. "First person who asked me something useful. Fine. I'm in."
success.art: A young mechanic sketching a map of junkyard rows in the dust on a garage floor with a red rag, a teenager crouched beside him

failure.text: "So is it, like, haunted?" Joey's sigh comes from under the truck, long and weary as a tired engine. "No. Come back tomorrow with a better question." Behind you, the car maze creaks in what sounds a lot like agreement.
failure.art: A teenager standing in a junkyard garage doorway, rows of wrecked cars creaking behind them, work boots sticking out from under a truck

arc.title: Her Truck
arc.place: Joey's garage, Rusty's Junkyard, after school
arc.text: Joey is sitting on the tailgate of the 1968 pickup with a letter in one hand and a socket wrench in the other, and he hasn't moved either in a while. The letter is from his grandma in Shiprock, written in pencil on lined paper: she's proud of him, she's saving the summer for him, and is her truck running yet. It isn't. The transmission died in the fog on Monday, and the only match in fifty miles is in a '68 wreck deep in the car maze, which rearranges itself every night. "I'll get it," Joey says. "Myself. Tonight."
arc.art: A Diné teen mechanic in a grease-stained work jacket sitting on the tailgate of a faded 1968 pickup in a cinderblock garage, a penciled letter in one hand and a socket wrench in the other, a towering maze of junked cars visible through the open door in fog

choices.label: Tell him you're coming into the maze with him, no arguments

success.text: "No," Joey says. You stand there. He says no again. You keep standing there. Finally he tosses you a flashlight. "Fine. You hold the light, you don't touch anything, and if the cars start honking, we leave." From Joey, that is basically a hug.
success.art: A teen mechanic tossing a heavy flashlight underhand to a teenager in a junkyard garage doorway, his expression grudging, the fog-wrapped car maze looming behind them at dusk

failure.text: You insist; he refuses; it turns into a staring contest you lose to a guy who once outlasted a seized engine for six hours. "Tomorrow," he concedes, "if the wreck's still there." Behind the garage, the maze creaks, as if it heard.
failure.art: A teen mechanic and a teenager locked in a stubborn staring contest across the hood of an old pickup, rows of junked cars creaking in the fog outside the garage window

choices.label: Ask him about the truck's first owner

success.text: Joey turns the letter over. "She drove it eighteen years. Hauled water, hauled feed for the sheep, hauled me to school when the bus got stuck in the mud." He almost smiles. "When we moved, she gave me the keys and said, bring it home running." He folds the letter into his shirt pocket, over his heart, without seeming to notice.
success.art: A teen mechanic sitting on a pickup tailgate folding a penciled letter into his shirt pocket with a faint smile, a teenager beside him, a faded snapshot of a grandmother beside the same truck taped to the dashboard

failure.text: "It's a truck," Joey says flatly, and slides underneath it, and that seems to be the end of that. But a few minutes later, from under the chassis, he says, "She calls it the Old Lady. Don't tell her I told you." It's a start.
failure.art: A pair of work boots sticking out from under a faded 1968 pickup in a cinderblock garage, a teenager sitting on an upturned bucket nearby, a radio on the workbench

choices.label: Help him chart where the wreck has drifted this week

success.text: Working from his dusty-floor sketch, you chart it: the maze shifts toward Crystal Street every night, and the '68 wreck drifts with it like a log on a slow river. By your math it'll be near the east fence by dusk. Joey studies the map, then you. "Okay. That's actually useful."
success.art: A teenager and a teen mechanic crouched over a map drawn in chalk on a dusty garage floor, arrows sweeping toward one corner, the teen mechanic pointing at the east edge with a wrench

failure.text: Your map puts the wreck in three places at once, which, Joey points out, is physically impossible. Then the maze groans outside, and you both look out the window, and he scuffs the chalk away with his boot. "Fine. It's possible. I hate it here."
failure.art: A teen mechanic scuffing out a chalk map on a garage floor with his boot, a teenager staring out the window at junked cars that have visibly shifted into new rows in the fog

arc.title: The Cracked Block
arc.place: Joey's garage, Rusty's Junkyard, late
arc.text: The transmission is out of the maze and bolted in, and it was all for nothing: last night's cold snap cracked the engine block clean through. Joey stands over it with his hands black to the wrist, silent, which is how you know it's bad. A new block costs more than he makes in three months. "I'll work doubles," he tells the engine, not you. "I'll figure it out. I don't need anybody to..." He stops, and you watch him swallow the rest.
arc.art: A teen mechanic standing over an open pickup engine bay under a single hanging work light late at night, hands blackened with grease to the wrist, a jagged crack visible across the engine block, his jaw set

choices.label: Ask what he's really afraid of, under the truck

success.text: For a long minute he doesn't answer. Then: "When it runs, I can hear her. The way she hums when she drives. When it's broken, I'm just a guy in the fog, a thousand miles from home, forgetting words I used to know." He wipes his hands on a rag. "Don't make it weird." You don't. You just stay.
success.art: A teen mechanic sitting on the garage floor with his back against the pickup's front tire, wiping his hands on a red rag and gazing into the dark rafters, a teenager sitting quietly beside him under a hanging work light

failure.text: "I'm not afraid," Joey says, too fast, and tosses a wrench into the parts bin hard enough to startle a crow off the rafters. Then he apologizes to the crow. Then, more quietly, to you. "Rough day. Rough week. Thanks for sticking around."
failure.art: A startled crow flapping off a garage rafter as a wrench clatters into a parts bin, a teen mechanic looking up apologetically, a teenager leaning against the workbench

choices.label: Go scrounging through the maze for a block, right now

success.text: You come back after dark, filthy, with a lead: a '67 delivery van at the bottom of a stack, same engine, block intact. Joey shines a light on it, then on you. "You went in there alone?" He's angry for exactly four seconds before he grins. "That's the dumbest, best thing anybody's done for this truck."
success.art: A rust-streaked teenager pointing a flashlight at an old delivery van wedged at the bottom of a stack of junked cars at night, a teen mechanic beside them breaking into a grin

failure.text: The maze turns you around three times and spits you out by the car crusher, empty-handed and covered in rust. Joey finds you there with a flashlight and a grim face. "Next time, you tell me." A pause. "Next time, we go together." He doesn't seem to notice what he just said.
failure.art: A teen mechanic with a flashlight finding a rust-covered teenager sitting beside a hulking car crusher in a foggy junkyard at night

choices.label: Remind him he built Sunny's racing chair with help

success.text: "You didn't build Sunny's chair alone," you say. "She bossed you around the whole time." Joey snorts. "She did." He looks at the cracked block for a while. "Maybe I could ask around. Wade has a chain hoist. Sunny knows a guy." Saying it seems to cost him a lot. He says it anyway.
success.art: A teen mechanic leaning on a workbench beside a framed snapshot of a grinning woman in a homemade racing wheelchair, half-smiling at a teenager, the cracked engine behind them

failure.text: "That's different," Joey says. "That was her chair. This is my problem." He goes back to work, shoulders set. But at closing time he writes Wade's phone number on the wall in grease pencil, right next to the phone, and doesn't explain why.
failure.art: A phone number freshly scrawled in grease pencil on a cinderblock garage wall beside an old rotary phone, a teen mechanic turning away from it, a teenager noticing from the doorway

arc.title: Let Her Hear It
arc.place: The lot outside Joey's garage, Rusty's Junkyard, dusk
arc.text: Joey made the calls. Wade Whitfield rolled up with a chain hoist in his van, Sunny Castellanos came with a coffee can of bolts and a lot of opinions, and half the crew stood around the pickup while the swapped engine went in. Joey kept trying to do every job himself and kept getting told to sit down. Now it's dusk, the garage phone's cord is stretched out the door as far as it will go, and the receiver is resting on the dashboard with his grandma on the line from Shiprock. "First try," Joey says, his hand on the key. "I want her to hear it on the first try."
arc.art: A teen mechanic in the driver's seat of a faded 1968 pickup at dusk, hand on the ignition key, a telephone receiver resting on the dashboard on a long coiled cord running back into a cinderblock garage, a crowd of friends gathered around the open hood

choices.label: Climb in the passenger side and talk him through the start

success.text: "Pump it twice," you say, the way he taught you, "then let her catch." He turns the key. The engine coughs, catches and roars, and over it you hear a tiny voice from the receiver, laughing and saying something in Navajo that makes Joey cover his eyes. He drives you one slow, triumphant lap around the lot, honking, while the crew cheers. You'll never hear a sick engine the same way again.
success.art: A teen mechanic covering his eyes with a grin in the driver's seat of a roaring old pickup, a teenager in the passenger seat cheering, exhaust curling in the dusk, friends whooping in the junkyard lot

failure.text: First try, it floods. Joey's face falls. Then from the receiver on the dash his grandma says, loud and clear, "Again. That truck always made me ask twice." The second time, it roars. Joey laughs so hard he has to put his forehead on the steering wheel.
failure.art: A teen mechanic laughing with his forehead pressed to the steering wheel of an old pickup as the engine finally roars, a telephone receiver on the dashboard, a teenager grinning from the passenger seat

choices.label: Hold the receiver to the engine so she can hear every note

success.text: You crouch by the open hood with the receiver held out like a microphone, and the engine catches on the first turn. On the line, his grandma starts to hum along with it. Joey hears it from the cab and goes very still, then leans out the window and says, "Grandma, it's running. I'm bringing it home in June."
success.art: A teenager crouched at the open hood of a rumbling old pickup holding a telephone receiver toward the engine, a teen mechanic leaning out the driver's window with an expression of quiet joy, dusk light over the junkyard

failure.text: The cord yanks out of the wall the second the engine fires, and the line goes dead. Joey stares at the phone, then at the truck rumbling under him, and starts laughing. "She'll call back," he says. She does, twelve minutes later, and he holds the receiver up to the tailpipe and lets her listen for a long, long time.
failure.art: A teen mechanic kneeling at the tailpipe of an idling old pickup holding a telephone receiver to the exhaust, a long phone cord trailing back to the garage, a teenager laughing beside him in the dusk

choices.label: Get the whole crew behind the tailgate for a push-start, just in case

success.text: It turns out it doesn't need a push, but you're all already pushing, so the truck lurches forward with six people shoving and Joey yelling, "It's running! Let go! It's running!" Everyone piles into the bed for a victory lap. On the dash, his grandma laughs at the racket and asks who all those people are. "My friends," Joey says.
success.art: A crowd of whooping teenagers and adults piled into the bed of a rumbling 1968 pickup on a victory lap around a junkyard lot at dusk, a teen mechanic at the wheel laughing, a phone receiver on the dashboard

failure.text: Everyone shoves at once, the truck rolls six feet and stalls in a puddle, and the crew goes down in a heap of mud and laughter. Joey climbs out, looks at all of you, filthy and grinning, and something in his face gives way. "Thanks," he says. "For showing up." On the next try, the engine catches clean.
failure.art: A heap of mud-splattered friends laughing in a puddle behind a stalled old pickup, a teen mechanic standing by the open driver's door looking at them with a softened, grateful face

reactions.tech: It's a machine. Machines have off switches. Give me five minutes.
reactions.paranormal: It's not a ghost. It's a draft. ...Okay, it's a ghost. Hand me the flashlight.
reactions.cosmic: My grandma had stories for things like this. Wish I'd listened closer.
reactions.creature: Whatever it is, it's got joints. Anything with joints, I can jam.

name: Barnaby
role: Junkyard stray and nightmare early-warning system
bio: Barnaby is a tricolor basset hound with ears that drag in puddles, a notch in his left ear from a fight he presumably won, and a nose that can smell a nightmare coming an hour before it arrives. He has lived at Rusty's Junkyard for three winters, sleeping in the back seat of a gutted station wagon; Joey Benally feeds him, Dr. Haddad has stitched him up twice, and nobody has ever successfully given him a bath. He howls at sirens, at the KGLM sign-off and at the Heartstone, which he will not walk past. Barnaby is loyal, brave, deeply food-motivated and stubborn as a parked car; his flaws are sandwich theft and lying down in the exact middle of wherever you are trying to go.

perk.name: Nightmare Nose
perk.text: Barnaby smells a bad dream coming and howls before it lands: +2 on every roll against dream nightmares.

poster: Full-body heroic 1986 pose of a long, low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes and a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one, a brown and black saddle coat, big white paws, a faded red bandana knotted around his neck, standing heroically on the hood of a junked car under a huge full moon, head thrown back mid-howl, ears streaming, red bandana fluttering, a wall of nightmare shadows recoiling from the sound

neutral.line: *sniffs your shoes thoroughly, then sits on your foot*
neutral.art: Portrait of a long, low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes and a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one, a brown and black saddle coat, big white paws, a faded red bandana knotted around his neck, sitting on a patch of gravel looking up with droopy eyes, ears pooled on the ground

happy.line: *full-body tail wag, ears flapping* Boof!
happy.art: Portrait of a long, low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes and a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one, a brown and black saddle coat, big white paws, a faded red bandana knotted around his neck, mid-wiggle with his tongue out, ears flying, red bandana askew

scared.line: *low whine, pressing his whole weight against your shins*
scared.art: Portrait of a long, low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes and a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one, a brown and black saddle coat, big white paws, a faded red bandana knotted around his neck, ears flattened, eyes wide and white-rimmed, huddled low in the shadow of a junked car

angry.line: *hackles up, a deep rumbling growl* Grrrrrrr...
angry.art: Portrait of a long, low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes and a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one, a brown and black saddle coat, big white paws, a faded red bandana knotted around his neck, lips curled back, hackles raised, legs planted wide, bandana bristling

sad.line: *sighs enormously and rests his chin on his paws*
sad.art: Portrait of a long, low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes and a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one, a brown and black saddle coat, big white paws, a faded red bandana knotted around his neck, lying flat with his chin on his big white paws, eyebrows tilted up mournfully

determined.line: *nose to the ground, then a long baying howl* AROOOOOO!
determined.art: Portrait of a long, low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes and a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one, a brown and black saddle coat, big white paws, a faded red bandana knotted around his neck, nose to the ground on a scent trail, tail straight up like a flag, ears dragging

meet.title: Something on the Wind
meet.place: The car maze, Rusty's Junkyard
meet.text: Halfway through Rusty's, something heavy leans against your legs. A basset hound with a red bandana and ears like dish towels is sitting on your foot, looking up at you with enormous sorrowful eyes and also at the sandwich in your hand. Then, all at once, his head whips toward the car maze. His hackles rise, and a growl comes out of him from somewhere deep in the earth. The wind shifts. It smells, faintly, like burnt hair and hairspray.
meet.art: A long low tricolor basset hound with droopy brown eyes, a white muzzle going gray, enormous velvety ears with a notch in the left one and a faded red bandana, sitting on a teenager's sneaker in a junkyard with his hackles raised, staring down a dark row of stacked rusted cars, a half-eaten sandwich in the teenager's hand, wind lifting his ears, gray late afternoon light, low medium shot

choices.label: Crouch down and share your sandwich with him

success.text: You split the sandwich. He takes his half with tremendous dignity, then leans his whole warm weight against you and sighs. When you stand up to leave, he follows. When you stop, he sits on your foot again. Apparently that settles it.
success.art: A teenager crouched in a junkyard sharing a sandwich with a basset hound, the dog leaning contentedly against their side

failure.text: He takes his half. Then he takes your half, and the bag, and vanishes under a rusted tail-finned sedan with a smug thump of his tail. He'll be back tomorrow. He knows where your lunch lives now.
failure.art: A basset hound's tail sticking out from under a rusty tail-finned sedan, an empty sandwich bag nearby, a teenager staring at their empty hands

choices.label: Follow him into the car maze toward the smell

success.text: He leads you nose-down through the maze to a rusted salon hair dryer someone dumped between two wrecks, still warm. Barnaby plants himself between you and it and howls, long and loud, until it goes cold. Then he looks back at you, tail thumping: so, we're a team now.
success.art: A basset hound howling protectively in front of a rusted vintage salon hair dryer between stacked wrecked cars, a teenager behind him

failure.text: The rows shift behind you while you walk. You spend an hour lost with an increasingly nervous basset hound before he finds the way out by smell alone. He sits down at the gate and won't follow you further. Tomorrow, maybe.
failure.art: A teenager and a basset hound lost between towering walls of stacked wrecked cars at dusk, the gaps between rows narrowing

arc.title: The Hoard in the Station Wagon
arc.place: Barnaby's station wagon, Rusty's Junkyard, afternoon
arc.text: Barnaby leads you to his gutted station wagon at a stately waddle, looking back every few steps to make sure you're keeping up. The back seat is a museum of stolen goods: a fuzzy slipper, a church program, one of Coach Pruitt's softballs, a bow tie that might be Chip's and half a bologna sandwich he is clearly saving for a special occasion. He climbs in, circles three times and settles on top of a faded red collar. Then he looks up at you with enormous wet eyes, waiting to see what you'll do.
arc.art: A tricolor basset hound with a red bandana lying regally in the back seat of a gutted rusty station wagon heaped with a fuzzy slipper, a softball, a bow tie and a half sandwich, his chin resting on a faded red collar, a teenager peering in the window

choices.label: Start sorting the stolen goods so they can go back to their owners

success.text: You make piles by owner while Barnaby supervises, nudging each item with his nose before he lets it go. He surrenders the slipper, the program and the bow tie with heavy sighs. The red collar he keeps. When you reach for it, he puts one paw on it, gently, and holds your gaze.
success.art: A teenager sorting a slipper, a bow tie and a softball into neat piles on a junkyard tailgate, a basset hound resting one paw protectively on a faded red collar and gazing up solemnly

failure.text: Every time you take something out of the car, Barnaby calmly takes it back and replaces it exactly where it was. After twenty minutes the hoard is precisely as you found it, and he's asleep on top of it, snoring. You sit in the front seat and keep him company, which seems to be what he wanted all along.
failure.art: A basset hound snoring on a pile of stolen odds and ends in the back of a rusty station wagon, a teenager slouched in the cracked front seat keeping him company, afternoon sun through the dusty windshield

choices.label: Gently ease the red collar out from under him to read the tag

success.text: He lets you, which feels like an honor. The tag is dented brass: BARNABY, 22 CRYSTAL ST, and a phone number with an old exchange. When you read his name out loud, his tail thumps once, twice, against the vinyl seat. Then he lays his chin on your knee and looks toward town.
success.art: A teenager holding a dented brass dog tag on a faded red collar up to the light, a basset hound resting his chin on their knee and gazing toward distant suburban rooftops beyond the junkyard fence

failure.text: The moment your fingers touch the collar he lets out a low, sorrowful rumble, sad rather than angry, and you pull your hand back. He sighs and tucks his nose into the collar. You catch a glimpse of a brass tag and the word CRYSTAL before it vanishes under his jowls.
failure.art: A basset hound tucking his long nose protectively over a faded red collar in the back of a station wagon, a glint of brass peeking out, a teenager drawing their hand back gently

choices.label: Offer your own lunch in exchange for the bologna

success.text: You hold out your sandwich. Barnaby considers the offer with the gravity of a supreme court justice, then accepts. In return he pushes the old bologna toward you with his nose, and the red collar slides out with it, brass tag and all. He watches you pick it up, tail sweeping the seat.
success.art: A basset hound solemnly accepting a fresh sandwich from a teenager's hand while nosing a stale bologna half and a faded red collar across the station wagon seat toward them

failure.text: He eats your sandwich. He also eats his sandwich. He looks at you with deep satisfaction and falls asleep on the red collar with one ear flopped over his eyes. You leave with less lunch and, somehow, a lot more friendship.
failure.art: A blissfully satisfied basset hound asleep with one ear flopped over his eyes and crumbs on his jowls, a teenager holding an empty lunch bag and laughing

arc.title: Number 22
arc.place: The junkyard gate, then Crystal Street, at dusk
arc.text: Today Barnaby is waiting at the junkyard gate with the red collar in his mouth, and the moment he sees you, he sets off toward town. He takes the long way around the Heartstone, giving it a wide, growling berth, and stops outside number 22 Crystal Street. A new family lives there now, with a minivan and a plastic jack-o'-lantern on the step. Barnaby lies down in the exact middle of their front walk, collar between his paws, and waits. Dr. Haddad, passing by with a grocery bag, stops short when he sees him.
arc.art: A basset hound lying in the middle of a suburban front walk at dusk with a faded red collar between his paws, a split-level house with a plastic jack-o'-lantern on the step, a giant purple geode glowing faintly on a roundabout down the street

choices.label: Ask Dr. Haddad what he knows about number 22

success.text: "Mrs. Odell," Dr. Haddad says softly. "She lived here alone with him. When her hip went, her son moved her to a retirement home in Tucson that doesn't allow dogs. She asked me to find him a family, and he ran off to the junkyard the day she left." He kneels beside Barnaby. "She still writes to me every Christmas. She always asks about him."
success.art: A veterinarian in a cardigan kneeling on a suburban sidewalk at dusk to stroke a basset hound's long ears, a grocery bag set down beside him, a teenager listening, porch lights glowing

failure.text: Dr. Haddad starts to explain, and Barnaby, hearing his voice, rolls over for a belly rub and refuses to stop being rubbed. By the time you're both done, all you've learned is that the name Barnaby was a Mrs. Odell's idea and that he still remembers the porch. "Come by the clinic," Amir says. "I have letters."
failure.art: A basset hound sprawled belly-up on a suburban front walk, a veterinarian and a teenager both crouched rubbing his tummy, a grocery bag tipped over with oranges rolling away

choices.label: Knock on the door and explain the dog on their walk

success.text: A girl about Bea's age answers, and her face lights up. "Is that Barnaby? He comes every Halloween week! He sits right there all night." Her mom brings out a bowl of water. Barnaby drinks politely, looks at the door one last time, as if checking who else might come out, then gets up and comes with you.
success.art: A young girl in a doorway beaming down at a basset hound drinking from a water bowl on the front step, her mother behind her holding the door, a teenager on the walk, a plastic jack-o'-lantern glowing

failure.text: Nobody's home except a very territorial cat in the front window, who puffs up at the sight of Barnaby. Barnaby gazes back, unbothered, and stays planted on the walk until the streetlights come on. You sit on the curb beside him the whole time. Eventually he leans against you, and you walk back together.
failure.art: A puffed-up cat glaring from a front window at a basset hound lying calmly on the walk below, a teenager sitting on the curb beside him as the streetlights flicker on

choices.label: Lie down on the walk beside him and wait with him

success.text: You stretch out on the cold concrete beside him. He shifts until his back is pressed against your side, and the two of you watch the porch light come on and the street go dark. After a while he lets out the biggest sigh you have ever heard, gets up, shakes his ears and looks at you. Okay. He's ready to go.
success.art: A teenager lying on a suburban front walk at nightfall beside a basset hound pressed against their side, both gazing up at a glowing porch light, autumn leaves scattered around them

failure.text: A sprinkler kicks on. Barnaby stays put. You get soaked through, he gets soaked through, and the new family's kids giggle at you from the window until their dad brings out a towel for each of you. Barnaby accepts his with the bearing of a visiting duke.
failure.art: A soaked basset hound and a soaked teenager sitting on a front walk in the spray of a lawn sprinkler, a dad in a cardigan walking out holding two towels, kids laughing at the window

arc.title: Bath Day
arc.place: Joey's garage, Rusty's Junkyard, noon
arc.text: Somehow the whole junkyard has turned out for Barnaby's first bath in three winters. Joey has filled a galvanized tub with warm water from the garage boiler, Dr. Haddad has brought oatmeal shampoo and a towel the size of a tent, and on the workbench sits a letter in shaky blue ink from Tucson: Mrs. Odell has heard he's found a crew, and she would dearly love a picture. Barnaby looks at the tub. He looks at all of you. Then he lies down in the exact middle of the garage floor and becomes as heavy as a parked car.
arc.art: A stubborn basset hound flopped flat in the middle of a cinderblock garage floor beside a steaming galvanized washtub, a teen mechanic holding a hose, a veterinarian holding an enormous towel, a letter in blue ink on the workbench

choices.label: Lure him toward the tub with a trail of bologna

success.text: One piece of bologna, then another, then a tactical piece floating on the water itself, and Barnaby steps into the tub of his own free will, looking deeply betrayed and deeply fed. Twenty minutes later he is clean, fluffy and furious about it. Joey takes his picture, wrapped in the giant towel, with everyone crowded around, for Mrs. Odell.
success.art: A freshly bathed fluffy basset hound wrapped in an enormous towel looking indignant, a crowd of grinning friends squeezed around him in a junkyard garage, a teen mechanic snapping a photo with an instant camera

failure.text: Barnaby eats the entire bologna trail, stops one inch from the tub and sits. When Joey tries to lift him, he goes boneless and slides out of his arms like a sack of wet sand. In the end you all bathe him right where he lies, with buckets, on the floor, and he enjoys every minute.
failure.art: A blissful basset hound lying on a sudsy garage floor while a teen mechanic, a veterinarian and a teenager pour buckets of water over him, a galvanized tub sitting unused nearby

choices.label: Climb into the tub first to show him it's safe

success.text: You step into the warm water with your shoes on. Barnaby watches, head tilted, then heaves himself up, plods over and climbs in after you with an enormous splash that soaks the whole crew. He lets you scrub him, leaning his full weight against your shins the way he did the day you met. Planting yourself where you're needed and staying put: he has been teaching you that all week.
success.art: A teenager standing ankle-deep in a galvanized washtub with shoes on, a sudsy basset hound leaning his full weight against their shins, a wave of water splashing a laughing crew in a junkyard garage

failure.text: You slip getting in and sit down hard in the tub. Barnaby, alarmed, rushes over to rescue you, and the two of you end up in the water together in a tangle of ears and elbows. Mission accomplished, technically. Dr. Haddad laughs so hard he has to lean on the workbench.
failure.art: A teenager sitting fully clothed in a galvanized washtub with a basset hound scrambling in on top of them, ears flying, a veterinarian doubled over laughing against a workbench

choices.label: Line up the whole crew around him for Mrs. Odell's picture

success.text: Damp and smug, Barnaby sits front and center as the crew squeezes in around him, and at the exact moment the shutter clicks, he howls. It's perfect. While the photo develops, Joey stamps him a new brass tag at the workbench: BARNABY, RUSTY'S JUNKYARD, ASK ANYONE. You mail the picture to Tucson with a two-word note: He's home.
success.art: A damp basset hound howling front and center in a group photo, a grinning crew of teenagers and adults squeezed in around him in a junkyard garage, a shiny new brass tag on his red collar

failure.text: Every photo catches Barnaby mid-shake, a blur of ears and flying water, with the crew shrieking behind him. You pick the best blur and mail it to Tucson anyway. Joey stamps him a new tag regardless: BARNABY, RUSTY'S JUNKYARD, ASK ANYONE. Barnaby shakes once more, directly onto the envelope.
failure.art: A blurry instant photo of a basset hound mid-shake spraying water over a shrieking crew, the same hound beside it shaking again onto an addressed envelope on a workbench

reactions.dream: *twitches in his sleep, wakes with a growl, then plants himself firmly across your feet*
reactions.paranormal: *stares at an empty corner, ears forward, for a long and deeply unsettling time*
reactions.creature: *hackles up, then a hopeful tail wag, as if it might be the type to share a sandwich*
reactions.camp: *sneezes at the glitter and declines, with enormous dignity, to wear the little cape*
